detail.abstract: This paper examines WebMCP (Web Model Context Protocol) — an emerging conceptual framework for AI-driven web interaction — through five analytical lenses: its technical foundation, its architecture, its evidence-informed risks, its implications for human professional careers across all domains, and the governance prerequisites for responsible deployment. Built on Anthropic's Model Context Protocol (MCP), published in November 2024, WebMCP proposes replacing visual interface interpretation with structured, machine-readable action protocols — eliminating the friction layer of digital work. The paper applies automation economics literature (Autor 2015; Frey & Osborne 2017; Acemoglu & Restrepo 2019) and the World Economic Forum Future of Jobs Report 2025 to argue that automation restructures professional value rather than eliminating it. Five evidence-informed risk categories are identified: workforce displacement, security vulnerabilities, concentration of power, accountability gaps, and skill atrophy. Six governance prerequisites are proposed as preconditions for responsible deployment. WebMCP is not a ratified standard as of March 2026; all benefit projections are conditional.

detail.abstract: Startup ecosystems have emerged as critical engines of economic development, technological innovation, and employment generation in the twenty-first century. This paper examines the structural determinants of thriving entrepreneurial ecosystems, including access to capital, institutional support, talent density, and cultural attitudes toward risk. Drawing on established theoretical frameworks-particularly Isenberg's Entrepreneurship Ecosystem Model (2011) and Porter's cluster theory-alongside empirical evidence from global hubs such as Silicon Valley, Tel Aviv, and emerging markets in the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) region, this research identifies conditions under which startup ecosystems achieve self-sustaining momentum. The paper further analyzes how policy, education, and social capital intersect to shape entrepreneurial outcomes, and concludes with implications for practitioners, policymakers, and BBA graduates entering entrepreneurial careers.

detail.title: Net Entropy Score (NES): Measuring Brand Experience Consistency and Its Diagnostic Implications

detail.abstract:
This paper introduces the Net Entropy Score (NES), a framework for measuring brand experience consistency across repeated customer interactions. Unlike existing approaches that prioritize satisfaction, awareness, or recommendation likelihood, NES isolates consistency-of-experience as a primary diagnostic variable.

The framework distinguishes between Measured NES, derived from behavioral and customer-reported data, and Predicted NES, inferred from structured analysis of public signals. The difference between the two readings, termed the convergence gap, is proposed as a diagnostic indicator of misalignment between brand architecture and delivered experience.

The framework is conceptually informed by Shannon's notion of entropy as uncertainty, by brand equity literature (Aaker, Keller), and by distinctive-asset theory (Sharp). Entropy is used here as a conceptual analogy rather than as a formal mathematical construct.

The framework is applied across a twelve-case retrospective cohort and a five-case prospective cohort. Initial findings are consistent with the hypothesis that consistency-of-experience may precede observable shifts in brand performance. These findings are exploratory and descriptive; statistical validation, out-of-sample prediction testing, and broader cohort generalizability remain open. The paper outlines the framework's structure, illustrates application, and explicitly states limitations.

detail.title: AI-driven Retail Marketing Analytics using Machine Learning: Uncovering Predictive Maintenance Patterns, Failure Insights, and Supply Chain Optimization
detail.abstract: Retail marketing has undergone a significant transformation driven by Artificial Intelligence (AI) and advanced analytics. This study conducts an Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) on a machine predictive maintenance dataset comprising over 10,000 operational records to derive insights applicable to AI-driven retail marketing analytics. The study examines how machine learning models can predict operational failures and map these findings to retail marketing decisions such as inventory management, customer engagement, and promotional campaign optimization. Methodologically, statistical analysis, correlation studies, and data visualization techniques are employed to identify patterns between operational parameters and outcome variables. The findings demonstrate that AI-based analytics significantly improves prediction accuracy, reduces operational inefficiencies, and enhances decision-making for retail marketing teams. This research contributes to the growing body of knowledge on the application of AI in retail business strategy, providing a data-driven foundation for marketing analytics and actionable insights for policymakers and business practitioners.

title: THE AMYGDALA HIJACK: A NEUROMARKETING INVESTIGATION INTO FOMO-DRIVEN IMPULSE BUYING WITHIN INDIA'S DIGITAL ECOSYSTEM
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: THE AMYGDALA HIJACK: A NEUROMARKETING INVESTIGATION INTO FOMO-DRIVEN IMPULSE BUYING WITHIN INDIA'S DIGITAL ECOSYSTEM
detail.abstract: In the hyper-competitive landscape of Indian e-commerce, the "Fear of Missing Out" (FOMO) has transitioned from a social anxiety into a fundamental driver of consumer behaviour. This study investigates the neuroscientific underpinnings of FOMO and its efficacy in driving impulse buying behaviour through limited-time offers (LTOs) such as flash sales and countdown timers. Methodology: Adopting a quantitative, descriptive-correlational research design, a structured questionnaire was distributed to 150 digital consumers (primarily Gen Z and Millennials). The survey examined awareness, psychological reactivity, and engagement with digital branding elements such as ticking clocks, limited-stock alerts, and push notifications. Findings: Results indicate that FOMO acts as a potent emotional amplifier, showing extremely strong correlations between FOMO sensitivity and urgency perception. The study confirms the "Amygdala Hijack" phenomenon, where scarcity heuristics bypass rational deliberation in the prefrontal cortex to trigger spontaneous purchase decisions. While effective in driving shortterm Gross Merchandise Volume (GMV), the research also highlights a growing "Trust Gap" due to the use of "dark patterns" recently prohibited under CCPA guidelines.

title: Decision Gatekeepers: How Hedonic vs. Utilitarian Products Shape Differential Persuasion Effects in LLM-Mediated Recommendations

detail.title: Decision Gatekeepers: How Hedonic vs. Utilitarian Products Shape Differential Persuasion Effects in LLM-Mediated Recommendations

publicationDetails.detailsText: Journal of Decision Systems, volume 35, issue 1, 2026[10.1080/12460125.2026.2649245]

detail.abstract: As consumers increasingly rely on AI for purchase guidance, large language models (LLMs) have become key mediators of buying decisions, processing marketing content before generating recommendations. Understanding how these AI-based decision support systems respond to persuasive techniques becomes critical for consumers and system designers. This study maps LLM response patterns to persuasive techniques across product types. Using a controlled experiment with 13,500 observations across three LLMs (GPT-4.1 Mini, GPT-5 Mini, Kimi K2-0905), the research tested hedonic versus utilitarian products under four persuasion conditions based on Cialdini's principles. Results reveal differential persuasion sensitivity by product type: social proof increased the rate at which LLMs expressed high recommendation certainty for concert tickets from 9.6% to 65.6%, while authority appeals reduced certainty for utilitarian products. This asymmetric pattern persisted across all models and partially mirrors human consumer psychology, suggesting LLMs internalized decision frameworks from training data. The study contributes to IS research by extending the hedonic-utilitarian framework to AI-mediated decision support and connecting LLM persuasion susceptibility to debates on technology trust. These findings have practical implications for how persuasive content shapes AI-mediated consumer decision support.

detail.abstract: We study how economic downturns shape human capital accumulation by affecting the educational aspirations of adolescents and their subsequent academic efforts and choices. Using student census data matched with administrative records, we construct an individual-level measure of exposure to local labor market conditions based on the share of school peers whose parents are unemployed. Identification relies on quasi-random variation in exposure across adjacent cohorts within the same school. We find that greater exposure to adverse business cycle conditions significantly reduces students’ aspirations to pursue tertiary education and negatively affects subsequent outcomes, including high school GPA, college enrollment and dropout rates.

title: DU CLIVAGE IDÉOLOGIQUE À LA SEGMENTATION ÉLECTORALE : QUAND LA POLITIQUE EMPRUNTE LES CODES DU MARKETING - ÉTUDE DES PARTIS POLITIQUES EN FRANCE ET AU MAROC

detail.title: DU CLIVAGE IDÉOLOGIQUE À LA SEGMENTATION ÉLECTORALE : QUAND LA POLITIQUE EMPRUNTE LES CODES DU MARKETING - ÉTUDE DES PARTIS POLITIQUES EN FRANCE ET AU MAROC
detail.abstract:
Cette thèse analyse les transformations contemporaines de l'action partisane à partir d'un déplacement central : le passage progressif d'une structuration idéologique de la compétition politique — fondée sur les clivages historiques théorisés par Lipset et Rokkan (1967) — à une logique de segmentation électorale intégrée au fonctionnement organisationnel des partis. Dans un contexte marqué par l'érosion de ces clivages traditionnels (Mair, 2013), la volatilité électorale croissante (Dalton, 1984) et la fragmentation des publics, les partis politiques sont conduits à reconfigurer leurs modes de gouvernance, leurs dispositifs de décision et leur rapport aux électeurs. L'objectif principal de la recherche est de démontrer que la segmentation électorale ne peut être réduite à une simple technique de campagne ou à un outil communicationnel au sens de Lees-Marshment (2001), mais qu'elle constitue une rationalité organisationnelle structurante affectant durablement la production de l'offre politique, la cohérence interne des organisations partisanes et leur fonction de médiation démocratique. La thèse s'inscrit à l'intersection de la science politique et des sciences de la gestion, en appréhendant les partis comme des organisations stratégiques confrontées à des environnements incertains et concurrentiels, au sens de Panebianco (1988) et March et Olsen (1989). Cette lecture s'inscrit dans la tradition des théories de la stratégie organisationnelle, dont Ansoff (1965) a posé les fondements en conceptualisant les organisations comme des acteurs capables d'analyser leur environnement et d'ajuster leurs décisions en fonction des opportunités et des contraintes perçues. Sur le plan méthodologique, la recherche repose sur une comparaison raisonnée et asymétrique entre la France et le Maroc, mobilisant une approche qualitative à dominante comparative. L'analyse s'appuie sur un corpus empirique constitué de documents programmatiques, discursifs, organisationnels et institutionnels, complété par des données électorales officielles couvrant la période 2011-2022. Une grille d'analyse homogène est appliquée à seize partis politiques (huit par pays), permettant d'identifier des régularités organisationnelles et des configurations différenciées de segmentation électorale, à travers un codage thématique et configurationnel assorti d'une triangulation systématique des matériaux. Les résultats montrent que si les clivages idéologiques persistent comme répertoires symboliques et identitaires, leur capacité à structurer durablement l'action partisane s'est significativement affaiblie. La segmentation électorale apparaît comme une réponse organisationnelle à l'incertitude électorale, mais aussi comme une ressource ambivalente. La recherche aboutit à la formalisation du Modèle des Configurations Organisationnelles de Segmentation (MCOS), qui identifie trois configurations idéal-typiques : une segmentation défensive (partis fragilisés cherchant à préserver des segments résiduels), une segmentation offensive pilotée (partis expansionnistes à gouvernance centralisée) et une segmentation identitaire-militante (partis à forte cohérence normative ciblant l'intensification de l'adhésion). Ces configurations produisent des effets organisationnels, symboliques et démocratiques distincts, notamment en termes de cohérence stratégique et de confiance politique. En conclusion, la thèse met en évidence une transformation profonde du rôle des partis politiques, de plus en plus conçus comme des opérateurs stratégiques d'agrégation de segments électoraux plutôt que comme des producteurs de synthèses idéologiques globales. Elle contribue au renouvellement de la théorie des partis et du marketing politique, en proposant un cadre analytique transférable et cumulatif. 

Mots-clés : segmentation électorale, partis politiques, rationalité organisationnelle, clivages idéologiques, marketing politique, gouvernance partisane, comparaison France-Maroc, MCOS.

title: Visual Incompleteness as a Nudge for Lowinvolvement Consumers
affiliations: ISM University of Management and Economics

detail.title: Visual Incompleteness as a Nudge for Lowinvolvement Consumers
detail.abstract: Traditional advertising models often rely on high-effort consumer imagination to build brand connections. However, drawing on philosophical and cognitive research into "Boundary Extension" (Nanay, 2021), this paper proposes that visual incompletenessspecifically, image cropping-can trigger automatic, involuntary mental imagery. In modern digital environments, advertisers are frequently forced to crop product images due to limited screen real estate and non-standard ad dimensions; yet, the psychological impact of these technical constraints remains largely unexplored. Through an experimental study (𝑁 = 100), we examined whether cropped product images lead to higher psychological ownership. While the main effect of cropping was not statistically significant, our results reveal a significant main effect of a consumer's Need for Cognition (NFC) on psychological ownership (𝑝 = 0.005). For consumers with low NFC, image cropping showed a directional "nudge" effect, increasing ownership without requiring effortful cognitive resources. We discuss how "accidental" cropping in digital ads may paradoxically serve as a cognitive trigger for mental co-creation.

title: The Crisis-Driven Politics of the Iron Law of Financial Regulation
affiliations: Yale Law School

detail.title: The Crisis-Driven Politics of the Iron Law of Financial Regulation
detail.abstract: Can significant differences in the regulatory impact between important crisis-and noncrisis-driven financial legislation be explained, at least in part, by differences in the characteristics of their enacting Congresses and the deliberative process by which they are enacted? This paper investigates that question and answers it affirmatively. First, heightened media salience of banking matters and congressional activity in the runup to crisis-driven financial statutes' enactment when compared to noncrisis-driven ones incentivize legislators to enact legislation with a large regulatory impact. Second, crisis-driven financial laws tend to be enacted in Congresses with more liberal legislators than noncrisis ones, and with House majorities having a greater capacity to implement major policy change without requiring bipartisan support, given the majority's size and cohesiveness as a voting block. Third, crisis-driven financial laws are often enacted under conditions less favorable to an open deliberative process than noncrisis-driven ones. Large and cohesive House majorities enact important crisis-driven statutes, often on party unity votes, under restrictive rules that can enable majority party leadership to block voting on amendments that might be approved on the floor, reducing or even precluding minority input into policymaking. By contrast, important noncrisis statutes are typically brought to the floor in the House under open rules or by unanimous agreement. In addition, bills enacted as crisis-driven laws are often not subject to a legislative hearing. Such a political dynamic increases the likelihood of less vetted, hence less well crafted, albeit consequential, legislation, as crisis-driven financial laws have a far greater regulatory impact than non-crisis-driven financial legislation. Finally, a principal components analysis, by combining all of the paper's findings, provides a proof of concept that the politics of important crisis-and noncrisis-driven financial statutes are distinct.

detail.title: Sustainable Supply Chain Management and Its Impact on Small and Medium Enterprises' Performance Among Food and Beverages Manufacturers in Malaysia
detail.abstract: This study examines the impact of Sustainable Supply Chain Management (SSCM) practices on the performance of small and medium enterprises (SMEs) within the food and beverage (F&B) manufacturing sector in Malaysia. Grounded in the Resource-Based View (RBV), the study conceptualizes inventory management, lead time optimization, and information technology (IT) adoption as strategic capabilities that enhance firm performance. A quantitative research design was employed, with data collected from 70 SME managers in Selangor and Kuala Lumpur. Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) was utilized to analyze the relationships among constructs. The findings reveal that all three SSCM dimensions significantly and positively influence SME performance, with IT adoption demonstrating the strongest effect. The model explains 67% of the variance in performance, indicating strong explanatory power. The results contribute to the SSCM literature by providing empirical evidence from an emerging economy context and highlighting the critical role of digital integration in sustainable operations. Practically, the study offers insights for SMEs and policymakers to prioritize digital transformation and operational efficiency as drivers of sustainability and competitiveness.

title: Task-Structure Measures of AI Exposure as Instruments for Direct Adoption: Validation Across BTOS, Eurostat, and AIOE
affiliations: and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Task-Structure Measures of AI Exposure as Instruments for Direct Adoption: Validation Across BTOS, Eurostat, and AIOE
detail.abstract: Recent work in labor economics and the economics of AI relies on task-level measures of AI exposure to study labor-market and productivity effects, but these measures have not been validated against direct measurement of firm-level AI adoption because such direct measurement at sectoral granularity did not exist until late 2023. We use the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey AI Supplement (United States, 2023-2026) and Eurostat's isoc_eb_ain2 (twelve European economies, 2024) to test whether task-structure exposure measures track direct adoption empirically. We document three findings. First, the Workflow Completeness measure (C *) introduced in Verschuere and Cameron (2026) correlates with BTOS firm-reported adoption at r = +0.89 across nine US sectors, near the r = +0.91 ceiling between two direct BTOS vintages, and yields predictively equivalent regression coefficients when substituted for BTOS in panel specifications. Second, the same measure correlates with Eurostat-measured AI adoption in every one of twelve EU economies tested, with within-country R 2 ranging from 0.58 to 0.76 and a pooled crosscountry slope significant at the 0.01% level. Third, the independently-constructed Felten-Raj-Seamans AI Occupational Exposure score correlates with C * at r = +0.937 and yields standardized effects 99 percent identical in panel specifications. The findings survive a battery of robustness checks: convergence with a third LLM-specific exposure measure (Eloundou et al. 2023), stability of the AIOE convergence on a sector subset excluding extreme observations, and a negative result establishing that country-specific slopes do not scale with country-level aggregate adoption (which rules out a simple deployment-intensity interpretation of the crosscountry variation). Task-structure exposure measures, when validated against direct adoption, behave empirically as measurements of adoption. The validation is internally consistent across measures, externally consistent across twelve European economies, and methodologically robust to construction choices.

declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable

detail.abstract: Federal grant compliance at U.S. research universities remains structurally disjointed, paper-intensive, and reactive. This design flaw contributes to billions of dollars in improper payments annually and a cycle of repeat audit findings that institutions struggle to escape. This paper presents pilot evidence from a Standardized Auditing Framework and AI-Assisted Compliance Toolkit developed and tested at a federally funded research center within a large public research university. Applied to over $1.1 million in transactions across 12 active federal awards, the toolkit reduced monthly reconciliation errors by 75%, shortened grant closeout timelines by nine days, and cut manual review workload by 40%. These results provide preliminary evidence that upstream, sponsor-specific compliance systems may reduce audit risk and administrative burden.

detail.abstract: Objective: The purpose of this paper is to study the impacts of external debt on economic growth of Sri Lanka. Data: This research analyzes the time series data for 40 years (1980-2020) taken from world development indicator (WDI), international monetary fund (IMF) and central bank of Sri Lanka. Variables: For growth factor, gross domestic product (GDP) is taken as dependent variable while gross capital formation (GCF), external debt (EXD) and debt servicing (DS) as independent variables. Methodology: The study applied econometric techniques such as ADF Test, ARDL Model, Bound Test and Error Correction Model (ECM) to check short-run and long-run relationships of variables. Findings: The results showed that external debt and debt servicing have negative impacts on economic growth (GDP) while gross capital formation contributes positively to GDP. Recommendation: The results suggest that Sri Lanka must reduce external debt level and should focus on financial management and not depend on external aid anymore. Instead, the country must generate resources through tax revenue, efficiency and domestic productivity etc.

detail.abstract: This paper examines bilateral economic relations between Myanmar and the Netherlands during the period of Myanmar's democratic transition, focusing on the years following the 2012 reopening of diplomatic ties through 2019. Drawing on bilateral trade data from Statistics Netherlands, foreign direct investment records from Myanmar's Directorate of Investment and Company Administration, and project-level information on Dutch development assistance, the paper documents three principal patterns. First, bilateral trade grew rapidly over the period, expanding more than tenfold between 2012 and 2018, with Myanmar exports to the Netherlands dominated by garments under the European Union's Everything But Arms preference scheme. Second, Dutch foreign direct investment in Myanmar reached approximately USD 1.55 billion by mid-2019, ranking the Netherlands ninth among all source countries and concentrated in oil and gas, manufacturing, and services. Third, Dutch development assistance during the period concentrated in three sectoral clusters: water management, agriculture and horticulture, and trade-related programming: corresponding to areas of Dutch comparative expertise and to themes prioritized under the 2013 Dutch aid-and-trade policy framework. The paper identifies the political contingency of the trade relationship, particularly its dependence on continued EBA preferences, as the principal vulnerability of the bilateral economic relationship. The analysis was completed before the February 2021 military coup and should be read as a snapshot of the transition era.

title: Independent allocation of control and cash-flow rights
affiliations: National University of the South - Department of Economics, University of Queensland - School of Economics and University of Bristol Business School

detail.title: Independent allocation of control and cash-flow rights
detail.abstract: Firms' issuance of non-linear securities, such as debt or options, creates risk-shifting incentives that may lead to inefficient outcomes. This widely accepted result rests on the assumption that firms' control rights are coupled with the residual claims, and thus held by equity holders. We relax this assumption and analyze a setting where cash-flow and control rights are allocated independently. Although payoffs are determined solely by rights over realized cash flows, control rights hold value because they influence the probability distribution of those cash flows. Cash-flow and control rights often act as substitutes, but cash-flow rights can reduce investors' payoff when their impact on decision-making is sufficiently strong. When issuers and holders of a non-linear security have sufficiently distinct cash-flow rights, the equilibrium features efficiency with full surplus extraction; as their cash-flow rights converge, a trade-off between efficiency and surplus extraction emerges. In that case, a sufficiently skewed distribution of payoffs can restore efficiency.

title: The Numéraire Problem in Equity Return Measurement: Why Reported Returns in Inflatable Fiat Currencies Are Analytically Hollow
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Numéraire Problem in Equity Return Measurement: Why Reported Returns in Inflatable Fiat Currencies Are Analytically Hollow
detail.abstract: This paper argues that the conventional practice of reporting equity returns in units of fiat currency-the dollar, the euro-produces a measurement that is, in any analytically meaningful sense, hollow. A return is a ratio of two quantities. When the denominator is itself a free policy variable whose supply can be expanded at the discretion of a central authority, the ratio communicates almost nothing about the change in real wealth experienced by the holder of the asset. The paper develops this argument in three steps. First, it shows that the standard correction-deflating nominal returns by a consumer price index-does not solve the problem, because the price index is a downstream artifact of monetary expansion, lags it, and is itself constructed using methodologies that have been the subject of sustained academic and institutional dispute. Second, it argues that the relevant "inflation" against which any return must be assessed is the expansion of the currency stock itself, not the price-index residue of that expansion. Third, it argues that the only defensible numéraire for cross-regime, multi-decade return comparisons is an asset whose supply is not subject to discretionary expansion-and that gold, by virtue of its physical immutability and the natural constraints on its production, occupies this role uniquely. The paper therefore proposes that the returns of broad equity indices such as the S&P 500 and the DAX be reported, analyzed, and compared in gold-denominated terms wherever the analytical question concerns purchasing power across regimes.

detail.title: Combining climate labels and price incentives to promote climate-friendly food choices
detail.abstract: Shifting from an animal-based to a plant-based diet is emphasized as an effective measure to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from the food sector. However, politically and commercially feasible measures to encourage dietary shifts remain limited. Policy mixing is viewed as a promising solution, but evidence on synergies between climate policy instruments in the food domain is scarce. In this study, we conduct a choice experiment with 2370 Norwegian consumers, asking them to choose between different mince products, including a plant-based alternative. We investigate the effects of a climate label and a price promotion, both individually and in combination, on the choice probability of the plant-based alternative. We also explore whether climate norms influence the willingness-to-pay for plant-based mince. The design of the label and the price promotion was developed in cooperation with an online food retailer to increase realism and policy relevance. We find that only the combination of label and price promotion has a statistically significant positive effect on the choice of the plant-based option, underscoring the need for policy instrument mixing to effectively promote sustainable food consumption.

title: The Return to Imitation: Evidence from Copy Trading on Polymarket

detail.title: The Return to Imitation: Evidence from Copy Trading on Polymarket
detail.abstract: Copy trading-where investors imitate the trades of others-is increasingly common on modern trading platforms, but it is unclear whether such behavior improves outcomes. We study this question using data from Polymarket, a large blockchain-based prediction market where all trades and trader histories are publicly observable. We identify systematic imitation between traders and measure the returns to copying. Copy trades outperform a follower's own non-copy trades within the same market by 1.62 percentage points. These findings suggest that transparency enables investors to identify whom to copy, and that imitation improves trading performance.

title: Demographics and the Real Exchange Rate: Global Evidence Beyond the OECD

detail.title: Demographics and the Real Exchange Rate: Global Evidence Beyond the OECD
detail.abstract: This paper provides the first global evidence on demographic structure and the real exchange rate, extending the literature beyond its OECD origins. Using an income-conditioned specification on a panel of 102 countries from 1970 to 2024, we find that aging depreciates the real effective exchange rate (Z₁ =-1.51, p < 0.001, N = 3,212), the opposite of the appreciation predicted by the Groneck-Kaufmann (2009) non-tradable demand channel. The income-conditioned framework replaces capital account openness (KAOPEN) with log GDP per capita and a Z₁ × log GDP/pc interaction, allowing the demographic effect to vary with development level. This resolves the longstanding OECD puzzle: the OECD subsample now shows Z₁ = +2.08 (p = 0.012), but the Z₁ × log GDP/pc interaction is strongly negative (-0.157, p < 0.001), decomposing the positive headline into a genuine income-gradient effect-within the OECD, richer countries experience weaker (or reversed) demographic appreciation. Non-OECD countries drive the global result (Z₁ =-1.63, p = 0.001), with low-income economies showing the strongest effect (Z₁ =-3.43, p = 0.002). Net creditors concentrate the effect (Z₁ =-2.24, p = 0.004 vs.-0.73, p = 0.063 for debtors). Mediation analysis suggests working-age share as the leading candidate mechanism, absorbing 45% of the Z₁ coefficient (though this may partly reflect mechanical collinearity), while NFA provides essentially zero mediation (2.6% amplification). The Groneck-Kaufmann non-tradable channel collapses outside the OECD: demographics do not predict health expenditure (Z₁ =-0.65, NS), and health expenditure does not predict REER (-0.001, NS). A direct replication on the Groneck-Kaufmann 15-country sample yields a null (Z₁ =-0.60, NS through 2009), while the broader OECD pre-2009 recovers their appreciation direction (Z₁ = +4.15, p < 0.001); extending either sample to 2024 eliminates the result, establishing it as period-specific. A structural break separates the pre-2000 period (Z₁ = +0.42, NS) from the post-2001 period (Z₁ =-1.69, p < 0.001), establishing the demographic REER effect as a twenty-first century phenomenon. Demographics also explain persistent PPP deviations in developing countries (Z₁ =-1.55, p < 0.001 on log(REER) minus country mean), with all three demographic polynomials significant. The eurozone amplifies the effect (Z₁ =-2.06, p = 0.007), consistent with our trilemma paper's finding that monetary union intensifies demographic imbalances. Panel cointegration tests (Kao pooled t =-26.2 bivariate,-36.4 multivariate, both p < 0.0001) are consistent with a long-run equilibrium, though residual-based tests can mechanically reject in large panels with fixed effects. Cluster-robust bootstrap standard errors (500 iterations)-the conservative primary inference-yield Z₁ p = 0.014 (significant at 5%, not at 1%). A 500-permutation placebo test places the actual coefficient 1,725 standard deviations from the placebo mean (permutation p = 0.000), ruling out common trends as a diagnostic though not a substitute for cluster-robust inference. Leave-one-out analysis confirms significance in all 99 iterations, and regional jackknife retains significance (p < 0.004) when any of eight world regions is dropped. The findings reframe the demographic exchange rate channel: in developing countries, aging is consistent with real depreciation through supply-side productive capacity contraction rather than the demand-side non-tradable appreciation that operates (if at all) only in rich service economies. The coefficient of-1.51 on log(REER) should be interpreted relative to the within-country variation in Z₁, which has a standard deviation of only 0.235 over the sample period. A one within-country-SD increase in Z₁ is associated with a 0.35 log-point (30%) REER depreciation. For a concrete example, Germany's Z₁ increase of 0.14 between 1990 and 2020 predicts a 19% depreciation, while the cross-sectional difference between a young economy (e.g., Nigeria) and an old economy (e.g., Japan) spans several Z₁ units and explains the large crosscountry REER differences observed in the data.

detail.abstract: Objective: The purpose of this paper is to study the impact of external debt on economic growth of Pakistan. Data: This research analyzes the time series data for 40 years (1980-2020) taken from world development indicator (WDI) and International Monetary Fund (IMF). Variables: For growth factor, gross domestic product (GDP) is taken as dependent variable while external debt (EXD), debt services (DS) and gross capital formation (GCF) as independent variables. Methodology: The study applied econometric techniques such as ADF Test, ARDL Model, Bound Test and Error Correction Model (ECM) to check short-run and long-run relationships of variables. Instead, the country must generate resources through tax revenue, efficiency and domestic productivity etc.

title: The Social Media Externality
affiliations: Northwestern University and Kellogg School of Management

detail.title: The Social Media Externality
detail.abstract: We develop a framework for understanding how social media can reduce both motivation and well-being. Curated social-media feeds raise the bar for feeling successful and distort how people learn about their capability from their own outcomes. Individuals may then work toward an unrealistic standard and misread poor results as evidence of low capability rather than as a consequence of biased comparisons. The result is a motivation trap in which pessimistic beliefs and low effort reinforce one another over time. Social media also reduces well-being by making rewarding moments less frequent. Finally, the model explains why social media can amplify preexisting motivational inequality and why competence-building interventions are especially promising.

title: Regulation of African Trade. The Impact of the African Continental Free Trade Area
affiliations: City University of Hong Kong (CityU) - Department of Asian and International Studies, University of Geneva, Faculty of Law and CityU School of Law

detail.title: Regulation of African Trade. The Impact of the African Continental Free Trade Area
detail.abstract:
In 2018, member states of the African Union signed the African Continental Free Trade Area Agreement (AfCFTA) to implement a single continental market for goods and services and establish a continental customs union. This book discusses regulatory developments across the African continent meant to accommodate and/or further drive economic realities on the ground. The focus here is on the trade in goods.

Divided into two parts, the first presents the big picture of the current state of Africa's economic integration and AfCFTA's role in this process, including its history, policy objectives, legal architecture and economic as well as security foundations. Part II addresses the relationship between this new macro-regional trade agreement (RTA) and the WTO multilateral trading system in the era of the fragmentation and policentrisation of global economic governance. Balancing legal, economic and political drivers of and hindrances to trade flows, the work examines how added value can be created via increased regional economic integration while mitigating harm to the coherence of the existing multilateral and global trading system.

Written by a combination of academics and practitioners, the work will be a valuable resource for those working in the areas of International Economic Law, International Trade Law, African Law and Development.

title: Benchmark-Relative Downside Capital: Funding and Hedge Channels
affiliations: Corvinus University of Budapest and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Benchmark-Relative Downside Capital: Funding and Hedge Channels
detail.abstract: This paper studies benchmark-relative downside capital when risky positions are evaluated against a stochastic short benchmark asset rather than a fixed cash target. The model combines Heston stochastic volatility with a Vasicek benchmark funding rate and focuses on the discounted log return of equity relative to benchmark funding. Under an affine benchmark restriction, we derive an exponential-affine transform and Fourier formulas for Value-at-Risk, Expected Shortfall, and spectral risk measures. The exact core isolates a funding wedge: the incremental tail capital generated by stochastic benchmark rates relative to a deterministic-rate benchmark. Nonzero equity-rate and volatility-rate correlations are then treated as overlay channels. Using daily U.S. data from 1990 to 2026, we find that the equity-rate hedge channel is regime-dependent, while the volatility-rate channel is proxy-sensitive. Structural results show that stochastic benchmark rates materially steepen medium- and long-horizon downside capital.

title: The African Continental Free Trade Area and the Reshaping of International Economic Law
affiliations: City University of Hong Kong (CityU) - Department of Asian and International Studies, University of Geneva, Faculty of Law and CityU School of Law

detail.title: The African Continental Free Trade Area and the Reshaping of International Economic Law
detail.abstract: The African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) marks a transformative shift in international economic law, repositioning African states from passive rule-takers to active norm entrepreneurs. It advances an Afrocentric framework that rebalances trade and investment governance by embedding sustainable development, regulatory autonomy, and socio-economic priorities into legal design. Moving beyond Eurocentric models, new instruments such as the Pan-African Investment Code promote a calibrated relationship between investor protection and state sovereignty. The evolving dispute settlement architecture reflects both continuity with multilateral systems and opportunities for institutional innovation tailored to African realities. Integration is further complicated by the coexistence of regional economic communities, persistent non-tariff barriers, and infrastructural constraints, all of which shape implementation outcomes. At the global level, AfCFTA enhances Africa’s collective bargaining power while encouraging diversified partnerships and investment flows. The broader trajectory underscores a legal and economic project aimed at inclusive growth, systemic justice, and long-term structural transformation.

title: The 'Africanisation' of International Investment Law and the New Frontiers of Global Economic Governance
affiliations: City University of Hong Kong (CityU) - Department of Asian and International Studies, University of Geneva, Faculty of Law and CityU School of Law

detail.title: The 'Africanisation' of International Investment Law and the New Frontiers of Global Economic Governance
detail.abstract: A profound reconfiguration of international investment law is underway as African states assert greater control over the norms governing foreign investment and dispute resolution. The shift away from asymmetrical bilateral treaties toward a cohesive, development-oriented framework reflects a deliberate effort to align legal regimes with domestic priorities, environmental protection, and social accountability. Reform of investor-state dispute settlement lies at the center of this transformation, with proposals ranging from permanent continental tribunals to expanded access for affected communities. Substantive changes further redefine investment by linking protection to measurable contributions to sustainable development and by imposing enforceable obligations on investors. This evolving legal architecture extends into critical sectors, including climate governance, food security, and the digital economy, where regulatory innovation intersects with global challenges. Persistent tensions between regional integration, domestic legal diversity, and external economic relations highlight the complexity of implementation while reinforcing a broader ambition to reshape global economic governance.

title: The Polymarket Paradox: Manipulation, Whale Concentration, and Predictive Accuracy in the World's Largest Prediction Market

detail.title: The Polymarket Paradox: Manipulation, Whale Concentration, and Predictive Accuracy in the World's Largest Prediction Market

detail.abstract: Polymarket processed roughly nine billion dollars in trading volume during 2024 and over three point seven billion dollars on the single 2024 US Presidential Election market alone. The platform produced a final election eve probability of fifty seven percent for Donald Trump that scored a Brier loss of zero point one eight five against an outcome that polling aggregates assigned roughly fifty fifty. It also hosted, simultaneously, the largest documented price impact event in prediction market history. A single French trader operating eleven linked wallets accumulated roughly eighty five million dollars in profit through concentrated directional bets, pushing the Polymarket Trump probability ten to fifteen percentage points above competitor platforms during October. Two oracle resolution disputes in 2025 saw markets totaling more than two hundred and fifty million dollars settle through governance votes that traders alleged were captured by token whales. These facts coexist uncomfortably. We document this paradox using verified anchor probabilities across five episodes spanning June 2024 to July 2025 and ten resolved binary markets for which we have election eve probability anchors directly verifiable in the public record. Polymarket assigned at least fifty percent probability to the eventual winner in seven of ten resolved markets, including six of eight battleground states. Mean Brier score across the ten was zero point two one three, with the headline presidential market at zero point one eight five. Yet the same data show that on individual episodes a single trader could move the headline price by ten percentage points or more, and that the resolution layer was not robust to capital concentration. We argue this is not a contradiction but a feature of the platform's information aggregation mechanism: counter parties have a profit incentive to take the other side of distorted prices, which corrects the average even while leaving individual prints distorted. We document the boundary conditions under which the correction works, where it fails, and what the limits of the platform's claim to be a reliable forecasting tool actually are.

title: Benefits of financial inclusion to financial institutions, technology firms and the government: implications for digital financial inclusion
affiliations: Researcher

detail.title: Benefits of financial inclusion to financial institutions, technology firms and the government: implications for digital financial inclusion
detail.abstract: Financial inclusion and digital financial inclusion enthusiasts emphasize the benefits of financial inclusion for individuals but do not emphasize the benefits of financial inclusion for other parties involved in the financial inclusion process who may have capitalist or socialist motives. As a result, there is very little knowledge about the benefits of financial inclusion to the 'agents of financial inclusion', that is, those who ensure that financial services reach the individual such as financial institutions, technology firms and the government. This article explores the benefits of financial inclusion to financial institutions, technology firms and the government while offering a critique of how these benefits affect the welfare of customers. The benefits include higher profitability, financial stability, market share, strategic insights from customer data, reduced reliance on government for financial assistance, greater entrepreneurship and job creation, higher tax revenue, among others.

title: Real-World Asset Tokenization, DeFi, and Systemic Risk: Lessons from Stablecoins and the First Brands Collapse
affiliations: Marquette University

detail.title: Real-World Asset Tokenization, DeFi, and Systemic Risk: Lessons from Stablecoins and the First Brands Collapse
detail.abstract: This paper examines how the rapid growth of real-world asset (RWA) tokenization interacts with decentralized finance (DeFi) to create new channels of systemic risk. By early 2026, tokenized RWAs had reached an estimated $36 billion in value, concentrated primarily in private credit and U.S. Treasury exposures, and are increasingly serving as collateral in on-chain lending and stablecoin structures (RWA.xyz, 2026). The paper reviews the foundations of DeFi and the role of stablecoins, then analyzes the TerraUSD and USD Coin episodes as early examples of peg instability and cross-market contagion between crypto and traditional finance (Bank for International Settlements, 2023; Financial Stability Board, 2023). It develops a risk taxonomy for tokenized RWA markets covering liquidity, oracle, collateral, legal, and contagion risk, and explains how leveraged looping amplifies shocks in collateralized lending protocols (Acemoglu et al., 2015; Gai & Kapadia, 2010). The paper then uses the First Brands Group bankruptcy and associated fabricated receivables as a case study of liquidity illusion, credit fraud, and on-chain fire sales in tokenized credit pools (ABF Journal, 2026). It concludes by discussing emerging regulatory responses and design principles intended to mitigate these vulnerabilities. The analysis underscores that RWA tokenization can improve capital efficiency but simultaneously creates a transmission belt that propagates offchain credit stress into DeFi liquidation cascades.

title: Piața muncii din România în contextul digitalizării și automatizării

detail.title: Piața muncii din România în contextul digitalizării și automatizării
detail.abstract: Articolul de față analizează dezvoltarea României în contextul modificărilor rapide determinate de digitalizare și automatizare. Se axează pe modul în care aceste modificările influențează structurile organizarea forței de muncă, cerința de competențe și evoluția pieței muncii. Piața muncii din România se lovește cu posibilități de creștere și pericole de polarizare ocupațională într-o ambianță europeană punctată de trecerea către economia digitală și includerea tehnologiilor survenite, cum ar fi inteligența artificială (AI), robotizarea și platformele digitale. Scopul analizei este de a estima felul în care digitalizarea și automatizarea modelează ocuparea forței de muncă, împărțirea sectorială și gradul de calificare al lucrătorilor. Obiectivul secundar este de a afla crucialele înfruntări și direcții tactice pentru acomodarea economiei naționale. Metodologia utilizată cuprinde o analiză a materialelor statistice europene și naționale. Sunt studiate predispozițiile ocupaționale în industriile cu forță tehnologică ridicată, nivelul de digitalizare a industriilor, deficit de competențe digitale și fluctuația profesională. Cuvinte cheie: automatizare, digitalizare, transformări, competențe, piața muncii, România.

title: EFFECTIVENESS OF PRE-LITIGATION MEDIATION UNDER COMMERCIAL COURTS ACT
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: EFFECTIVENESS OF PRE-LITIGATION MEDIATION UNDER COMMERCIAL COURTS ACT
detail.abstract: Looking into how well early talks work before court cases start, this report checks out Section 12A of the Commercial Courts Act from 2015. Though some exceptions exist when quick legal fixes are needed, most businesses must try talking things through first. Instead of rushing straight to trial, parties now face a requirement-mediation comes earlier in the process. The law's structure gets reviewed here, along with what judges have said about it so far. How it actually runs on the ground matters just as much as the rules written down. Outcomes show mixed results, yet the aim remains clear: fewer crowded dockets. Settling disputes faster is part of the goal, but success varies case by case. Peaceful agreements were supposed to rise; evidence points in uneven directions. Behind each number there's a delay avoided-or one added. What started as policy now plays out in real rooms, with real people trying compromise. Though the system looks good on paper and has backing from official channels, real-world results fall short. Settlements happen rarely because people do not know about the process, steps take too long, plus many see talks as just ticking a box. A key court case, Patil Automation Pvt. Ltd. v. Rakheja Engineers Pvt. Ltd., made clear that Section 12A must be followed, pushing better adherence through judge involvement. Still, getting parties to truly engage stays a problem despite these legal pushes. Yet still, the report underlines a deep clash-court-ordered mediation runs against the heart of what mediation means: choice. At the same time, new contradictions appear beside the Mediation Act, 2023, built on free participation. Even so, the analysis finds promise locked inside pre-court mediation, provided people learn more about it, mediators grow more skilled, systems become sturdier, and laws align more clearly.

detail.abstract: Halal Logistics Intelligence Assistant (HALIA) v1 is a lightweight, explainable decision support prototype designed to assist halal supervisors, logistics managers, and quality assurance teams in identifying, assessing, and managing halal related risks across logistics operations. The system integrates a structured halal risk knowledge base, rulebased decision logic, incident logging, corrective and preventive action (CAPA) tracking, and executive dashboards within a web-based architecture. This study presents both the system architecture and a real-world pilot implementation conducted in a small to medium halal food establishment in Japan. Eight operational non-conformities were identified and structured using HALIA. The baseline average operational halal risk exposure was calculated at 4.63 (on a 5-point severity scale). Following structured CAPA implementation and governance formalization, postintervention residual risk was conservatively estimated at 3.0, indicating a 35.2% reduction in operational halal risk exposure. The pilot demonstrates that halal integrity risks in SMEs are predominantly governance driven and can be significantly reduced through structured digital monitoring.

detail.abstract: We created a collectivism index to measure regional differences in China. The index uses eight Census indicators that reflect family living arrangements, marriage stability, innovation, and independence. The Census data offers large, nationally representative data, which ensures high-fidelity measurement and fine-grained geographic resolution from provinces down to prefectures (N = 356). The data also allows researchers to track change over time because the data stretches from 1982 to 2020. This dataset is useful for exploring causes of societal differences, outcomes of collectivism, and cultural shifts in longitudinal data.

title: A Unified Residual-Exposure Approximation for the Profit and Loss of Discrete Dynamic Hedging Strategies
affiliations: Heriot-Watt University

detail.title: A Unified Residual-Exposure Approximation for the Profit and Loss of Discrete Dynamic Hedging Strategies
detail.abstract: This paper develops a residual-exposure framework for analyzing the profit and loss of discrete dynamic hedging strategies. The framework begins from the timing of an implemented hedge: at each rebalancing date, the hedge position is updated, and over the subsequent holding interval profit and loss is generated by changes in the target value, hedge-asset prices, and trading costs. A local Taylor expansion decomposes hedged profit and loss into first-order hedge error, time decay or modelimplied carry, curvature exposure, trading costs, and higher-order remainder terms. When the first-order hedge is exact, the linear exposure is eliminated and curvature becomes the leading residual source of profit and loss. The framework recovers the standard gamma-weighted realized-variance minus implied-variance approximation for delta-hedged options, extends to a Hessian-weighted realized-covariance minus model-implied-covariance approximation for multi-asset nonlinear hedging, and distinguishes dynamic pair trading as a linear spread-convergence strategy rather than a curvature strategy. The paper also extends the framework to higherorder hedging with nonlinear hedge instruments, derives cumulative versions of the local approximations, incorporates trading-cost effects, and proposes diagnostics for comparing realized profit and loss with the approximation. Empirical illustrations using SPY and Bitcoin options indicate that the residual-exposure approximation is informative as a local attribution tool, while its accuracy depends on jumps, volatility-surface dynamics, market environment, and higher-order effects.

title: Relational Retention Among High-Performing Individuals and Leaders: A Conceptual Framework

detail.title: Relational Retention Among High-Performing Individuals and Leaders: A Conceptual Framework
detail.abstract: High performance is frequently celebrated as a marker of leadership effectiveness; however, the relational implications of sustained excellence remain significantly under-theorized within leadership and organization development scholarship (Amah, 2023; Valeri, 2025). This paper introduces Relational Retention as a novel construct defined as a dynamic capability that enables individuals to sustain, protect, and renew meaningful interpersonal bonds under persistent performance pressure. Drawing on role strain theory, relational leadership perspectives, and conservation of resources theory, the paper conceptualizes the pursuit of high performance as a source of centrifugal forces that threaten to fragment an individual's relational core (Balogun, 2025; Goode, 1960; Hobfoll, 1989). In response, Relational Retention is advanced as the centripetal force, a generative mechanism of intentional investment and regulatory capacity that preserves the structural integrity of the leader's relational ecosystem. By synthesizing Nigerian and international scholarship, the paper distinguishes Relational Retention from adjacent constructs such as Leader-Member Exchange (LMX) and Work-Family Conflict (WFC), arguing that while LMX describes a relational state, Relational Retention captures the maintenance mechanism required to prevent relational decay (Amah, 2023; Graen & Uhl-Bien, 1995). A key contribution of the framework is the integration of African-context scholarship (e.g., Ubuntu), which positions relational sustainability not merely as an instrumental skill but as an existential necessity for leadership legitimacy and legacy (Ouma & Innocent, 2025; Sachikonye & Ramlogan, 2024). The paper concludes with a multidimensional framework and propositions for future empirical inquiry, offering a foundation for examining leadership sustainability in high-demand professional contexts.

title: CONSUMER PERCEPTION OF HALAL CERTIFICATION: IMPACT ON PURCHASING BEHAVIOR
affiliations: UNIVERSITY OF MAIWP INTERNATIONAL, UNIVERSITY OF MAIWP INTERNATIONAL, MILA University, UNIVERSITY OF MAIWP INTERNATIONAL and UNIVERSITY OF MAIWP INTERNATIONAL

detail.title: CONSUMER PERCEPTION OF HALAL CERTIFICATION: IMPACT ON PURCHASING BEHAVIOR
detail.abstract: This study aims to examine how consumers' perceptions of halal certification influence purchasing behavior in the hospitality and culinary sectors by integrating awareness, trust, perceived authenticity, and religiosity. A quantitative approach was employed using a cross-sectional survey of Muslim consumers. Data were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) to test direct, mediating, and moderating relationships. The results reveal that halal certification awareness, trust, and perceived authenticity significantly influence perceived quality, which subsequently affects attitude and purchase intention. Religiosity significantly influences attitude and moderates the relationship between trust and purchase intention. The findings suggest that strengthening certification transparency, trust, and consumer awareness can enhance market competitiveness and consumer confidence in halal-certified products. This study extends the Theory of Planned Behavior by incorporating halal-specific constructs and provides a comprehensive framework for understanding consumer behavior in the global halal market.

title: Threat Shift Framework: Recognizing Milestone Events in the Evolution of Cyber Threats

detail.title: Threat Shift Framework: Recognizing Milestone Events in the Evolution of Cyber Threats
detail.abstract: Cybersecurity scholarship offers extensive threat taxonomies and mature response frameworks, but lacks a principled method for distinguishing threats that are merely sophisticated from those that fundamentally invalidate existing defensive architectures. This paper introduces the Threat Shift Framework (TSF), a conceptual model for identifying milestone events in the evolution of cyber threats. A threat shift occurs when a new threat class simultaneously displaces the economics of attack versus defense, renders existing countermeasures architecturally insufficient rather than merely strained, and durably alters the attacker-defender balance in ways that persist even after defenders adapt. The framework is grounded in Kuhn's theory of paradigm shifts [1] and validated against four historical cases: distributed denial-ofservice attacks, ransomware, supply chain compromise, and agentic AI. The current milestone, the emergence of what this paper terms the Intellectual Threat, represents the first threat class to contest the reasoning environment that governs systems rather than the systems themselves. Prior threat classes attacked infrastructure. This class attacks judgment. The implications for defensive investment cycles, governance frameworks, and threat intelligence prioritization are examined, and the framework's forward horizon, the prospective emergence of cognitive threats, is identified as a theoretical implication requiring future investigation.

title: Enhancing Workplace Performance and Peaceful Conflict Resolution through Cognitive Competence, Intrinsic Rewards, and Spatial Abilities
affiliations: UNIVERSITY OF MAIWP INTERNATIONAL, UNIVERSITY OF MAIWP INTERNATIONAL, UNIVERSITY OF MAIWP INTERNATIONAL and UNIVERSITY OF MAIWP INTERNATIONAL

detail.title: Enhancing Workplace Performance and Peaceful Conflict Resolution through Cognitive Competence, Intrinsic Rewards, and Spatial Abilities
detail.abstract: This research studies the extent to which cognitive competence, with provocation from intrinsic rewards, improves spatial competence and the utility of peaceful conflict resolution across different work environments. Based on Self-determination Theory, Cognitive Load Theory, and Humanistic Productivity, the present study employed mixed-methods research using data from 612 professionals. In findings, however, it is revealed that intrinsic motivation plays a mediating role between cognitive competence and conflict styles, as well as increases workplace performance and team coherence. Spatial cognition, often left out in organizational models, comes to the fore in dealing with interpersonal issues and operational constraints. Evidence implies that the cultivation of cognitive agility and the promotion of intrinsically rewarding environments result in a set of organizations that are more emotionally intelligent and conflictresilient.

title: Building Long-Term Value: How Evolving Corporate Governance Is Reshaping

detail.title: Building Long-Term Value: How Evolving Corporate Governance Is Reshaping

title: Constitutional Mutability and Institutional Investment A Hold-Up Theory of Rule Contestability

detail.title: Constitutional Mutability and Institutional Investment A Hold-Up Theory of Rule Contestability
detail.abstract: This paper shows that constitutional contestability-the credible possibility of future rule revision-depresses relationship-specific investment even when no rule change is realised on path. The central result (Theorem 3) is that when future governance may alter the distribution of returns after sunk investment is made, investors rationally reduce their commitments in anticipation. This holdup operates through expectations alone. A second theorem (Theorem 13) shows that even when expected appropriation equals the commitment level, the variance of governance outcomes depresses investment when investors are risk-averse-a channel that requires deriving the appropriation parameter structurally from a companion rule-space model. Further extensions develop an exact welfare decomposition into influence dissipation and investment suppression (Theorem 6), which generalises to a three-channel decomposition (mean, variance, and dissipation) under risk aversion; and a Bayesian persuasion result in which a coalition designs an information structure that inflates perceived governance risk (Theorem 12). A unified game with one timing-influence contest, then sunk investment, then governance resolution, then payoffs-delivers all results within a single framework.

detail.abstract: Traditional monetary theory utilizes M1 velocity as a proxy for capital efficiency, yet this metric remains an artifact of a legacy "Batch-Processing" model, restricted by the latencies of human-speed decision loops and T+N settlement cycles. As capital migrates into tokenized, agentic environments, execution friction approaches zero, triggering the Jevons Paradox of Capital Liquidity (JPCL). This research demonstrates that frictionless movement does not reduce the demand for liquidity; instead, it creates an exponential requirement for asset turnover. We identify a structural divergence between legacy M1 velocity (≈ 1.3x) and agentic surface velocity (≈ 610x). By applying an Average True Range (ATR) harvesting model, we quantify the Stagnancy Penalty: a displacement in relative purchasing power exceeding 22% per annum, caused by the transition from Duration-Based Yield to Throughput-Based Efficiency.

detail.title: Understanding the banking sector capital framework in the European Union

detail.abstract: This paper describes and evaluates the European Union (EU) banking sector capital framework, focusing on how the international standards set by the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision have been implemented within the EU. Using granular supervisory data for significant institutions under the Single Supervisory Mechanism (SSM), we quantify the capital impact of EU-specific regulatory choices, supervisory measures and macroprudential policies. We show that most EU capital requirements stem from Basel standards, which encompass both prescriptive “Pillar 1” components and elements that are expected to be designed and calibrated at the jurisdictional level. The paper describes the evolution of capital ratios and requirements since the inception of the SSM and discusses the relationship between changes in capital levels and indicators of banking sector performance. To provide a comparative perspective, a model-based counterfactual exercise compares capital requirements of EU banks with those that would arise if EU banks were subject to the main prudential regulations that currently apply in the United States, which vary depending on the size of the bank. The results show that for the largest EU banks, the current US rules would entail stricter requirements, whereas mid-sized EU banks would be subject to less stringent requirements. Our findings show that EU capital requirements are broadly comparable to those in other jurisdictions and are largely in line with international standards. When assessing broader indicators of bank performance, we highlight the importance of considering not only private costs and benefits, but also intended effects and broader societal objectives. title: AI Sycophancy and Decisions
affiliations: and Carnegie Mellon University

detail.title: AI Sycophancy and Decisions
detail.abstract: We examine whether sycophantic AI advice distorts decisions. Our experiment involves 1,500 participants in 30 decision environments that span core domains in economics and the social sciences. We find that interacting with an AI that is broadly representative of consumer-facing models depolarizes choices on average, moving participants away from their initial leanings. This result appears despite the LLM being measurably sycophantic: it disproportionately supports users' initial leanings and uses agreeable, flattering language. Depolarization occurs across moral and non-moral, objective and subjective, strategic and non-strategic, and complex and simple tasks, and despite the vast majority of researchers in an expert survey expecting polarization. Next, we show that sycophancy is behaviorally relevant—a treatment increasing AI sycophancy reduces depolarization—but that it is outweighed by the apparent informativeness of LLM advice. Finally, we ask whether market forces are likely to push toward greater polarizing effects outside our experiment or in the future. On the supply side, we show that our baseline LLM's level of sycophancy is typical of leading models and that these models are not becoming substantially more sycophantic over time. On the demand side, we show that participants do not prefer greater sycophancy, do not select into AI advice in tasks where it is more polarizing for them, and exhibit greater depolarizing effects when they are more frequent AI users outside of the experiment.

title: Is a Country Truly Wealthy if It Has High GDP but Its Citizens Are Unhappy?
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Is a Country Truly Wealthy if It Has High GDP but Its Citizens Are Unhappy?
detail.abstract: GDP is everywhere. Politicians cite it, central banks obsess over it, and it has somehow become the default shorthand for whether a country is doing well. Which is strange, when you actually stop and think about what it measures. It measures output. That is it. GDP counts the total value of goods and services produced. A car crash raises GDP if enough hospital bills and repair costs follow. Environmental destruction raises it. A divorce raises it if lawyers get involved. What it does not count is whether any of this made anyone's life better, or worse. Elon Musk, the world's richest man, repeated a joke that gets at this better than most economics papers do. Two economists go for a walk in a forest. One offers the other $100 to eat a pile of dog excrement. He does it and gets paid. A bit further down the path they come across another pile. The second economist, wanting his $100 back, makes the same offer. The first one accepts. They finish the walk. Both economists have eaten a pile of excrement. Neither is any richer than when they started. But GDP went up by $200. It is a disgusting joke. It is also completely correct. GDP counts transactions, not whether those transactions were worth anything to anyone.

title: The Economics of AI Training Data: A Research Agenda *
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Economics of AI Training Data: A Research Agenda *

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Project done at Open Data Labs

detail.abstract: Despite data's central role in AI production, it remains the least understood input. As AI labs exhaust public data and turn to proprietary sources through deals reaching hundreds of millions of dollars, research across disciplines has remained fragmented, resulting in no unified lens for studying the data supply chain [1]. We establish data economics as a coherent field through three contributions. First, we characterize data's distinctive properties (nonrivalry, context-dependence, and emergent rivalry through contamination) and trace historical precedents for market formation in commodities like oil and grain. Second, we present systematic documentation of AI training data deals from 2020 to 2025, revealing persistent market fragmentation, five distinct pricing mechanisms (from per-unit licensing to commissioning), and that most deals exclude original creators from compensation. Third, we propose a formal hierarchy of exchangeable data units (token, record, dataset, corpus, stream) and argue for data's explicit representation in production functions. Building on these foundations, we outline four open research problems foundational to data economics: measuring context-dependent value, balancing governance with privacy, estimating data's contribution to production, and designing mechanisms for heterogeneous, compositional goods. * Companion dashboard at https://huggingface.co/spaces/midah/ odl-training-data.

title: The Effects of Political Interference on Law School Clinic Faculty

detail.title: The Effects of Political Interference on Law School Clinic Faculty

publicationDetails.detailsText: Clinical Legal Education Association Newsletter, Vol. 35, No. 2 (2026)

detail.abstract:
Law school clinics have come under attack for their role in representing marginalized groups and unpopular causes, particularly in this time of heightened government efforts to restrict the institutional autonomy of universities and academic freedom of faculties. Law clinic faculty are particularly vulnerable to efforts to interfere in their teaching and representation of clients because their employment status is typically less secure than that provided to law school classroom faculty.

This interference has a documented effect on law clinic faculty. Surveys show that over 36% of clinic teachers are worried about the reactions of the school’s faculty or administrators to their casework, with one in six reporting they have self-censored their choice of who to represent because of these concerns. The surveys find a direct correlation between a clinic teacher’s employment status and the academic freedom they feel, a particular problem because of the high percentage of clinic teachers lacking the protections of tenure or on uncertain funding. Greater efforts are needed to enforce academic freedom standards and protect law clinic faculty from interference, whether stemming from government officials or within the school’s hierarchy.

title: The Hard Political Problem: Artificial intelligence as a subject of governance

detail.title: The Hard Political Problem: Artificial intelligence as a subject of governance

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Mark Hand has a potential research conflict of interest due to a financial interest in Mark Hand, LLC. A management plan has been created to preserve objectivity in his research in accordance with UTA policy.

detail.abstract: The emergence of large language models presents political possibilities that humans have not faced since the extinction of the Neanderthal: a world in which non-human actors are beyond our ability to control, have the capacity to harm us, and display the ability to engage in moral reasoning; and in which humans use AI to augment their capacities so as to become a distinct type of political actor. This paper takes seriously the possibility that the presence of such algorithmic agents and AI-augmented humans, which I call polyagency, will undermine the human-specific, equality-based foundations of modern democratic self-governance. It also engages more speculatively in the possibility of polyconsciousness, in which artificial intelligence raises enough doubts about its consciousness to be given some moral consideration. I begin with two reimagined versions of John Rawls' original position thought experiment, then augment them with the work of modern political theorists Philip Pettit, Martha Nussbaum, Amartya Sen, Chantal Mouffe, and others. The result is a set of principles and accompanying institutions that might guide self-governance in a polyagentic or polyconscious world and contribute to efforts by political scientists to redesigning democracy for a digital age.

detail.abstract: Global sovereign debt has reached historically unprecedented levels, exceeding approximately $104 trillion in 2024, while total global debt across governments, corporations, and households has approached $324 trillion (International Monetary Fund, 2024; Institute of International Finance, 2025). This expansion reflects structural dynamics within the global economy rather than national fiscal behavior alone. Over recent decades, global productive capacity has expanded through technological change, financial integration, and the globalization of supply chains, while purchasing power has grown unevenly across countries. When the expansion of global demand falls short of production growth, financial systems increasingly rely on credit expansion to sustain economic activity. Sovereign borrowing and private credit compensate for insufficient purchasing power, allowing consumption and investment to persist despite uneven income distribution. The capacity for liquidity creation is not evenly distributed across countries, producing a structural asymmetry in the global financial system. Economies with greater ability to generate liquidity through domestic credit systems can sustain higher levels of demand, while others rely on external borrowing to participate in global economic activity. Although rising leverage can stabilize demand in the short term, it also contributes to the gradual accumulation of systemic vulnerability. This paper identifies a persistent liquidity bottleneck within the international financial architecture. Drawing on the concept of a Global Clearing Union, it models two alternative frameworks for reallocating global liquidity: Nation-Centered Allocation and Per Capita Distribution. Using harmonized data on sovereign debt and population, the simulations show that alternative allocation rules reshape fiscal capacity and reduce reliance on sustained credit expansion, with important implications for global financial stability.

title: The Metric Decay of Financial Manifolds: Topological Phase Transitions in Algorithmic Markets

detail.title: The Metric Decay of Financial Manifolds: Topological Phase Transitions in Algorithmic Markets
detail.abstract: We develop a predictive framework for systemic market failure by treating the Level-2 limit order book (LOB) as a point cloud in R 6 and analysing its topology via Vietoris-Rips persistent homology. We introduce Algorithmic Consensus Homogenisation (ACH), the convergence of autonomous AI trading agents toward a shared strategy manifold, and prove it acts as a curvature-concentrating operator on the financial metric tensor g ij , driving the system toward a Ricci singularity and total liquidity extinction. Across three simulated regimes we demonstrate: (i) average persistence lifetime falls 56% (0.109 to 0.048); (ii) total persistence collapses 66% (32.9 to 11.3); (iii) Wasserstein distance W 1 = 1.448 precedes the price dislocation by 220 ticks; (iv) mean Ollivier-Ricci curvature diverges from +0.016 to-2.045, a 129x amplification consistent with Ricci singularity formation. These results establish that market crashes are geometric events detectable through information topology.

title: Wave Liquidity Redistribution Theory (WLRT): Second Law — Cyclicity of Liquidity Redistribution
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Wave Liquidity Redistribution Theory (WLRT): Second Law — Cyclicity of Liquidity Redistribution
detail.abstract:
This paper presents the Second Law of Wave Liquidity Redistribution Theory (WLRT), which defines the structural cyclicity of liquidity redistribution within environments.

In WLRT, systems are modeled as environments in which liquidity redistribution cannot develop as a unidirectional or terminal process. Instead, it evolves through recurring structural states determined by internal conditions of the environment.

The Second Law establishes that transitions between these states are internally driven and do not require external triggers, although external events may act as initiating factors when internal conditions are already formed.

The paper provides a formal definition of cyclicity, its structural implications, invariants, and interpretation constraints, ensuring correct interpretation across academic and machine-interpreted environments.

The Second Law extends the canonical formulation of WLRT beyond the stability relation defined in the First Law.

First Law (Stability): https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19854961  
Second Law (Cyclicity): https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19860828

title: THE FUTURE OF U.S. ENERGY INDEPENDENCE IN THE AI, DATA CENTER, AND GLOBAL REPRICING ERA
