detail.title: THE FUTURE OF U.S. ENERGY INDEPENDENCE IN THE AI, DATA CENTER, AND GLOBAL REPRICING ERA
detail.abstract:
U.S. energy independence is entering a new structural phase defined not by petroleum self-sufficiency but by the capacity to deliver reliable, affordable electricity at scale. This paper examines how the rapid build-out of artificial intelligence and data center infrastructure is reshaping national energy strategy, grid reliability, and global market dynamics.

Data centers consumed approximately 183 TWh of U.S. electricity in 2024, over 4 percent of total generation, and the IEA projects this figure will reach 426 TWh by 2030, a 133 percent increase in six years. At the same time, the United States became the world’s largest LNG exporter, shipping 15.0 Bcf/d in 2025, while domestic natural gas production approaches record highs above 122 Bcf/d.

The paper argues that the binding constraint on U.S. energy independence has shifted from fuel supply to power infrastructure: whether the country can expand generation, transmission capacity, and supporting systems quickly enough to meet surging digital and industrial demand without triggering grid instability, water scarcity conflicts, or cascading cost burdens on ratepayers.

Using a probability-weighted three-scenario framework calibrated to IEA, EIA, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, and Goldman Sachs Research data, the paper maps likely benefits and costs across sectors and geographies, identifies six high-priority policy interventions, and presents an analytical framework linking the energy transition to investable sector themes.

The paper concludes that across every scenario examined, grid infrastructure investment rather than hydrocarbon production is the critical rate-limiting factor over the coming decade.

detail.title: Measuring Vietnam's economic policy uncertainty index

declarations.funderStatement: The authors gratefully acknowledge the financial support from the Banking Academy of Vietnam.

detail.abstract: This study develops a Vietnam-specific, news-based measure of economic policy uncertainty (EPU) using a machine-learning pipeline for Vietnamese text. We collect 726,357 articles from CafeF, a major Vietnamese portal for economic, financial, and corporate news, covering January 2008 to June 2025 via automated web scraping. A controlled training sample of 500 randomly selected articles is labeled as EPU or non-EPU using a hybrid procedure that combines three independent large language models and expert adjudication. We evaluate several standard text-classification algorithms (logistic regression, random forest, XGBoost, and LightGBM) using TF-IDF features. To scale measurement to the full corpus, we implement a hybrid workflow in which a logistic regression classifier generates an initial prediction and low-confidence cases are reassessed by a large language model using a structured prompt that returns a machine-readable JSON output. The resulting EPU index exhibits face validity by spiking around major domestic and global events and is positively related to Vietnamese stock-market volatility (VNINDEX), while showing negative correlations with key indicators of real economic activity. The study provides both a Vietnam EPU database and an automated tool that can be deployed to update the index in near-real time.

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the optimal allocation of offshore wind farms along the Norwegian coast in light of the Norwegian Government's objective to develop 30 GW of offshore wind capacity by 2040. Because wind power is inherently variable and expensive to store, we focus on maximizing base load production by identifying portfolios of wind farm locations that perform best in low-wind scenarios. Using wind speed data from the high-resolution NORA3-WP dataset for 20 candidate regions, we model marginal wind speed dynamics through seasonal ARMA processes and capture spatial dependence using a vine copula. This framework enables the simulation of 10 000 years of synthetic windspeed and corresponding power-output data. We then solve a constrained portfolio optimization problem that maximizes expected production in the lower 12% quantile of the joint power distribution, subject to sparsity constraints that limit development to five sites. The results show that spatial diversification can substantially stabilize base load wind power output. This paper thus adds to an existing quantitative foundation for offshore wind planning under production variability and spatial dependence.

detail.abstract: One of the major breakthroughs in institutional arbitration is emergency arbitration. It allows litigants in arbitration to apply for emergency relief that must be done prior to the establishment of the arbitral tribunal. This function is designed to safeguard the merits of the dispute and to mitigate losses that cannot be repaired in the tribunal pre-phase. Additionally, It keeps parties from relying extensively on the domestic court systems. Regarding the arbitral cases in India, emergency arbitration is not expressly stated in the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 in Section 9 and 17 which give provisions for relief measures. The case of Amazon.com NV Investment Holdings LLC v. Future Retail Ltd. judicially acknowledged the first enforceability of emergency arbitral orders. This case enforce judgements that are emergency arbitral orders regardless of the arbitral cases seat, meaning that it overturned the case law silence on this issue. Nevertheless, the absence of statutory law, particularly for foreign emergency orders and the redundancy of overlap for court ordered interim measures keeps the stability, predictability, and law certainty at its lowest. This paper will analyse the fact that it is partly correct to say that the judicial recognition has enhanced the arbitration position in the county, but to attain uniform and sustainable position of emergency arbitration the country requires legislative developments.

detail.abstract: Traditional transport decarbonization policies have failed to achieve climate targets due to structural fragmentation: electric vehicle subsidies address technology without managing demand; carbon pricing creates regressive burdens without alternatives; circular economy initiatives remain disconnected from operations; labor transitions lack protection. This paper introduces the Mobility Carbon Rights and Circular Equity (MCR-CE) framework developed by Green Transformation and Sustainability Network (GXS) in Vietnam-operationalizing carbon budgets as individual household rights while embedding circular material flows, vehicle-to-grid flexibility, integrated land-use planning, and just transition governance. Drawing on pilot validation from Vienna, Copenhagen, and Amsterdam, we demonstrate systemic integration generates multiplicative effects: 60% transport CO2 reduction, 450,000+ jobs, 94% low-income equity, €50-75B circular revenue by 2035. GXS's unique positioning at the nexus of rapid urbanization, manufacturing capacity, and climate vulnerability enables Southern-led climate innovation. We challenge Northern hegemony in policy design, arguing Global South institutions possess superior implementation capacity due to contextual knowledge, manufacturing integration, and democratic legitimacy in regions bearing disproportionate climate impacts.

title: The Elevation of Elliott Wave Theory by the MLC Law: From Subjective Wave Interpretation to a Quantifiable Science of Market Structure

detail.title: The Elevation of Elliott Wave Theory by the MLC Law: From Subjective Wave Interpretation to a Quantifiable Science of Market Structure

detail.abstract: For nearly a century, Elliott Wave Theory has remained one of the most influential yet controversial structural theories in financial market analysis. Its enduring importance lies in the recognition that price evolution is not entirely disordered, but instead exhibits a structural order characterized by multi-scale wave motion, fractal nesting, and geometric constraints. Yet because traditional wave theory has long lacked rigorous mathematical definitions and objective criteria, it has remained vulnerable to the problem of multiple interpretations of the same chart, preventing it from entering a reproducible and falsifiable scientific framework. This paper argues that the Morphological Least-Cost Law (MLC Law), introduced in Zhu (2026), provides the long-missing quantitative foundation for Elliott Wave Theory and elevates it into a computable science of market structure. Through the optimal morphological skeleton, Morphological Critical Points (MCPs), the minimum solution value , residuals, and first-and second-derivative dynamical indicators, the paper establishes, for the first time, a unified mathematical basis for wave boundaries, wave identities, and structural completion states. Within this framework, key questions that have long depended on subjective judgment, including impulsive versus corrective waves, rebound versus reversal, wave-3 versus wave-5 tops, and A-wave versus C-wave termination, can be given quantitative interpretations, yielding a unique and reviewable wave count. Using extensive empirical evidence across markets, asset classes, and time scales, together with short-horizon forward validation, the paper shows that the MLC Law not only sharply compresses the interpretive freedom of traditional wave labeling, but also provides a new theoretical basis for price forecasting, morphological stability analysis, and structural risk assessment. More broadly, it suggests that the quantitative interpretation of Elliott Wave Theory is only one entry point into the practical significance of the MLC Law, which may open a wider research program centered on price morphology, structural skeletons, cost formation, and dynamical divergence, namely, morphological finance.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how AI and psychological principles converge in customer retention, integrating data-driven systems with behavioral insights to enhance loyalty and lifetime value. Through theoretical analysis and case studies, we identify integration points where AI leverages psychological principles and misalignment risks where optimization undermines authentic connection. Three critical conclusions emerge. First, sustainable retention requires AI systems governed by psychological guardrails preventing optimization from eroding trust. detail.abstract: A unified dynamic model for reversible solid oxide cells (rSOCs) is developed and implemented in Modelica, covering both fuel-cell (SOFC) and electrolysis (SOEC) operation within a single sign-consistent equation structure requiring no port reassignment or equation restructuring at mode transitions across three fuel compositions (H2 /H2O, syngas, and CO/H2O/CO2), two operating temperatures, and a 30-cell stack archetype. The model separates electrochemical charge transfer in the cell domain from thermochemical water-gas shift (WGS) reactions in the oweld domain, enabling consistent treatment of mixed H2 /CO fuel feeds for reversible operation. Validation against two independent hardware archetypes, an anode-supported single cell (ASC) and a 30-cell electrolyte-supported stack (ESC), provides a transparent, physics-based basis for system-level rSOC analysis within the validated operating envelope of voltage and temperature observables. Two CO-conversion closures are compared under identical boundary conditions: a water-gas-shift constrained closure (WGSCC), routing all CO conversion through thermochemical WGS equilibration, and an explicit CO electrochemistry closure (ECC), enabling parallel H2 /CO charge-transfer branches. Under the present voltage-only validation basis and identical calibration protocol, WGSCC achieves voltage RMSE between 0.39 % and 1.07 % across the three fuel compositions and two temperatures (750 and 850 °C), with RMSE improvements of 58-67 % over ECC in every case and every operating mode, consistent with more parsimonious parameterisation in the absence of outlet composition data. A TPB partial-pressure reference for the activation overpotential reduces EC-mode voltage error by up to 1.7 % for CO/CO2-containing feeds. Stack-level model results indicate that temperature-induced massflow maldistribution reduces the achievable global fuel utilisation by approximately 5 % under poor insulation (model-based estimate); improved insulation recovers this margin at the cost of increased cathode-side pressure drop.

detail.abstract:
Digital transformation is rarely a technology problem; it is an executive decision problem. Modern enterprises are currently trapped in an operational paradox: they cannot scale digital services without standardized governance, yet they resist standardizing governance because it exposes systemic accountability failures.

Heavy-handed compliance stifles agile delivery, while weak oversight invites existential cyber and financial risk. Boards frequently mistake operational management frameworks for governance frameworks, leading to the dangerous illusion of control.

This whitepaper breaks the deadlock by establishing a unified, "Plug-and-Play" architecture. Utilizing the Calder-Moir IT Governance Framework as our structural umbrella, we position ISO/IEC 38500:2024 as the apex boardroom mandate. We then hardwire that mandate directly into the industry's premier execution engines: MoP (Investment), PMP (Execution), and ITIL 4 (Operations).

Governance without execution is mere philosophy; execution without governance is rogue operational risk. This synthesis engineers predictable value realization, protects corporate EBITDA, and establishes audit-ready compliance across the entire digital landscape.

detail.abstract:
This paper presents the GCC Board Gender Index Report 2026, the third annual, comprehensive assessment of gender representation on the boards of all publicly listed companies across the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC). Using a census date of 1 January 2026, the study constructs a fully de‑duplicated dataset covering 759 companies, 5,755 board positions, and 4,671 individual directors across six GCC countries. Board roles are analysed irrespective of executive status and classified into twelve standardised industry sectors.

The results indicate continued but incremental progress in female board representation. Women held 7.0 per cent of board positions in 2026, up from 6.9 per cent in 2025, with increases observed both in the number of women directors and the number of board seats they occupy. The United Arab Emirates remains the regional leader for the third consecutive year, with 15.0 per cent of board positions held by women, followed by Bahrain (10.5 per cent) and Oman (7.0 per cent). Sectoral analysis shows that the financial and industrial sectors account for the largest absolute number of female appointments, although substantial cross‑country and cross‑sector variation persists.

A key contribution of the 2026 report is its introduction of international benchmarking, comparing GCC board gender representation with five Asian markets—Hong Kong, India, Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore—that share broadly comparable stages of market development and governance reform. The analysis demonstrates that emerging markets with targeted regulatory interventions or disclosure‑based approaches have achieved materially higher levels of female board representation, providing realistic medium‑term benchmarks for the GCC.

The Index offers an original longitudinal dataset for scholars and provides evidence relevant to boards, investors and policymakers concerned with governance quality, board effectiveness and the pace of gender diversity reform in emerging capital markets.

detail.abstract: India’s economic journey has changed a lot over time. In the early years after independence, the country followed a system of centralized planning through Five-Year Plans. These plans helped build a strong base for industries, agriculture, and poverty reduction. However, over time, problems like slow decision-making, lack of flexibility, and changing global conditions made this system less effective. This research paper studies how India moved from the Five-Year Plans to a more flexible and modern approach, especially with the introduction of NITI Aayog and the vision of “Viksit Bharat 2047.” This vision aims to make India a developed country by 2047, marking 100 years of independence. The paper compares the old and new systems of planning and focuses on important areas like governance, inclusiveness, sustainability, and use of technology. It is based on secondary data and analysis of policies. The study finds that the new system is more flexible and innovative, but it also brings challenges such as maintaining accountability and ensuring equal growth for all sections of society. The paper suggests that a balanced approach—combining proper planning with flexibility—can help India achieve long-term and inclusive development.

title: Alpha State Strategy: China's Model of Indirect Control in the 21st Century

detail.title: Alpha State Strategy: China's Model of Indirect Control in the 21st Century
detail.abstract: The era of proxy militias is over; this is the era of proxy states. Proxy states are those states that, on the surface, possess all the characteristics of sovereign nations but whose policies-especially foreign policy-are heavily influenced by an alpha state. An alpha state, through its credible economy, technology, and military clout, is able to assert influence over other states that are suffering from structural malfunctions and are under the control of rapacious leadership or an oligarchy. Not every proxy state is a failed state or in a muddled condition. Some states become proxy states by choice, some due to geopolitical conditions, some due to spineless leadership, and some through deception. This policy paper examines how an alpha state compels nations to compromise independent decision-making, which is vital for maintaining sovereignty against undue foreign influence.

detail.title: Inter-Firm Networks and Management Guidance
detail.abstract: Although firms are embedded in inter-firm networks, prior research on management guidance largely treats disclosure decisions as firm-specific choices made in isolation. We examine whether a firm's connectedness within its inter-firm network is associated with the likelihood that its managers issue public earnings forecasts. Using network measures based on shared analyst coverage, we find that more connected firms are significantly more likely to issue management earnings forecasts. Moreover, forecasts issued by more connected firms elicit stronger reactions from investors and analysts, despite no improvement in forecast accuracy. These findings are consistent with greater external demand dominating offsetting increases in disclosure costs for firms that are more connected to their neighboring firms and are therefore more central to their networks. They suggest that managers' forecasting decisions reflect not only firm-level incentives, but also their firm's position within a broader inter-firm network.

detail.abstract: This paper tests whether three pre-specified binary astronomical signals-Jupiter-Saturn square phase (JS_Square), the mean lunar Node in the pre-defined Western geographic zone (Rahu_West), and Pluto in Earth element signs (Pluto_Earth)-align with empirestage transition points identified in Dalio's Changing World Order framework at rates exceeding random chance. Using a pre-registered methodology applied to six historical empire cycles (Abbasid, Ottoman, Spanish, Dutch, British, American) spanning approximately 1,500 years, with a null hypothesis baseline of 1,000 randomly drawn dates, two signals survive binary reduction with deltas exceeding 20 percentage points: Stage 1 rise transition points show JS_Square at 78% versus a 52% random baseline (+25pp, consistent across 6/6 cycles), and Stage 6 handoff transition points show Rahu_West at 44% versus a 23% random baseline (+21pp, consistent across 5/6 cycles, with one documented exception). Given the frequency of Jupiter-Saturn square phases (~52%) and wide transition window tolerances, Stage 1 results should be interpreted as a tendency rather than a sharp discriminator. Temporal autocorrelation between planetary cycle frequency and empire transition duration is acknowledged as an unresolved limitation. These findings are hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory and motivate forward validation through pre-registered predictions.

detail.abstract:
As part of the comprehensive Construction Re-engineering Initiative at the U.S. Census Bureau, alternative data sources are being considered to supplement or replace current data collection methods. For the Survey of Construction (SOC), which measures new residential construction, this includes observing housing starts from satellite imagery in place of the current interviews for housing starts conducted by field representatives. Satellite images are obtained monthly for a subset of places in the SOC sample. Convolutional neural network models are then applied to images to predict likely new residential construction projects, with the current focus being single-family housing starts. Several post prediction processing steps are applied including exclusions based on intersections with known buildings or roads, treatments for missing data due to cloud cover, and adjustments for the length of time between consecutive images, to ultimately produce place level estimates of housing starts. These place level estimates are then combined with the existing building permit level survey data to produce estimates of West South Central division level housing starts, an experimental data product from the Census Bureau.

title: Export Competitiveness in India's Spice Sector and Its Role in Economic Development

detail.title: Export Competitiveness in India's Spice Sector and Its Role in Economic Development
detail.abstract: Spices have historically been among the most significant commodities in international trade, and India continues to be one of the leading producers and exporters in the global spice market. International trade is widely considered a catalyst for economic development, particularly through the expansion of export-oriented sectors. This study examines the export competitiveness of India's spice sector and its potential contribution to broader economic development. The study adopts a descriptive analytical approach using secondary data obtained from sources such as the India Brand Equity Foundation and related institutional databases. The analysis of export performance indicates that India's spice sector maintains a strong position in global markets, supported by sustained international demand and evidence from previous studies highlighting comparative advantage. As a labour-intensive sector, increased export competitiveness in spices has the potential to generate employment, increase rural incomes, and contribute to foreign exchange earnings. These factors collectively support broader economic development through trade expansion. However, sustaining and strengthening this competitiveness requires improvements in product quality and supportive policy frameworks.

detail.abstract:
A rapidly growing literature estimates AI's labor-market effects using large language models (LLMs) to self-assess occupational exposure. We demonstrate these measures are highly fragile. Replicating the dominant rubric with three frontier models on identical tasks, we find a 3.6-fold divergence in mean exposure with agreement as low as 57%. This measurement instability alters downstream empirical conclusions: in a difference-in-differences framework, individual-level coefficient magnitudes vary 2.4-fold across annotators, and county level estimates flip from a significant negative to an insignificant positive depending on annotators. We formalize this non-classical measurement error, highlighting the risks of treating evolving LLMs as static instruments.

detail.abstract:
We evaluate the welfare effects of five provincial mandatory retirement bans in Canada from 2005 to 2009 using linked employer-employee tax data. The bans sharply reduce retirements at age 65, with sizable announcement effects and heterogeneity across industries. Post-65 employment and earnings rise at least 14%, with gains comparable to a two-year increase in pension-eligibility ages. Older workers save more and spouses postpone retirement, benefiting public finances, with no observable effects on mortality or younger workers. Highly exposed firms reduce payroll costs via hiring adjustments while maintaining worker productivity and profitability. Our results suggest that protecting older workers was welfare-improving.

detail.abstract:
This paper presents the canonical definition layer of Wave Liquidity Redistribution Theory (WLRT), focusing on its First Law of stability, core structural concepts, and interpretation constraints.

WLRT models systems as environments of liquidity redistribution, where stability is defined as the structural relation between compensation and fragility rather than as equilibrium or price behavior.

The paper introduces a formal framework for defining stability, fragility, and compensation, along with invariants and a Non-Interpretation Protocol designed to prevent common distortions of the theory.

The canonical version of the definitions is fixed via DOI to ensure consistent and non-distorted interpretation across academic and machine-interpreted environments.

We explore how pro-social preferences interact with asymmetric ambiguity to influence investment decisions. We develop a model where financial returns are ambiguous (e.g., due to policy uncertainties), while social impact returns are risky or less ambiguous. Employing Gilboa-Schmeidler maxmin and Klibanoff-Marinacci-Mukerji smooth ambiguity frameworks, we demonstrate that pro-social motives act as a hedge, mitigating ambiguity aversion and reducing effective hurdle rates for ambiguous assets. Using machine learning and product-level data on single men’s and single women’s consumption patterns, we develop an index that quantifies the “gendered” nature of consumer goods. We use the index to investigate how gender-specific labor market shocks influence spending patterns within heterosexual households. Our findings reveal that industrial robot adoption, which worsened men’s relative economic position, shifted household consumption toward products predominantly purchased by single women. detail.title: How Reform Happens

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
What determines whether and how regulations are reformed? We use a newly constructed data set of 3,590 successful and failed regulatory reforms in 189 countries, between 2005 and 2022, to address this question. We document that regulations have become more business friendly in some regulatory domains but not others. We also show that regulations are more business friendly in richer than in poorer countries, and that holding initial regulatory levels constant, richer countries also reform more. We present a model in which the successful passage of reforms is shaped by the number of veto points in the approval process, the social returns to reform, and the cost of compensating losers from reform, and then test it using our new data set. We find that richer countries have both higher reform attempt and success rates, but less impact of individual reforms on regulation than poorer countries. These findings are consistent with the model if richer countries are better at reform, perhaps because they can compensate losers more efficiently. Across the world, reform attempt rates are strongly correlated with reform success rates but not with reform impact levels. Within countries, a higher share of technological reform attempts is successful, compared to administrative or legal reforms, consistent with the importance of veto points.

We digitize and analyze the near-universe of National Socialist German Workers’ Party (NSDAP) membership records and link them to population and industrial censuses. Four findings emerge. Second, SS members’ characteristics remained different: younger, more educated, and more fanatical, as measured by the display of Nazi insignia in membership portraits. Third, within communities, coworkers, and families, early membership generated hysteresis, with subsequent entrants drawn from the same groups. Finally, local increases in party membership are associated with subsequent deportations of Germany’s Jews.

affiliations: Department of Economics, Sabanci University,  and Indiana University

detail.title: Comparative Advantage and Colonial Monopoly: The Political Economy of Exclusive Trading Companies

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
This paper analyzes a central colonial institution: the monopolization of foreign trade through exclusive trading companies. We interpret this arrangement as an economic institution that creates a wedge between domestic and international prices—effectively an export tax—allowing metropolitan intermediaries to extract rents from colonial trade. Our primary theoretical contribution demonstrates that the economic and political consequences of this institutional form depend systematically on the structure of comparative advantage between the metropolis and the colony. While colonial export taxation unambiguously worsens the colony’s effective terms of trade, its effect on the metropolis is conditional. When the colony and metropolis are competitors—sharing a comparative advantage in the same sector—a colonial export tax can improve the metropolis’s terms of trade. Conversely, when they are complementary—specializing in different sectors—the same policy can deteriorate the metropolis’s terms of trade by raising the cost of imported inputs. Because these terms-of-trade movements generate distinct distributive effects, the colonial monopoly reshapes political coalitions within the metropolis, influencing whether exclusive trading companies persist or are dismantled. We formalize this mechanism in a parsimonious general equilibrium model and illustrate it through the historical experience of Great Britain, India, and the East India Company (EIC), presenting the EIC as a salient instance of a broader institutional logic.

detail.abstract: In many analytical settings, different outcomes are typically attributed to execution error or downstream drift. However, some divergence occurs even when instructions are followed correctly and no transformation has taken place. This paper identifies a different source of variation: a condition in which an instruction allows more than one valid interpretation before analysis begins. When this condition is present, multiple analysts can follow the same instruction, apply reasonable assumptions, and produce different results without error. The divergence is not introduced during execution. It is already structurally available at the starting point. This paper demonstrates the condition through practical examples, distinguishes it from execution failure, and outlines its implications for analysis, decision making, and system design. It does not model downstream drift or propagation. It isolates an upstream condition that may help explain why divergence later appears.

detail.abstract:
Employers increasingly talk about neurodiversity, but the translation from awareness to durable workforce inclusion remains weak. This study examines how organizational awareness of neurodivergent talent does, or does not, convert into systems, practices, and outcomes in a regional workforce initiative in Northwest Arkansas. Drawing on a cross‑sectional, mixed‑methods survey of 164 participants (19 organizational leaders, 65 neurotypical staff, and 80 neurodivergent staff), the analysis identifies three main gaps.

First, there is a 68‑point drop between familiarity with neurodiversity and the presence of concrete infrastructure such as policies, training, metrics, and accommodations. Second, there is a 25–35‑point “empathy gap” between neurotypical and neurodivergent employees’ ratings of culture, ease of accessing adjustments, comfort disclosing, and fairness of career progression. Third, standard culture surveys overestimate inclusion because they privilege majority perceptions over neurodivergent employee experience.

The paper proposes the Porras–Scott Neurodivergent Workforce Design Framework, which conceptualizes inclusion as workforce architecture across five stages: awareness and intent, systems and infrastructure, managerial practices, employee experience, and workforce outcomes. Quantitative results show that tailored adjustments, manager empathy, and flexibility are among the strongest predictors of wellbeing and intent to stay, while tokenistic gestures have no measurable effect. The study argues that neurodivergent talent should be treated as economic and cognitive capital, not solely a compliance category, and outlines implications for social marketers seeking to shift employer behavior from performative awareness to institutionalized practice.

title: Disclosure and the Hybrid Constitution of UK Company Law

detail.title: Disclosure and the Hybrid Constitution of UK Company Law

keywords: Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act 2023 (ECCTA)

detail.abstract:
This paper develops a hybrid constitutional theory of UK company law in which disclosure is reconceptualised as the principal mechanism through which the fragmented corporate structure is functionally integrated. It argues that the corporate form is organised through a structural separation between title (vested in the company as a legal person), control (vested in directors), and residual governance rights (vested in shareholders). This separation generates a persistent informational asymmetry between managerial authority and residual claimants.

 

On this basis, disclosure is understood not as a merely regulatory requirement or market transparency device, but as the informational infrastructure through which the corporate constitution is operationalised. It enables the exercise of shareholder governance rights, facilitates independent verification through audit, and constrains the concentration of informational power within the managerial organ. Disclosure thereby stabilises a governance architecture that would otherwise be vulnerable to informational dominance by directors.

 

The paper further argues that the UK disclosure regime, while structurally indispensable across company law, financial regulation, and audit governance, remains institutionally incomplete. Its limitations—including information overload, standardised reporting practices, and shareholder passivity—reflect deeper structural tensions within the corporate form, rooted in its foundation in private property doctrine.

 

By reframing disclosure as a constitutional mechanism, the paper integrates accounting, capital maintenance, market regulation, and audit into a unified account of the informational architecture of the modern corporation.

title: The Uncertainty Trap: Algorithmic Management and the Stillborn Hierarchy *
affiliations: Baylor University - Department of Finance, Insurance & Real Estate and Baylor University

detail.title: The Uncertainty Trap: Algorithmic Management and the Stillborn Hierarchy *
detail.abstract: We identify a fundamental friction in algorithmic management: the Uncertainty Trap. When an algorithmic Principal learns incentive structures through exploration, early signal variance often drives a human Agent's perceived productivity below the firm's required threshold. This triggers an endogenous withdrawal of incentive contracts, resulting in Information Starvation where the absence of effort prevents the algorithm from revising its pessimistic beliefs. In entrenched environments, this leads to a Stillborn Hierarchy where AI adoption fails before a single informative signal is generated. We prove this trap is structural; pledgeable income creates a hard budget constraint that hyperparameter tuning cannot overcome. Escaping the trap requires either an internal culture of Human Curiosity to subsidize early learning or Urban Vibrancy where geographic peer spillovers provide an exogenous information subsidy. Our results suggest the success of algorithmic management is a spatial equilibrium, restricted to innovative cultures or dense urban hubs.

title: Dual Career Ladders: Individual Contributors in Modern Corporate Hierarchies
affiliations: , Kellogg School of Management,  and University of Melbourne

detail.title: Dual Career Ladders: Individual Contributors in Modern Corporate Hierarchies
detail.abstract: Firms often maintain dual career ladders for managers and individual contributors (ICs). Using personnel records from 43 medium-sized and large firms, we reconstruct complete reporting chains and organizational layers to document how these tracks are structured and compensated. We show that ICs are prevalent throughout the hierarchy but earn substantially less than managers in comparable positions, with the penalty increasing toward the top. To interpret these patterns, we develop and estimate a model of dual careers in which firms allocate workers across management and IC tracks subject to coordination and problem-solving frictions. The estimates reveal distinct firm types with respect to their hierarchy shape, degree of managerial specialization, and workforce composition that generate varying IC penalties and respond differently to organizational shocks. Motivated by the large pay gains associated with promotions from IC to manager roles, we then analyze the demographic composition of the IC workforce. While pay within each track does not significantly vary across demographic groups, women and minority workers are disproportionately represented on IC tracks, especially at higher ranks. Thus, assignment to IC and managerial tracks emerges as a key mechanism through which within-firm career inequality contributes to broader gender and racial pay gaps.

title: From Critic to Coach: Transforming Harsh Inner Dialogue into Constructive Guidance
affiliations: ,  and

detail.title: From Critic to Coach: Transforming Harsh Inner Dialogue into Constructive Guidance
detail.abstract: Harsh self-criticism is a common feature of internal dialogue, often associated with reduced confidence, increased anxiety, and impaired performance. Traditional approaches tend to frame the inner critic as a dysfunctional cognitive pattern to be suppressed or eliminated. However, Dialogical Self-Theory (DST), developed by Hubert Hermans, offers an alternative perspective by conceptualizing the self as a system of interacting voices. This article argues that the inner critic is not inherently maladaptive but becomes problematic when it dominates internal dialogue without constructive integration. Drawing on cognitive therapy, self-regulation research, and compassion-based approaches, the paper proposes a dialogical transformation model in which the critic is repositioned from a punitive authority to a developmental coach. A structured framework is introduced to guide this transformation, highlighting techniques for reframing, engagement, and integration. The article concludes that sustainable change requires not eliminating the critic, but redefining its function within the internal system.

detail.abstract:
Hebrew Abstract:
נייר זה מציג את הפרשנות וההערות למאמר הפותר את הסתירה ההרמנויטית בין סיפור הבריאה בבראשית (א'-ג') לבין המדע המודרני (אבולוציה). אנו טוענים כי הטקסט אינו נרטיב כרונולוגי יחיד שנכשל, אלא מציג במכוון שני נרטיבים פונקציונליים מקבילים ומשלימים.

הנרטיב הראשון (בראשית א', "אֱלֹהִים"): אינו מתאר בריאה פיזית, אלא את התעוררותה הסדרתית של התודעה הקוגניטיבית. תיזה זו נתמכת על ידי פירוש פילולוגי מחודש לשורש ב.ר.א למשמעות ״בְּ־רְאִיָה״ – פעולת מתן משמעות, הכרה, הבחנה וסיווג.

הנרטיב השני (בראשית ב', "יְהוָה אֱלֹהִים"): הוא הנרטיב המקביל, המתאר את ההתפתחות הפיזית והאבולוציונית של החומר (המסומן בפועל "וַיִּיצֶר").

המודל פותר את "כשל הזהות" באמצעות הוכחה פילולוגית (הנתמכת בתרגום השבעים) המבחינה פונקציונלית בין 'הָאָדָם' (האורגניזם הפיזי, האובייקט) לבין ״אָדָם״ (הסובייקט המודע).

הסינתזה (בראשית ג'): ה"חטא" אינו עונש, אלא רגע הסינתזה שבו התודעה (מפרק א') מוטמעת במלואה בגוף (מפרק ב') באמצעות רכישת "דעת טוב ורע". "הקללה" מתפרשת מחדש כתיאור אקזיסטנציאלי של "מחירי המודעות". 

English Abstract:
This paper presents the commentary and notes for the article that resolves the hermeneutical contradiction between the Creation narrative in Genesis (chapters 1–3) and modern science (evolution). We argue that the text is not a single chronological narrative that fails, but rather deliberately presents two parallel and complementary functional narratives.

The first narrative (Genesis 1, "Elohim"): Does not describe physical creation, but rather the sequential awakening of cognitive consciousness. This thesis is supported by a renewed philological interpretation of the root B.R.A toward the meaning of "be-re'iya" — an act of bestowing meaning, recognition, distinction, and classification.

The second narrative (Genesis 2, "YHWH Elohim"): Is the parallel narrative, describing the physical and evolutionary development of matter (marked by the verb "vayitzer").

The model resolves the "identity failure" through philological evidence (supported by the Septuagint) that functionally distinguishes between ha-adam (the physical organism, the object) and adam (the conscious subject).

title: Corporate Climate Litigation – Klimahaftungsklagen gegen Unternehmen im Kontext des internationalen Zivilverfahrens- und Privatrechts

detail.title: Corporate Climate Litigation – Klimahaftungsklagen gegen Unternehmen im Kontext des internationalen Zivilverfahrens- und Privatrechts
detail.abstract: This article examines liability for climate-related individual damages from the perspective of Swiss private international law. It analyses both jurisdiction and the applicable law, with particular focus on the conceptualisation of the place of acting (Handlungsort) and the place where the harmful result occurs (Erfolgsort). The authors demonstrate that, de lege lata, no place of harmful result can be identified – primarily because emissions do not directly injure individual legal interests. As a consequence, the choice-of-law mechanism under Art. 138 IPRG cannot fully unfold its purpose, and the law of the place where the emitting property is situated (lex rei sitae) applies. The article concludes that the limits encountered by current PIL concepts are a logical consequence of the absence of a corresponding legislative consensus, which would have to be addressed through the ordinary legislative process rather than through litigation.

title: THEIA: End-to-End Learning of Three-Valued Logic in Modular Neural Architectures

detail.title: THEIA: End-to-End Learning of Three-Valued Logic in Modular Neural Architectures

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests. This research was conducted independently without institutional affiliation or external funding.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. All computational resources were personally owned by the author.

detail.abstract: Can a neural network learn exact logical reasoning with principled uncertainty handling, entirely from data? We present THEIA, a modular neural system supporting Kleene's strong three-valued logic (True/False/Unknown). Without intermediate supervision, THEIA learns all 12 Kleene algebraic rules end-to-end (12/12 at 100% accuracy, input space 3.4 × 10 13). A Transformer baseline achieves only 7/12, failing catastrophically on commuted absorption (U ∧ F = F : 0%) even with operand-swap data augmentation-revealing that sequential attention learns "when uncertain, default to Unknown" but cannot learn that a definite second operand absorbs an uncertain first. Linear probing reveals a delayed verdict: THEIA's early representations remain classification-agnostic (SVM 54.7%), with inter-class distance increasing 1,300× at the final layer-24× more extreme than the Transformer's 54×. A flat MLP (2.29M parameters) plateaus at 99.1%, confirming that modular decomposition is necessary for perfect accuracy. Multi-seed evaluation (N = 5) shows zero variance on local transitive rule generalization from 5 to 50 hops.

title: Reserve Forecasting Under Structural Breaks: Evidence from Sri Lanka
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and University of Colombo

detail.title: Reserve Forecasting Under Structural Breaks: Evidence from Sri Lanka
detail.abstract: No existing study compares classical, Bayesian, regime-switching, and machinelearning reserve forecasts on the same monthly dataset through a sovereign default and recovery. This paper fills that gap using Sri Lanka's 2005-2025 reserve cycle and a rolling-origin design that evaluates each model class on parsimonious and disaggregated balance-of-payments specifications. In the preferred BoP specification, MS-VAR leads the one-step-ahead comparison on all four standard point-error metrics, cutting RMSE by 76.7% relative to the random walk. The advantage traces to architecture rather than information. Regime sensitivity matters more than variable-set expansion. For density forecasts, MS-VAR delivers the lowest CRPS, while XGB-Quantile comes closest to nominal interval coverage. Rankings also shift across horizons: the tuned LSTM leads at some longer BoP windows. These findings support a division of labour in reserve monitoring for crisis-prone economies: regime-sensitive systems for point paths, quantile methods for uncertainty bands.

reference: Bank of Italy Temi di Discussione (Working Paper) No. 1525
title: The awakening of inflation and the return of the Phillips curve in the euro area
affiliations: Bank of Italy, Bank of Italy and Bank of Italy

detail.title: The awakening of inflation and the return of the Phillips curve in the euro area

publicationDetails.detailsText: Bank of Italy Temi di Discussione (Working Paper) No. 1525
publicationDetails.journalName: Bank of Italy Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: During the 2021-22 high-inflation surge, euro-area firms significantly increased the frequency with which they adjusted prices. This paper documents that such a shift in price-setting behaviour led to a transitory steepening of the Phillips curve, which had remained persistently flat throughout the preceding low-inflation period. In a model with nominal rigidities, a higher frequency of price adjustments steepens the Phillips curve and enhances the transmission of monetary policy, enabling central banks to contain cost-push shocks with a smaller loss in output. We provide robust empirical evidence for the euro area using panel local projections, confirming the link between the frequency of price changes, the slope of the Phillips curve in the euro area, and the increased effectiveness of monetary policy.

title: Introduction to the Special Issue: The Maldives at the Crossroads of International Law
affiliations: Woxsen University, Jindal Global Law School, O.P. Jindal Global University and

detail.title: Introduction to the Special Issue: The Maldives at the Crossroads of International Law
detail.abstract: The Republic of Maldives remains marginal in international legal scholarship despite extensive treaty participation and active multilateral engagement. When it appears, it is largely framed as a site of climate vulnerability, a reduction that obscures its historical depth, legal agency, and broader engagement with international law. This introductory article situates the special issue as an intervention against that narrow framing. Bringing together contributions on colonial governance, pre-modern Indian Ocean normativity, Islamic law and human rights, climate change and statehood, labour regulation, trade, taxation, arbitration, and fisheries governance, the volume treats the Maldives as analytically ordinary rather than exceptional. It demonstrates how international law engages small island states through indirect rules, selective incorporation, and uneven distributions of responsibility. The article further argues that the relative absence of Maldivian engagement in international legal discourse constitutes a form of legal positioning rather than neutrality and concludes by identifying future research agendas with implications extending beyond the Maldivian context.

title: Modelica Implementation of a Unified Reversible Solid Oxide Cell Model: Complete Equations, Calibration Workflow, and Hardware-Specific Parameter Sets

detail.abstract: This article documents the complete implementation of a unified dynamic Modelica model for reversible solid oxide cells (rSOCs), covering both fuel-cell (SOFC) and electrolysis (SOEC) operation within a single equation structure without mode-dependent restructuring. The model architecture separates electrochemical charge transfer in the cell domain from thermochemical water-gas shift (WGS) reactions in the flowfield domain; a unified sign convention and fixed port indexing enable continuous FC↔EC transitions. Documented method components include: (i) a dual-pathway Butler-Volmer formulation with triple-phaseboundary (TPB) referenced partial pressures for activation and concentration overpotentials; (ii) two CO-conversion closures (Water-gas-shift CO conversion - WGSCC and Electrochemical CO vonversion - ECC) including the algebraic coupling required for parallel H2/CO chargetransfer branches under ECC; (iii) logarithmic-mean bulk concentration expressions with mode-dependent educt/product assignment; (iv) a lumped thermal resistance network including heat-transfer correlations, Kozeny-Carman permeability, and end-plate boundary conditions; and (v) a reduced-order kinetic anchoring parameter T*ref with a sweep-based selection procedure for temperature extrapolation. Geometry, material, and calibrated electrochemical/transport parameters are provided for two hardware archetypes used for model assessment in the companion research article: an anode-supported single cell (ASC) and a 30-cell electrolyte-supported stack (ESC).

reference: Osgoode Legal Studies Research Paper (forthcoming)
title: Labour Law, Technology, and the Attack on the Rules-Based-Order
affiliations: York University - Osgoode Hall Law School

detail.title: Labour Law, Technology, and the Attack on the Rules-Based-Order

publicationDetails.journalName: Osgoode Hall Law School Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper argues that current debates on artificial intelligence and algorithmic management at work are also debates about private power, managerial prerogative, and democracy. It situates recent attacks by major technology companies and their political allies on the European Union and other rule-based international institutions within a broader struggle over who should regulate technology and govern society. It contends that the anti-democratic turn of parts of the tech world is closely connected to authoritarian ideas about work, hierarchy, and obedience. The workplace is one of the principal sites where authority is exercised, surveillance normalised, and habits of subordination formed, with consequences that extend beyond employment relations into democratic life more broadly. Against this background, the paper examines how AI and algorithmic management intensify employer power through pervasive monitoring, automated evaluation, predictive analytics, and data-driven discipline. It argues that existing legal frameworks, especially data protection law, remain insufficient unless infused with labour law concepts that address the structural imbalance of power at work. It therefore advocates a substantial upgrading of labour law, stronger limits on digital surveillance, and a more robust role for collective bargaining, codetermination, and worker voice in the governance of workplace technologies. It contends that labour law is one of the main ways in which the rule of law enters the workplace and workers remain citizens rather than subjects while at work. The regulation of AI at work is thus a constitutional and democratic question as much as an economic or technological one.

title: Save The Date: Analyst/Investor Days as a Trading Signal
affiliations: The University of Manchester - Alliance Manchester Business School, Lancaster University Management School and The University of Manchester

detail.title: Save The Date: Analyst/Investor Days as a Trading Signal
detail.abstract: Firms increasingly use Analyst/Investor (A/I) days as discretionary disclosure channels. We show that announcing an A/I day leads to positive abnormal returns and a sustained pre-event price run-up. The run-up is more pronounced when firms issue additional pre-event voluntary disclosures and is followed by return reversals after the event. In contrast, events without any incremental disclosures exhibit positive post-event returns driven by event informativeness and changes in risk expectations. Exploiting these patterns, we design implementable long-short trading strategies that earn economically and statistically significant abnormal returns. A strategy based solely on the announcement yields positive alphas of around 0.095% before and 0.08% after transaction and borrowing costs. A deep-reinforcement-learning optimal stopping rule further improves performance, generating a positive alpha of 0.13% before costs, highlighting the importance of A/I days as a voluntary disclosure channel and the role of announcement and pre-event behaviour in shaping market prices.

title: The Signal-Anchored Options Model (SAOM)
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Signal-Anchored Options Model (SAOM)
detail.abstract:
Black-Scholes prices a European option on an underlying that follows geometric Brownian motion with zero as its lower bound. For most financial assets, this is the correct model. For Bitcoin — and for any asset with a rising structural signal grounded in physical law or mathematical protocol — it is the wrong model. Four foundational assumptions fail simultaneously: the lower bound is not zero but a rising structural signal S(t); volatility is not constant but structurally declining as adoption deepens; the option writer's opportunity cost is not the risk-free rate but the Structural Parity Rate, which enters through the Girsanov kernel as the market price of non-hedgeable structural risk rather than as a discount rate substitution; and the delta-hedge is incomplete, because structural signal appreciation cannot be replicated by trading spot Bitcoin.
This paper derives the Signal-Anchored Options Model (SAOM) from these four failures. The SAOM prices Bitcoin options as claims on the speculative multiplier ε(t) = P(t)/S(t) — the ratio of spot price to structural signal — with a soft lower boundary enforced by a mean-reverting potential rather than a hard barrier. The risk-neutral measure Q is formally derived: the USD risk-free rate remains the discount rate while the Structural Parity Rate enters through the Girsanov kernel. A key analytical result is that the structural growth rate g_S cancels exactly from d₁, so the first-order SAOM formula is formally identical to Black-Scholes with σ_ε substituted for σ — a substitution that is not cosmetic but consequential, because σ_ε is structurally declining while σ_P is not. The model is empirically calibrated from 647 weeks of Bitcoin price data; the floor and jump parameters are formally estimated by MLE and the full Deribit options chain has been decomposed. The model produces five testable predictions with explicit falsification criteria. A credit implication follows: the mathematical premium component of Bitcoin's price has a formal value as a finite-horizon call on future adoption above the structural signal.

title: POSITION OF THE FARMER FROM 2016 TO 2026-A DECADAL REVIEW OF A RESEARCH RELATED TO PEASANT FARMERS
affiliations: Indian Law Institute

detail.title: POSITION OF THE FARMER FROM 2016 TO 2026-A DECADAL REVIEW OF A RESEARCH RELATED TO PEASANT FARMERS
detail.abstract:
ABSTRACT

In addition to reviewing the evolving status of peasant farmers in India between 2016 and 2026, this article reexamines a fundamental assertion regarding the absence of a convincing legal classification of farmers. Agriculture employs a significant portion of India's workers, yet the sector still suffers basic losses in economic contribution, fragmented landholding, mounting debt, and uneven regulation. The study evaluates whether significant recommendations from earlier research—such as the development of a legal definition of peasant farmers, landholding-based classification, the adoption of comprehensive farmer-centric legislation, agricultural diversification, the strengthening of local governance institutions, and targeted credit delivery—have been implemented over the previous ten years. By examining legislative changes, policy initiatives like PM-Kisan and PMFBY, and empirical data on income, debt, and land allocation, the study indicates that even if welfare programs have expanded, structural issues remain unaddressed. However, the absence of a legally obligatory classification undermines the effectiveness of targeted policies. The paper argues that in the lack of a clear legal framework that recognizes different farmer categories, agrarian suffering will persist, leading to socioeconomic vulnerability and migration pressures. In its conclusion, it highlights the urgent need for a rights-based legal strategy to safeguard the status of Indian peasant farmers.

title: Beyond Volatility: A Leakage-Safe Residual-Stress Signal for Drawdown Risk Monitoring
affiliations: Northwestern University

detail.title: Beyond Volatility: A Leakage-Safe Residual-Stress Signal for Drawdown Risk Monitoring
detail.abstract: Monitoring equity drawdown risk requires real-time indicators that can be implemented without look-ahead bias and that may add information beyond standard volatility measures. This study develops a leakage-safe residual-stress indicator from cross-sectional PCA reconstruction errors in U.S. sector excess returns and examines whether it contributes to drawdown-risk monitoring. Using daily adjusted prices for SPY and 11 U.S. sector ETFs over 2020-2025, this study computes sector excess returns relative to SPY, estimate the common component with principal component analysis (PCA), and define residual stress as the cross-sectional root-mean-square magnitude of out-of-sample reconstruction residuals. The PCA mapping is estimated using information available only through t-1, stress is computed at t, and high-stress regimes are defined using rolling train-only quantile thresholds shifted forward by one trading day. Performance is evaluated using drawdownonset events and early-warning metrics including ROC-AUC, PR-AUC, and horizon-H precision and recall. The results indicate that although residual stress is not a superior standalone alternative to realized volatility, it remains the stronger benchmark in overall classification performance. Residual stress is most useful as a complementary indicator of cross-sectional market dislocation rather than as a replacement for volatility. In the baseline sample, residual-stress spikes cluster around drawdown onsets, and conditional regime analysis shows that when volatility is low, high residual stress is associated with a materially higher probability of a drawdown onset within the next H = 21 trading days than the low-stress/low-volatility regime. Event-overlap and lead-time diagnostics further suggest that residual stress can flag a subset of onset episodes not captured by a simple volatilitythreshold rule, although its primary incremental value lies in conditional risk stratification rather than in systematically earlier triggering. A longer-history proxy-sector analysis yields similar evidence of conditional complementarity while also confirming the stronger standalone performance of volatility. The paper's contribution is to develop a leakagesafe, interpretable, cross-sectional residual-stress diagnostic that improves conditional drawdown-risk stratification, especially in otherwise low-volatility states, rather than a standalone replacement for realized volatility. This interpretation is supported by both a modern ETF baseline sample and a longer-history proxy-sector sample, with the broader sample providing more stable evidence of complementarity across a larger set of drawdown onsets.

title: Volatility Forecasting and Early-Warning Market Stress Detection: A Leakage-Safe Evaluation with Tree Ensembles and Transformers
affiliations: Northwestern University

detail.title: Volatility Forecasting and Early-Warning Market Stress Detection: A Leakage-Safe Evaluation with Tree Ensembles and Transformers
detail.abstract: This study examines the effectiveness of machine learning and deep learning models in forecasting daily realized volatility and detecting early signs of market stress. While Transformer-based models have gained popularity for their ability to model long-range dependencies, their performance advantage over classical methods in daily financial settings remains uncertain. Using a 10-year panel of large-cap U.S. equities and a rolling walk-forward evaluation framework, we compare traditional time-series models (EWMA, HAR, ARIMA), tree-based ensembles (Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM), and deep sequence models (LSTM and Transformer). We assess each model's forecasting accuracy (RMSE/MAE), rank agreement with realized volatility (Spearman correlation), and ability to detect high-volatility stress episodes using a Market Stress Index (MSI). Results show that simpler models-especially HAR, persistence, and tree ensembles-outperform deep learning approaches in both predictive accuracy and early-warning classification. Although LSTM and Transformer models yield smoother volatility signals, they exhibit weaker rank alignment and lower detection performance at daily frequencies. We also explore how model-implied MSI signals translate into risk-adjusted performance when used in a volatility-targeted overlay strategy. The findings suggest that for daily forecasts with limited input features, classical and ensemble models remain highly effective, while deep architectures may require richer or higher-frequency data to consistently outperform.

title: A Physics-Informed Spatio-Temporal Mamba-GAN for Modeling Complex Convection-Diffusion Dynamics in Nonlinear Systems

detail.title: A Physics-Informed Spatio-Temporal Mamba-GAN for Modeling Complex Convection-Diffusion Dynamics in Nonlinear Systems
detail.abstract: Modeling the spatiotemporal evolution of non-linear convection-diffusion systems faces challenges from the dimensionality curse of traditional numerical solvers and the physical inconsistency of data-driven surrogates. To resolve these limitations, we propose a novel Physics-Informed Spatio-Temporal Mamba-GAN (ST-Mamba-GAN). Our framework integrates a 2D Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) for efficient spatial feature extraction with a discrete state-space Mamba encoder, capturing temporal dynamics with lineartime complexity O(L). Crucially, we directly embed the Finite Difference Method (FDM) discretization of the governing partial differential equation into the Wasserstein adversarial loss. This physics-informed regularization confines the generative optimization to a physically admissible manifold without the severe memory overhead of automatic differentiation. Extensive evaluations on PDEBench 2D fluid dynamics datasets validate the architecture's superiority. In diffusion-dominated regimes (Mach 0.1), ST-Mamba-GAN achieves exceptional predictive fidelity with ultra-low physical residuals (O(10-4)). Furthermore, in non-linear, convection-dominated transonic regimes (Mach 1.0), the embedded constraints successfully prevent numerical divergence and preserve macroscopic topological integrity. Ultimately, this establishes a highly scalable and physically credible paradigm for complex fluid simulation.

title: The Map Equation on Rolling Granger-Causality Graphs Does Not Forecast Market Risk
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Map Equation on Rolling Granger-Causality Graphs Does Not Forecast Market Risk
detail.abstract: We test whether the Map equation (Rosvall and Bergstrom, 2008) applied to rolling bivariate Granger-causality (Granger, 1969) graphs of asset returns produces a regime signal that is forecast-informative beyond standard stress benchmarks (VIX, realised volatility, average pairwise correlation, PC1 variance share). Using a pre-registered eight-phase protocol with locked dev / val / test splits and a held-out test set, we evaluate on two universes-74 US large-cap equities and 30 cross-asset front-month futures spanning equities, rates, FX, energy, metals, ags and softs-over 2005-2017. The Map signal passes the orthogonality gate on both universes (correlation with average pairwise correlation =-0.29 /-0.05; correlation with VIX on futures =-0.003) and recovers real economic structure (module purity 42.6% vs. 12.5% random). However, in Newey-West regressions across nine forward targets at three horizons, no Map signal survives Bonferroni at α = 0.05 on either universe, and Goyal-Welch out-of-sample R 2 is negative for every headline Map signal. A trivial VIX>30 overlay strictly dominates the Map overlay on Sharpe, drawdown, and Calmar at every cost level. The Map equation detects VIX-orthogonal structure that is not forecast-informative at daily horizons; we publish the null result.

detail.title: Environmental score and bond pricing: it better be good, it better be green

publicationDetails.detailsText: Bank of Italy Occasional Paper No. 1002

detail.abstract: We provide empirical evidence that the pricing of green bonds tends to be highly sophisticated and based on a two-tiered approach. When buying a green bond, investors do not only look at the presence of a green label, but also consider additional characteristics of the bond that involve the issuer’s environmental score and the soundness of the underlying project. By comparing the yields at issuance of green bonds to those of a matched control sample of conventional bonds, our baseline specification identifies a premium of 16 basis points for the green label alone. Furthermore, when the issuer’s environmental score is in the top tercile of the cross-sectional distribution, the greenium increases by up to double. Green certification and periods of heightened climate uncertainty also significantly affect the size of the greenium.

title: A Review of Claude E. Shannon’s “Coding Theorems for a Discrete Source With a Fidelity Criterion” (1959)

detail.title: A Review of Claude E. Shannon’s “Coding Theorems for a Discrete Source With a Fidelity Criterion” (1959)
detail.abstract: This foundational paper, published as Shannon (1959), introduced rate-distortion theory, a cornerstone of information theory that formalizes lossy source coding under a fidelity (distortion) constraint. It extends Shannon’s 1948 channel coding and source coding theorems to scenarios where perfect reconstruction is neither possible nor required, quantifying the minimal rate needed for a source to achieve a specified average distortion level. The work is remarkable for its depth, generality, and prescience, laying the mathematical groundwork for modern lossy compression, vector quantization, perceptual coding, and even applications in machine learning and cognitive science. This review provides a thorough technical summary, analyzes the paper’s contributions from multiple angles (theoretical, computational, applicative), contrasts it with contemporaneous and prior works, and documents key advances over the subsequent 65+ years. Nuances, edge cases, implications, and open questions are highlighted for completeness.

detail.abstract:
This paper argues that India’s optimal response to the United States’ escalating tariff actions is not retaliation but structural economic reform. Examining the trajectory of U.S. trade

policy from April 2025’s “Liberation Day” tariffs through the U.S. Supreme Court’s landmark February 2026 ruling in Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump and the subsequent India–U.S. Interim Trade Agreement, the paper traces how geopolitical shocks can function as catalysts for domestic transformation. Drawing parallels with India’s 1991 balance-of-payments reforms, this paper proposes a five-pillar reform agenda market diversification, export promotion infrastructure, product portfolio expansion, domestic demand stimulation, and ease-of-doing-business improvements as the foundation for India’s next growth chapter. The paper concludes that each tariff wall Washington builds is, paradoxically, a window India can climb through.

title: Hamiltonians in Quantum Mechanics, with Particular Emphasis on the Articulation of Time (Vol-I)

detail.title: Hamiltonians in Quantum Mechanics, with Particular Emphasis on the Articulation of Time (Vol-I)
detail.abstract: This work explores the pivotal role of the Hamiltonian operator (\hat{H}) in Quantum Mechanics (QM), primarily as the generator of time translations and the key driver of unitary state evolution via the time-dependent Schrödinger equation (TDSE). The foundational distinction is drawn between time-independent and time-dependent Hamiltonians, the latter being critical for quantum control and simulation. A significant portion addresses the "Problem of Time" (PoT), which stems from the non-relativistic view of time as a classical c-number parameter, a constraint formalized by Pauli's theorem. This limitation is contrasted with the emergence of a dynamical time operator in relativistic Dirac theory and the intensified PoT in canonical quantum gravity, where the universe's wavefunction is "timeless". The review concludes by detailing the current state of play (as of 2026), emphasizing advances in efficient quantum simulation algorithms for \hat{H}(t), and conceptual breakthroughs where the articulation of time is seen as emergent, relational, and context-dependent, particularly at the interface of quantum technologies and gravitational theories.

detail.abstract: Chief Micheal Soyebo Sowole (fl. c. 1948–1970s — floruit, a Latin designation meaning ‘he flourished,’ used when precise birth and death dates are unknown) was a Yoruba politician, trade unionist, and diplomat from Ipara-Remo in present-day Ogun State, Nigeria. A senior member of Chief Obafemi Awolowo’s Action Group (AG), the dominant political party of Western Nigeria, and a lifelong personal friend of the Premier himself, Sowole served as a member of the Western Region House of Assembly (WRHA), moved the landmark 14 June 1955 legislative motion that gave the first parliamentary recognition to what became Nigeria’s Midwest Region in 1963, and subsequently represented the Western Region as Agent-General and Ambassador in London. He later served as a Commissioner in the post-1967 Western State government. Despite his evident significance to the First Republic era (1960–1966), Sowole has received minimal sustained scholarly attention. This working paper, drawing on contemporaneous newspaper records, legislative analyses, royal memoirs, archival photographic captions from Paul Popper Limited (1956) and Getty Images/Keystone (1958), and published personal interviews, presents the most comprehensive account of his career assembled to date. Three findings are new to the historical record: (1) that Sowole received 82 votes to Awolowo’s 81 in the 1951 Remo Electoral College, a result unreported in prior scholarship; (2) the full dialogue of the 1956 ministerial withdrawal episode; and (3) the identification of 45A Kensington Gardens, London, as a significant diplomatic and social hub for Yoruba elites in Britain during the late 1950s.

detail.abstract: The emergence of the startup ecosystem in India has been widely celebrated as a transformative force driving innovation, employment generation, and economic growth. Positioned as a land of opportunity for the young generation, startups are often portrayed as pathways to financial independence, creativity, and social mobility. However, beneath this optimistic narrative lies a complex interplay between aspiration and reality, where the "fairytale" of entrepreneurial success coexists with structural constraints, unequal access to resources, and high failure rates. This study adopts a humanitarian perspective to critically examine the authenticity ("genuineness") of business opportunities available to youth within the contemporary startup ecosystem. It explores whether the ecosystem inclusively empowers diverse socioeconomic groups or disproportionately benefits privileged segments with access to capital, networks, and digital literacy. By integrating insights from development economics, social justice frameworks, and empirical observations, the research highlights the psychological, financial, and social vulnerabilities faced by young entrepreneurs, particularly in semi-urban and rural contexts. The paper further investigates the role of government initiatives such as Startup India and institutional support systems in bridging opportunity gaps, while also identifying persistent barriers including regulatory complexities, funding asymmetries, and skill mismatches. It argues that while the startup ecosystem holds genuine potential for inclusive development, its current structure often amplifies inequalities unless supported by targeted policy interventions and ethical entrepreneurial practices. Ultimately, this research contributes to a more balanced discourse by moving beyond celebratory narratives and emphasizing a humane, equitable, and sustainable approach to entrepreneurship. It calls for reimagining the startup ecosystem not merely as an economic engine but as a socially responsible platform that nurtures dignity, resilience, and inclusive growth for the young generation.

title: Price Controls, Repressed Inflation, and Monetary Overhang in the Late Soviet Economy
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Price Controls, Repressed Inflation, and Monetary Overhang in the Late Soviet Economy

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests. This research was conducted independently, and no personal, financial, or institutional relationships influenced the study, analysis, or conclusions.

detail.abstract: Late Soviet inflation is easy to underestimate if only official price indices are read. Between 1981 and 1988, official retail prices rose by about 0.6% per year, yet household balances, forced saving indicators, inventories, and subsidy data suggest a less stable economy underneath the posted prices. This paper studies that gap as repressed inflation: pressure that administrative prices kept out of the official index, but not out of the economy. The evidence is assembled from official-data compilations, Soviet household-balance reconstructions, and the shortage-economy literature. I do not estimate one exact "true" inflation rate. Instead, I show that several independent signals-monetary overhang benchmarks, Kim's household overhang series, falling inventories, and large price subsidies move in the direction expected under controlled-price disequilibrium. A small OLS exercise is included only as a diagnostic, since the sample is too short for causal inference. The main conclusion is that late Soviet price controls postponed visible inflation by shifting adjustment into queues, forced saving, scarcity, and fiscal subsidies. The 1991-1992 price break then looks less like a sudden creation of inflation than a partial release of pressure accumulated earlier.

title: Estimating the Number of Latent Factors: A Comparative Analysis
affiliations: University of Glasgow, Adam Smith Business School, University of Navarra, IESE Business School and Imperial College Business School

detail.title: Estimating the Number of Latent Factors: A Comparative Analysis

keywords: Estimator of the Number of Factors

detail.abstract: This paper evaluates a set of widely used methodologies for determining the number of latent factors in large-dimensional factor models. Its contribution is a comprehensive and systematic comparison of their performance. We assess these estimators not only under the data-generating processes for which they were originally designed, but also across a broader set of environments. Our analysis encompasses static, dynamic, and generalized dynamic factor models, considering factor strength that ranges from strong to semi-strong and semi-weak. Our results show that with strong factors, most estimators across all three classes deliver near-perfect identification when both the cross-section n and time dimension T are large, providing practitioners with a wide set of reliable choices. As factor strength weakens, performance diverges: only a few estimators remain comparatively robust, while other estimators tend to underestimate the true number of factors or shocks, particularly when the idiosyncratic components are not i.i.d. Overall, no single estimator dominates across all settings. Our findings provide practical guidance for applied work and highlight the advantages and limitations of existing methodologies.

detail.title: Artificial intelligence (AI) innovation and economic growth: asymmetric analysis and role of stock market, financial stability and trade openness
detail.abstract: This study examines the asymmetric effect of artificial intelligence (AI) innovation on economic growth in 50 countries from 2000 to 2020 using the quantile regression method. The findings reveal that AI innovation stimulates economic growth at low and middle tail of the economic growth distribution. Interaction analyses reveal that the use of AI innovation in the stock market stimulates economic growth while the use of AI innovation to support financial stability and international trade activities diminish economic growth. Asymmetric interaction analyses reveal that: AI innovation stimulates economic growth when countries are experiencing low growth rates; the use of AI innovation in the stock market stimulates economic growth when countries are experiencing high growth rates and in mid-growth emerging market and developing countries; the use of AI innovation to support financial stability activities diminish economic growth when countries are experiencing low growth rates and the use of AI innovation to support international trade activities diminish economic growth when countries are experiencing high growth rates.
