title: In U.S. Supreme Court, brief of National Assn of Patent Practitioners Inc and PTAAARMIGAN LLC as amici curiae

detail.title: In U.S. Supreme Court, brief of National Assn of Patent Practitioners Inc and PTAAARMIGAN LLC as amici curiae

declarations.declarationOfInterest: none
declarations.ethicsApproval: none
declarations.funderStatement: none

detail.abstract: The Federal Circuit’s presumption that prosecution laches attaches at six years disrupts policy balances set by Congress. In all fields of intellectual property, Congress carefully balances rights between the rightholder, against rights of the public to use nearly-similar subject matter, scope and duration of the right-holder’s right to exclude vs. the public interest in the right to use, lapse dates on which the subject matter passes into the public domain, etc.  Contrarily, the Federal Circuit’s prosecution laches presumption disregards those policy balances, and counts USPTO delay against a six-year clock. Congress allocated the burden of proof in the applicant’s favor; the Federal Circuit proposes to reverse that burden. When Congress draws those policy balances, they occupy the field, and courts have no discretion to coin equitable exceptions.  The Federal Circuit’s six-year presumption is not narrowly tailored to the facts of the case before it; instead the presumption cuts broadly, and falls most harshly on the most-innovative and commercially-important patent applications.

publicationDetails.detailsText: China Finance Review International, volume 12, issue 4, 2022[10.1108/CFRI-08-2021-0172]

detail.abstract: We examine the interest rate pass-through in Hong Kong (HK) and Macao to see if the monetary policy transmission mechanism has been impaired since the Global Financial Crisis (GFC). Our results show that, in the post-GFC period, both the long-run and short-run interest rate pass-through from policy rates to prime rates have disappeared in Macao and weakened significantly in HK. The long-term relationship between deposit rates and policy rates no longer exists in either market while the short-term relationship has been reduced significantly. The results indicate that the effectiveness of the monetary policy in HK and Macao has been seriously undermined after the GFC and alternative monetary policy tools were needed.

title: Vehicle Industry and Circular Economy: Mapping the Global End-of-life Vehicles

detail.title: Vehicle Industry and Circular Economy: Mapping the Global End-of-life Vehicles
detail.abstract: Vehicle industry is significantly improving our life quality and promoting economic development. However, the large number of end-of-life vehicles (ELVs) deserves more attention since many valuable resources are embodied in them. This work predicts ELVs generation for both commercial vehicles and passenger cars in 144 countries. Our results show that while typical developed countries such as the U.S., Japan, Germany, and France peaked their ELVs generation in the 2010s, China has experienced a dramatic increase in generation, with nearly 50 times increase from 2000 to 2020 and since 2020 become the largest generator of ELVs over Japan and the U.S. With the vehicle transition toward electric vehicles, its recycling through a circular economy is facing a new challenge since these ELVs contain different materials and therefore require more specific efforts. Key findings call for global efforts to improve ELVs circular economy through the full implementation of circular economy so that both resource concerns and associated environmental impacts from ELVs can be mitigated.

detail.title: Effects of Expanding Contraceptive Choice: New Evidence from Virginia's Contraceptive Access Initiative

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
In 2018, the Virginia Department of Health implemented the Contraceptive Access Initiative (CAI) to increase access to long-acting reversible contraceptives (LARCs). We use encounter-level data on contraceptive choice in participating CAI clinics and county-level natality data from 2014--2021 to estimate relative changes in LARC take-up and childbearing rates before and after the CAI. Difference-in-differences estimates indicate that the CAI reduced birth rates in participating counties by approximately 3 percent, or less than half of the effect size of other similar, state-level programs. We show that this smaller effect is likely due to existing high LARC take-up and contraceptive substitution.

title: Calibration-Gated Reputation
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Calibration-Gated Reputation
detail.abstract: How can reputation be made unforgeable in pseudonymous systems without external identity infrastructure? We introduce calibration-gated reputation: a mechanism in which agents commit cryptographic hashes of probabilistic predictions, reveal them after a mandatory delay, and accumulate reputation through a strictly proper scoring rule. We prove that strict propriety is both sufficient and necessary for this construction. Our first result (Theorem 3.1) is an impossibility: under any scoring rule that is proper but not strictly proper, a Sybil adversary controlling K identities can produce a wallet whose expected reputation matches that of a genuinely skilled predictor, making merit-based filtering impossible. Under strict propriety, we prove three positive results: (i) no pseudonymous identity proliferation strategy produces a high-calibration score without genuine predictive skill-a property we call merit-gating (Theorem 4.1); (ii) the cost of constructing fake reputation grows at least linearly in the number of Sybil identities (Theorem 4.3); (iii) under temporal decay, each predictor's reputation converges to a unique stationary value that is monotonically increasing in skill (Theorem 4.5). We complement our impossibility result with a second negative result showing that accuracy-only scoring (without calibration) admits polynomialcost Sybil attacks regardless of the number of predictions required (Theorem 3.3). All results are validated through Monte Carlo simulation with 10,000 independent trials. The mechanism is implemented as a protocol on Ethereum Layer 2; a companion technical specification is available separately.

title: Cyclical Behavior in Large Location Games
affiliations: University of California, Santa Barbara (UCSB) - Department of Economics, University of California, Santa Cruz - Department of Economics, University of California, Santa Cruz and University of Wisconsin at Madison - Department of Economics

detail.title: Cyclical Behavior in Large Location Games

declarations.declarationOfInterest: none
declarations.ethicsApproval: UCSC IRB HS3566

detail.abstract: Location games capture important economic phenomena ranging from preemption to choice of bank leverage. We explore a parametric family of location games with many players, each facing a conflict between maximizing a fundamental payoff component and a relative (or quantile dependent) component. Using simulations and human subject experiments we show that, behaviorally, the stationary Nash equilibria in such games are terrible predictions of behavior and payoffs when players can freely adjust their locations. Instead, large cycles consistently emerge, in which behavior slowly grows bolder over time. This corresponds to progressively earlier timing in pre-emption games or to increasingly later timing in wars of attrition. When locations are maximally bold, namely at the end of the domain of Nash play, behavior quickly reverts to the peak fundamental and a new cycle begins.

detail.title: Early Childcare Attendance and Cognitive skills in Adolescence

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
This paper examines the impact of early childcare on academic achievement for children in grade 5 and grade 9, based on a 2003 policy expansion that created quasi-random variation in slot availability for children aged 1–2. Starting childcare one year earlier increases math scores by 9.7% of a standard deviation (SD) in grade 9. Children whose mothers do not hold a high school diploma benefit by a significant 28% of a SD at grade 9, reducing the math achievement gap from children of higher-educated mothers by about one third. We also present evidence of strong improvements for children of immigrants.

Résumé Cette étude analyse la relation entre la croissance économique et le taux directeur en RDC 1990-2023 à l'aide d'un modèle VECM. Les tests de cointégration montrent l'existence d'un équilibre de long terme entre les deux variables, mais les mécanismes d'ajustement révèlent une forte asymétrie : le PIB réagit très faiblement, tandis que le taux directeur ajuste activement les déséquilibres. Les réponses impulsionnelles confirment que la politique monétaire exerce un impact limité sur la croissance, principalement en raison de la dollarisation élevée et de la structure minière de l'économie. Ainsi, le taux directeur joue un rôle stabilisateur, mais n'est pas un moteur de croissance. Pour progresser vers l'émergence d'ici 2030, la RDC devra renforcer les canaux de transmission monétaire, diversifier son économie et mener des réformes structurelles profondes.

detail.title: A lifecycle approach to the link of the saving rate with income inequality

keywords: Labor bargaining power JEL classification: JEL D30

publicationDetails.detailsText: Emerging Markets Finance and Trade, volume 58, issue 14, 4091-4102, 2022 [10.1080/1540496X.2022.2084378]

detail.abstract: Using an extended overlapping generations (OLG) model, we theoretically prove that functional inequality resulting from weak labor bargaining power can be a key driver of high saving rates, as observed in China and other labor-abundant Asian emerging markets. Income distribution that favors capital over labor may attract excess capital investments and hence lead to high saving rates. The link between inequality and saving is especially prominent for the household sector because excess return on capital motivates the working-age population to increase their retirement savings. We also find empirical support for our theoretical predictions using China's sectoral-level data.

title: Educational Architecture: A Human Conditions Theory of Learning System Stability

detail.title: Educational Architecture: A Human Conditions Theory of Learning System Stability
detail.abstract:
Education reform has historically focused on curriculum, instructional practice, and accountability systems used to measure academic performance. While these approaches have generated valuable insights into teaching and learning, they often overlook the upstream conditions that regulate learning itself. Students and educators do not engage in learning within neutral environments; rather, they operate within complex social, emotional, physiological, and institutional contexts that shape their capacity to sustain intellectual engagement. When system conditions across layers are unstable, instructional improvement alone cannot consistently produce positive outcomes.

This article introduces Educational Architecture, a conceptual framework proposing that learning outcomes emerge from the alignment of system conditions across layers within educational systems. These conditions are organized across four interacting domains: distributed ecosystem conditions, governance structures, adult regulatory capacity, and student capacity conditions. Together, these ideas are articulated through the Human Conditions Theory of Education, which conceptualizes learning environments as layered systems whose stability regulates the capacity for sustained intellectual engagement. Drawing on ecological systems theory, motivation theory, and organizational research on institutional coherence, the article argues that learning environments must be understood as human systems whose effectiveness depends on the alignment of system conditions across layers.

Within the student layer, readiness for learning is further specified through the Five Wells Framework, which describes five domains influencing students’ capacity to engage in sustained academic work: physical, emotional, environmental, relational, and cognitive conditions.

The article introduces four conceptual contributions to educational scholarship:

1. Human Conditions Theory of Education — a theoretical framework for examining the environmental foundations of learning systems 

2. Educational Architecture — a systems model describing how system conditions interact across institutional layers 

3. The Five Wells Framework — a model describing domains of student capacity that influence sustained learning engagement 

4. A dual-measurement system consisting of:

   - The Human Conditions Index (HCI), which assesses the stability of environmental conditions influencing learning 

   - The Coherence Index (CI), which evaluates the alignment of system conditions across layers 

Together, these contributions establish a multidimensional framework for understanding, measuring, and designing learning environments capable of sustaining intellectual engagement over time.

title: SWEET POTATO-BASED BIOETHANOL PRODUCTION IN NIGERIA: ECONOMIC POTENTIAL, POLICY CONSTRAINTS AND EXPERIMENTAL VALIDATION OF A RURAL BIOENERGY PATHWAY

detail.title: SWEET POTATO-BASED BIOETHANOL PRODUCTION IN NIGERIA: ECONOMIC POTENTIAL, POLICY CONSTRAINTS AND EXPERIMENTAL VALIDATION OF A RURAL BIOENERGY PATHWAY
detail.abstract: Nigeria has faced and continues to face persistent energy insecurity, high dependence on imported refined petroleum products, and pressure on foreign exchange reserves. In response, bio-ethanol has been identified as a strategic renewable energy that serves as an alternative within national energy policy frameworks. But due to domestic production, it remains limited due to weak industrial capacity, inconsistent policy enforcement, and underdeveloped agricultural value chains. This paper examines the economic and policy feasibility of sweet potatoes (Latin word ipomoea batatas) as a bio-ethanol feedstock in Nigeria. Drawing on established literature on bio-fuel economics, and agricultural energy systems, the study evaluates sweet potato's suitability as a rural bio-energy crop. It also incorporates a preliminary experimental observation conducted by the author (Tobalase da Silva) which provides qualitative validation of fermentation feasibility under low-resource conditions. The findings indicate that sweet potato has a strong technical potential and moderate economic viability under a structured policy support. However, commercialization is constrained by pricing instability, infrastructure deficits and weak coordination between agricultural and energy sectors. The study concludes that sweet potato based ethanol could significantly contribute to rural industrialization and energy diversification if supported by consistent policy instruments and investment incentives.

title: PARALLEL CIVILIZATIONAL EVOLUTIONA Comparative Framework for Understanding the Axial Transformation (c. 500 BCE)
affiliations: New York State Department of Taxation & Finance

detail.title: PARALLEL CIVILIZATIONAL EVOLUTIONA Comparative Framework for Understanding the Axial Transformation (c. 500 BCE)
detail.abstract:
Conventional historical analysis treats civilizations as discrete and geographically bounded entities, obscuring patterns of concurrent systemic transformation across regions. This paper advances a parallel systems framework to examine the period surrounding the 6th–5th century BCE—commonly associated with the Axial Age—as a moment of global structural convergence rather than isolated intellectual development.

Drawing on developments in the Indian subcontinent, China, the Greek world, and the Persian Empire, the study identifies the emergence of domain-specific systems—metaphysical, ethical, rational, and administrative—each addressing distinct dimensions of human organization. Rather than converging in content, these civilizations converged in their level of systemic abstraction and complexity.

The paper argues that this period reflects a transition from mythological explanation (mythos) to structured frameworks of analysis (logos). It proposes that human progress operates through parallel, differentiated responses to shared conditions of social and institutional complexity. This framework offers implications not only for historical interpretation but also for understanding contemporary globally distributed systems, including the modern digital economy.

title: Value Beyond Labor Time: Production and Participation in Contemporary Political Economy
affiliations: and

detail.title: Value Beyond Labor Time: Production and Participation in Contemporary Political Economy

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve human participants, patient data, or identifiable personal information. Ethics approval was therefore not required.

detail.abstract: This paper challenges the contemporary relevance of the Labor Theory of Value (LTV), arguing that labor time no longer provides an adequate metric for value creation in economies structured by automation and digital platforms. As economic activity becomes increasingly mediated by datadriven systems, value depends less on direct labor input and more on the conditions that enable participation in production. To account for this shift, the paper develops a structural framework in which value is modeled as a function of the means of production (Mₚ) and the means of participation (Mπ). While Mₚ captures technological capacity, infrastructure, and data systems, Mπ refers to the institutional, digital, and organizational conditions required to access and engage with these systems, including credentials, connectivity, and network position. By formalizing value as V = f(Mₚ, Mπ), the framework highlights the complementarity between production capacity and participation access. Constraints on participation limit value realization even in the presence of advanced technological systems. Where the Labor Theory of Value relies on socially necessary labor time (SNLT) to measure the quantity of labor required for production, the present framework emphasizes socially necessary participation (SNP) as the condition under which labor becomes economically effective. Within this structure, labor is reinterpreted as a cost-bearing participant that invests in its own participation capacity, thereby blurring the conventional distinction between labor and capital. The analysis extends to surplus allocation through a co-investment framework, in which multiple forms of capital, including human, financial, and technological, generate claims on output. This perspective supports a shift in the analysis of economic justice from post-production redistribution toward pre-distribution, emphasizing the role of participation conditions in shaping economic outcomes.

title: RESEARCH METHODS IN INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS: THE CHALLENGE OF COMPLEXITY
affiliations: Dept of Management, Mays Business School, Texas A&M University and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: RESEARCH METHODS IN INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS: THE CHALLENGE OF COMPLEXITY
detail.abstract:
International business (IB) research is designed to explore and explain the inherent complexity of international business, which arises from the multiplicity of entities, multiplexity of interactions, and dynamism of the global economic system. To analyze this complexity, IB scholars have developed four research lenses-difference, distance, diversity, and disparity-that create not only unique research opportunities for IB scholarship but also unique research methodological challenges. We therefore view complexity as the underlying cause of the unique methodological challenges facing international business research. We offer several recommendations to help IB scholars embrace this complexity and conduct reliable, interesting, and practically relevant research.

title: Modeling Demand-Responsive Pricing for India’s Power Sector: A Scenario-Based Analysis Using the Switch Electricity Planning Model
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and Indian Institute of Technology (IIT), Roorkee

detail.title: Modeling Demand-Responsive Pricing for India’s Power Sector: A Scenario-Based Analysis Using the Switch Electricity Planning Model

declarations.funderStatement: This work was supported by the 2025 MCET Small Grants Program funded by EDF. The authors gratefully acknowledge EDF’s support for and commitment to advancing research in this field.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Environmental Defense Fund Economics Discussion Paper Series, EDF EDP 26-03, April 2026

detail.abstract:
Demand response (DR) is increasingly positioned in India as a low-cost flexibility option to manage peak demand, support the integration of variable renewables, and enable time-of-day (ToD) pricing. Yet policy relevance depends on how DR is represented in planning models and whether it can materially improve reliability and costs under realistic constraints. This report evaluates three DR formulations within the switch planning model optimization framework using a stylized India 2030 test system. The model is implemented as a single load zone (NORTH) with hourly operations represented by a 24-hour profile scaled to a typical year under a fixed, predetermined supply portfolio (coal with CCS, gas with CCS, hydro, solar, wind, nuclear, biomass, batteries, and pumped hydro). Reliability is represented through an unserved-energy slack variable penalized for lost load, used here as a reliability-enforcing modeling parameter. CO₂ is priced at $15/tCO₂.

We compare (1) fixed or inelastic demand, (2) bounded energy-neutral load shifting with a flexible-load module (5% daily and 3% annual shiftable shares), and (3) endogenous price-responsive demand using a quadratic-utility function with an explicit DR program cost, allowing economically optimal curtailment in scarcity hours. Under the fixed-demand baseline, the system is structurally supply-constrained, yields 99.37 TWh/yr of energy not served (ENS), non-served energy share (NENS) of 13.67%, and a peak shortfall of 35.99 GW. Flexible loads improve reliability only partially (ENS 74.08 TWh/yr; NENS 10.19%; peak shortfall 30.65 GW), indicating that limited energy-neutral shifting cannot resolve multi-hour adequacy deficits. Price-responsive elastic demand produces the largest improvement (ENS 20.34 TWh/yr; NENS 2.80%; peak shortfall 9.14 GW) by allowing economically optimal demand reduction in scarcity hours. However, its objective is welfare-based and not directly comparable to cost-only cases.

Overall, the results suggest that DR benefits are highly sensitive to modeling choices and are constrained when adequacy is dominated by firm capacity limits. For policy, ToD pricing and DR programs should be assessed alongside complementary adequacy measures, and reporting should include reliability, costs, emissions, and explicit storage behavior metrics to avoid overstating flexibility impacts under scarcity-driven outcomes. These scenario results should be interpreted as estimates of technical DR potential under stylized response assumptions rather than forecasts of achievable real-world uptake. In practice, participation barriers, behavioral frictions, metering limitations, and institutional constraints would likely reduce the magnitude of observed impacts.

title: The Biodiversity of Singra Sal (Shorea robusta) Forests in North-western Bangladesh: Anthropogenic Disturbances
affiliations: Information and Communication Technology Division

detail.title: The Biodiversity of Singra Sal (Shorea robusta) Forests in North-western Bangladesh: Anthropogenic Disturbances

publicationDetails.detailsText: A keynote presented at the Regional Public Administration Training Centre (RPATC), 28 April, Dhaka, Bangladesh

detail.abstract: The overarching objective of the study was to explore the flora and fauna of the unexplored Singra Sal forests in Northwestern Bangladesh. The anthropogenic disturbances on the biodiversity were assessed. The study also aimed to evaluate the ecological impacts of anthropogenic disturbances. To do so, data was collected from the Singra Sal forests, the last abode of the natural ecosystem in that district. It was found that the forests were dominated by Sal tree (Shorea robusta), covering ~70-80% of the canopy, followed by associates like Arjun (Terminalia arjuna), Indian Nettle (Celtis australis), Madhuca (Madhuca indica), Jarul (Lagerstroemia speciosa), Rokto Kanchan (Bauhinia variegate), Lal Shimul (Salmalia malabarica), and others. The understory of the Singra Sal forests also supported a variety of shrubs, grasses, and medicinal plants. Some notable species included Babla (Acacia nilotica), Tridhara (Tridax procumbens), Shonpata (Crotalaria spp.), Bermuda grass (Cynodon dactylon) and Kalmegh (Andrographis paniculate). The Spotted deer (Axis axis) and the wild boar (Sus scrofa) were very rarely spotted, while the Barking deer (Muntiacus muntjak) became locally extinct. Among other mammals, the jackal (Canis aureus), Indian fox (Vulpes bengalensis), Jungle cat (Felis chaus), Hanuman langur (Semnopithecus entellus), Rhesus macaque (Macaca mulatta), squirrels, mongoose, civets, bats, and rodents were occasionally found in this forest. Among reptiles and amphibians, monitor lizard (Varanus bengalensis), cobras, kraits, rat snakes, vine snakes, skinks and geckos, frogs and toads were spotted in the moist areas. Many bird species were found occasionally. The forests suffered huge losses in biodiversity due to anthropogenic disturbances. Various conservation measures have been advocated.

title: Career Equity Model (CEM): A Meritocratic Redistribution Framework for Professional Football Transfers
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and

detail.title: Career Equity Model (CEM): A Meritocratic Redistribution Framework for Professional Football Transfers

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing interests. This research received no external funding and was conducted independently.

detail.abstract:
FIFA's Solidarity Contribution Mechanism, established under the Regulations on the Status and Transfer of Players (RSTP), distributes 5% of international transfer fees across a player's former training clubs based on registration years between ages 12 and 23. However, this system, despite aiming to reward every club involved in the development of a player's professional career, systematically concentrates value at the selling club regardless of developmental contribution from former clubs. It considers neither critical aspects such as league quality nor competitive performances while excluding the pre-age-12 development stage completely.
While demonstrating the mechanism's structural inadequacy, this paper introduces Career Equity Model (CEM), a meritocratic redistribution framework that considers the complete career history of a player and calculates the development contribution of each club within. CEM creates a career-indexed equity pool using six key variables: days under contract, competitive minutes, league points finish, FIFA/UEFA ranking coefficient, developmental tier, and continental participation. The equity pool is proportionally redistributed across all former clubs based on development contribution at the point of transfer. 
This paper presents case simulation for three of the most common archetypes in the modern market using three of the biggest recent football transfers: Florian Wirtz (€125M), Erling Haaland (€60M), and Moisés Caicedo (€116M). CEM recovered significant value for grassroots and youth clubs with developmental contributions and produced significantly different distributions from the existing system, where those clubs received minimal compensation.
Across all three cases, developmental clubs that contributed to 79.52% of combined career years received only 2.11% of combined transfer fees under RSTP, compared to 52.66% under CEM. This shift narrows the distributional gap between developmental and selling clubs from 94.75 percentage points to 5.32 percentage points, with the entire €152.16M redistribution flowing within the existing transaction value. 
The Career Equity Model (CEM) is designed to comply with the existing FIFA Clearing House and Electronic Player Passport infrastructure, and it does not require any new implementation or structural architectural overhaul.

title: Unstable Evidence, Stable Conclusion: A Critique of the GDP Overestimation Thesis of Anand, Felman, and Subramanian (2026)
affiliations: and

detail.title: Unstable Evidence, Stable Conclusion: A Critique of the GDP Overestimation Thesis of Anand, Felman, and Subramanian (2026)
detail.abstract: The Peterson Institute working paper by Anand et al. (2026) claims that Indian GDP growth has been overestimated by 1.5 to 1.9 percentage points per year over 2011 to 2023, with an implied level overstatement of 22 percent as of 2025. The paper is a direct continuation of the thesis advanced in Subramanian (2019), a Harvard working paper in which Subramanian (a co-author on the 2026 paper) argued the same position as sole author seven years earlier. This paper establishes that the 2026 magnitude claim is not supported by the evidence presented. Six findings support this conclusion. First, of the seventeen macro indicators the 2019 paper used to establish post-2011 correlation breakdown, thirteen are absent from the 2026 paper; on the extended 2012 to 2024 window, ten of the eleven indicators flagged by the 2019 paper as negatively correlated with GDP show positive correlation, including IIP Manufacturing, whose divergence from formal manufacturing GVA the 2019 paper used to argue for a substantial portion of the overall overestimation (on the order of 1 percentage point), and which now correlates with GDP at 0.92. Second, the informal sector contribution of 0.4 to 0.8 percentage points is computed as a compound annual growth rate between the NSS 73rd Round (2015 to 2016) and ASUSE 2023 to 2024, separated by a six year gap and by a change in survey instrument, sampling frame, and coverage. Third, the sales to GVA wedge presented as independent evidence is partly mechanical: the wedge correlates with the CPI to WPI gap at 0.81 by construction, because corporate sales are deflated by CPI while GVA is deflated substantially by WPI. Fourth, none of the five correlation changes in the paper's Figure 2 reaches statistical significance under the standard Fisher r-to-z test, and the reported India dummy in the cross country regression falls by 24 percent when two excluded observations are added back. Fifth, the 2026 paper reverses five specific positions from the 2019 paper without acknowledgment: on double deflation (from core mechanism to "relatively minor problem"), on the scope and weight of the informal sector channel (from narrowly-defined informal manufacturing ruled out for the baseline sample period to the full informal economy as a primary mechanism), on tax indicators (from excluded as "unreliable" to headline indicator), on magnitude (from 2.5 percentage points to 1.5 to 1.9, entirely within the lower half of the 2019 paper's reported 95 percent confidence interval of 1.5 to 3.5), and on the indicator set itself. Sixth, post-2020 tax performance contradicts the overestimation thesis: nonoil tax growth of 14.9 percent against nominal GDP growth of 10.5 percent yields a buoyancy of 1.4 that the paper's Appendix C attempts to explain through composition effects that, if true, imply aggregate nominal growth above official figures rather than below. The headline claim has remained stable across seven years and two papers; the indicators, mechanisms, decomposition, and magnitude supporting it have not. The pattern is conclusion-anchoring, not evidence-following.

title: Living Wage Benchmarks: Sri Lanka's Tea Estate and Urban Sectors, 2022-2025
affiliations: Sri Lanka Institute of Information Technology

detail.title: Living Wage Benchmarks: Sri Lanka's Tea Estate and Urban Sectors, 2022-2025

keywords: purchasing power parity JEL Codes: J31

detail.abstract: This paper examines the conceptual and empirical linkages between living wage estimates, cost of living measurements, and social policy, with specific application to Sri Lanka. Drawing on the International Labour Organization's normative definition and the Anker methodology, we analyze how living wage benchmarks translate a "basic but decent" consumption basket into a monthly wage requirement. Sri Lankan estimates for the tea estate sector (LKR 48,584 gross monthly) and urban areas (LKR 115,291 gross monthly as of June 2025) are presented and compared with regional PPP-based benchmarks such as the Asia Floor Wage. The analysis highlights significant gaps between prevailing wages and living wage thresholds, particularly after the 2022-2023 inflationary crisis. We conclude that living wage frameworks offer rigorous, rights-based tools for wage policy, social protection, and development planning, though careful attention must be paid to methodological transparency, updating frequency, and macroeconomic feasibility.

title: Teaching Case: Improving Government Operations with Large Language Models

detail.title: Teaching Case: Improving Government Operations with Large Language Models
detail.abstract: This fictionalized teaching case examines a real managerial problem at the intersection of artificial intelligence, public administration, and professional responsibility. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly attractive for government operations because they can reconcile messy, unstructured, and inconsistent data across disconnected systems, including records held by (for example, in the US) the Internal Revenue Service, Medicaid, Social Security, and other agencies. Yet these same systems can also hallucinate, project unwarranted confidence, and produce consequential errors unless subject to careful human oversight. This case centers on a consulting firm asked to lead a high-value government engagement to build AI-enabled data infrastructure supporting immigration enforcement, citizenship verification, and benefits screening. It also highlights a set of concrete design choices, including whether the LLM would merely reconcile records and flag discrepancies or would go further by drafting recommendations, escalating files, or prioritizing cases for review. In doing so, it raises a broader question that extends well beyond this particular context: how should firms evaluate lucrative opportunities when technical capability, legal authority, political controversy, reputational exposure, and the risk of serious human harm all converge? This case is designed to prompt discussion about: management judgment, implementation risk, organizational ethics, and the limits of policy neutrality in professional service firms.

title: Construction Intelligence (CI-DF) as a Decision Science: A Spatial-Temporal Adaptive Framework for Engineering Project Contracting
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Construction Intelligence (CI-DF) as a Decision Science: A Spatial-Temporal Adaptive Framework for Engineering Project Contracting

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve human participants or clinical data. Ethical approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received for this research.

detail.abstract: This study introduces SAITCO / Construction Intelligence Decision Framework (CI-DF) as an integrated construction intelligence ecosystem that transforms engineering project contracting from fragmented, document-based, experiencedriven practice into an adaptive, decision-centric, self-learning digital intelligence system operating across the full project lifecycle. The paper argues that persistent problems of cost overrun, payment delay, weak qualification, reactive claims, and construction disputes are not isolated failures; they are symptoms of a missing decision architecture across the project lifecycle. The proposed framework establishes Construction Decision Theory (CDT), where each project is treated as a dynamic system governed by data, constraints, objectives, and uncertainty. CI-DF integrates SCIM, CDS, PLDS, GACM, SECIM, DCIM, and CPOM. A central contribution is the principle that system validity does not mean producing the same price or decision everywhere; rather, validity means producing contextually correct outputs for each location, time, currency, market, resource environment, and risk profile. The framework is conceptually validated through five applied cases: a financial dispute and residual claim, a risk-adjusted pricing and contractual safeguard case, a project delivery and claims-recovery portfolio case, an organizational structuring and qualification readiness case, and a cost intelligence / BOQ analysis case. The cross-case analysis demonstrates that construction disputes are delayed manifestations of earlier decision failures and that cost is not the final output of construction intelligence, but one of its decision inputs. This paper introduces a fundamental principle: construction system validity is defined by contextual correctness rather than uniform outputs across different environments.

title: Algorithmic Nudging for Energy Savings and Environment: Evidence from an IoT Platform
affiliations: , University of Calgary - Haskayne School of Business, Ohio State University (OSU) - Fisher College of Business and University of North Carolina (UNC) at Chapel Hill - Kenan-Flagler Business School

detail.title: Algorithmic Nudging for Energy Savings and Environment: Evidence from an IoT Platform
detail.abstract:
Problem definition: Organizations are increasingly seeking innovative approaches to reduce energy consumption, with real-time algorithmic nudging emerging as a promising solution. Although nudges are shown to influence the behaviors of individual customers and households, their effects in commercial settings remain largely underexplored, particularly in environments where managers lack direct financial incentives to conserve energy. In this study, we empirically examine how real-time algorithmic alerts affect energy use in such a commercial context.

Methodology/results: We collaborate with one of Europe’s largest Internet of Things (IoT) energy platforms, which collects and monitors real-time electricity consumption data for organizations. When a facility’s energy use exceeds an algorithmically determined, dynamically updated threshold, the system generates an alert notifying managers of unusual usage. Using a rich IoT dataset from the retail sector, we show that receiving an alert leads to a 16% reduction in a store’s energy consumption in the subsequent hour, establishing the effectiveness o f algorithmic nudging in business environments where managers lack direct financial incentives to conserve energy. Unlike the prevailing view in the energy conservation literature, we find a distinct U-shaped relationship between the number of alerts and energy consumption in our commercial setting: energy use initially declines as alerts accumulate, but beyond a threshold, additional alerts are associated with higher consumption. This pattern reveals a fundamental design trade-off. Although real-time alerts generate immediate energy savings, issuing more alerts does not necessarily yield greater benefits for organizations or the environment; excessive alerting can erode effectiveness.

Managerial implications: Our results show that IoT-based nudging can effectively reduce organizations’ energy consumption and emissions, even in the absence of financial incentives for managers to do so. At the same time, its effectiveness depends on thoughtful implementation. These findings highlight the importance of careful design to avoid unintended consequences for organizations.

detail.title: Exploring the Legacies of Small and Medium-Sized Cultural Festivals: Evidence from a Qualitative Study

publicationDetails.detailsText: Venice School of Management - Department of Management Working Paper No. 6
publicationDetails.journalName: Venice School of Management - Department of Management Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
This study applies a hybrid thematic analysis to examine the long-term consequences of small and mediumsized
cultural festivals on host territories. It adopts a qualitative exploratory design based on semi-structured
interviews with festival organizers and stakeholders. Drawing on the framework developed by Preuss (2019),
the findings identify five interconnected domains of structural change; human, social, intellectual,
institutional, and environmental; which give rise to differentiated forms of legacy, predominantly cultural,
social, and economic. The evidence highlights the central role of festivals in fostering skills development,
cultural participation, and network formation, while long-term consequences in urban, environmental, and
institutional domains emerge more limited. 

This research advances event legacy literature by building on Preuss (2019) distinction between structural
changes and legacy within the context of cultural festivals, explicitly linking the two dimensions through an
empirical analysis. In doing so, it proposes a more systematic framework for investigating long-term effects
of events in non-mega-event settings. The study further expands the empirical scope of legacy research by
focusing on underexplored provincial contexts, showing how festivals contribute to human capital formation,
cultural diffusion, community building, and pathways to employability. The findings also provide practical
insights for organizers, emphasizing the role of data collection, youth engagement, continuous educational
initiatives, and multi-level collaboration in enhancing the enduring value of cultural festivals.

title: Anticipating corporate emissions depending on the ambition and early action of companies
affiliations: , University of Orleans - Laboratoire d'économie d'Orléans and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Anticipating corporate emissions depending on the ambition and early action of companies
detail.abstract: Anticipating future corporate greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions has tremendous potential to help develop cost-efficient long-term investment strategies and to assess climate risks for companies. Traditional projections mainly rely on global estimates broken down by sector and firm characteristics, but they overlook information contained in firms' own decarbonization strategies. In the meantime, many companies have set climate targets that specify their intended emission reductions over different time horizons. This paper presents a methodology to integrate these pledges into firm-level emission projections by aligning them with climate scenario-consistent abatement pathways. By doing so, this method provides a clearer view of future economy-wide emissions and of the stringency of corporate climate strategies. To account for the extent to which firms' GHG trajectories support or contradict their ambitions, we introduce a metric, called "carbon credibility", that reflects the recent evolution of their emissions relative to their stated targets. This measure serves both as an early indicator of target feasibility and as an adjustment factor in forward-looking projections. Accounting for the carbon credibility of nearly 300 STOXX 600 companies increases projected cumulative GHG emissions through 2050 by almost 5%. Credibility values indicate that half of the sectors in the panel fall short of the efforts required to align with their decarbonization ambition. These results imply higher expected climate risks and call for enhanced corporate actions.

title: Which Patents Go Open? External Value, Internal Value, and the Patent Licensing Decision
affiliations: SICIP,Tongji University, Beihang University (BUAA) and Tongji University

detail.title: Which Patents Go Open? External Value, Internal Value, and the Patent Licensing Decision
detail.abstract: Open patent licensing (OPL) systems aim to promote technology diffusion by incentivizing patent owners to declare their technologies available for non-exclusive licensing. This paper evaluates China's Open Patent Licensing system which is designed to screen out opportunistic declarations from low-value patents. Using the OPL declarations and a matched sample of comparable non-declared patents, we first show that corporate patentees are more likely to declare OPL for patents with higher external value. Participation is highly heterogeneous across owner types: small and medium enterprises (SMEs) declare a substantially larger share of their portfolios than large firms and universities. Second, we use a misclassification model to unpack the false open and the false non-open decisions. The results indicate that SMEs, despite few strategic incentives to withhold, exhibit markedly higher false non-open rates, suggesting that many potentially licensable patents remain undeclared. Additionally, we show that within-firm continuation development and accumulated commercialization experience are systematically associated with these deviation patterns. Managerial implications: Firms, especially SMEs, can improve licensing outcomes by adopting more structured portfolio triage (combining market signals such as external forward citations with internal indicators of follow-on development such as self-forward citations) to identify which patents to declare under OPL and which to retain for internal commercialization.

detail.abstract:
Italian Abstract: La Banca d’Italia ha stipulato un Accordo di collaborazione con l’Agenzia nazionale per le nuove tecnologie, l’energia e lo sviluppo economico sostenibile (ENEA) per stimare la variazione delle emissioni di gas serra e dei consumi di energia conseguenti all’adozione di un’organizzazione flessibile del lavoro. Nell’ambito del progetto, nel 2023 è stato elaborato e somministrato ai dipendenti della Banca un questionario volto a valutare gli impatti ambientali del modello di lavoro ibrido, introdotto nel 2022, in cui la prestazione a distanza si integra con quella in presenza. L’analisi delle 4.255 risposte, raccolte tra i dipendenti sia dell’Amministrazione centrale a Roma e Frascati, sia presso 38 Filiali presenti sul territorio nazionale, ha consentito di stimare, sulla base dell’evidenza empirica, l’impatto ambientale degli spostamenti casa-lavoro dei dipendenti e degli extra consumi domestici di energia connessi con il lavoro da remoto, finora poco studiati in letteratura. Tenendo conto anche dei giorni lavorati a distanza, le emissioni medie pro-capite per gli spostamenti casa-lavoro dei dipendenti risultano pari a 4,1 chilogrammi di anidride carbonica equivalente (kgCO2e) per ogni giornata di lavoro in ufficio (4,8 il dato calcolato nel 2020, prima dell’introduzione del modello). Le emissioni connesse agli extra consumi domestici legati al riscaldamento, al raffrescamento e all’utilizzo del computer e dell’illuminazione risultano pari a 1,1 kgCO2e per una giornata di lavoro da remoto. Il lavoro fornisce inoltre una stima delle emissioni medie connesse agli extra consumi domestici di energia per un giorno di lavoro a distanza, suddivise per zona climatica, potenzialmente utilizzabile da altre aziende e istituzioni per il calcolo delle emissioni indirette di gas serra (Scope 3) connesse con il pendolarismo dei dipendenti.
English Abstract: The study estimates the variation in greenhouse gas emissions resulting from the adoption of a flexible work organization, using data from a survey conducted among Banca d’Italia’s employees and a calculation tool developed by the Italian National Agency for New Technologies, Energy and Sustainable Economic Development (ENEA). The average per-capita GHG emissions for employees’ home-to-work commuting were found to be 4.1 kilograms of carbon dioxide equivalent (kgCO₂e) for each day worked in the office. GHG emissions associated with additional household energy consumption due to heating, cooling, computer use and lighting amount to 1.1 kgCO₂e for one day of remote work. Overall, the use of remote work had a net positive impact on the environment. The study also provides an estimate of the average GHG emissions due to increased domestic energy consumption for one day of remote work, broken down by climate zone, which can potentially be used by other companies and institutions to calculate the Scope 3 GHG emissions associated with remote work.

detail.abstract: The paper examines the capacity of higher education institutions to withstand and recover from violent conflict, using the University of Science and Technology (UST) in Omdurman Tagana, Sudan, as a case study (AD Scientific Index, 2025). Following a devastating attack by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) during the 2023 civil war, UST sustained catastrophic physical and financial damage (Sudan Tribune, 2026). This study analyzes the nature and extent of the destruction, the university's multi-faceted recovery strategy, and its subsequent efforts to diversify its operations. Through a review of available reports and literature on post-conflict higher education (Elhag & Baleela, 2024; Center for International Higher Education, 2025), the paper identifies key factors that enabled UST's recuperation, including the formation of rapid damage assessment committees, the utilization of multiple campuses to maintain operations, and the cultivation of partnerships for reconstruction (AllAfrica, 2024). The university's experience underscores the critical role of strategic planning, institutional flexibility, and multi-stakeholder engagement in rebuilding and reimagining higher education in fragile and conflict-affected states.

title: Rethinking Brokerage Enforcement in International Trade: The Institutional Brokerage Protection Architecture (IBPA)

detail.title: Rethinking Brokerage Enforcement in International Trade: The Institutional Brokerage Protection Architecture (IBPA)

detail.abstract:
This paper develops a conceptual framework addressing a persistent structural problem in international trade: the failure to enforce brokerage entitlements in intermediary-driven transactions. Rather than attributing this issue to contractual deficiencies, the study argues that enforcement failures arise from the absence of embedded mechanisms within transaction execution.

Drawing on institutional theory and transaction cost economics, the paper introduces the Institutional Brokerage Protection Architecture (IBPA), a multi-layer framework integrating identity verification, capability-based validation, transaction structuring, and payment-linked enforcement. As a conceptual contribution, the study proposes the notion of qualified financial validation, enabling financial institutions to verify transactional capability without disclosing sensitive information.

The framework shifts the focus from contract-based enforcement to structural transaction design, offers practical pathways for implementation within existing trade finance systems, and outlines directions for future empirical validation.

detail.abstract: Recent reports indicate that Meta and Microsoft may reduce or reshape thousands of positions while simultaneously increasing capital commitments to artificial intelligence infrastructure. Meta is reportedly preparing to cut approximately 8,000 employees and close roughly 6,000 open roles, while Microsoft is reportedly offering voluntary redundancy or retirement options to long-serving U.S. employees. These developments should not be viewed only as cost-cutting decisions. From the perspective of Ansoff's Strategic Success Hypothesis, the layoffs represent a broader strategic posture adjustment amid elevated environmental turbulence. Artificial intelligence has increased the speed, novelty, complexity, and unpredictability of competition in the technology sector. As a result, firms must align strategic aggressiveness and capability responsiveness with the external technological environment. This article introduces a Trend-Based Reality Benchmark to compare technological advancement trends with management perception and action. The framework helps identify three strategic gaps: the Environmental Turbulence Level (ETL) gap, the Strategic Aggressiveness gap, and the Capability Responsiveness gap. The article argues that Big Tech may not be suffering from a lack of strategic ambition, but from the difficulty of transforming organizational capability quickly enough to match the speed of AI-driven turbulence.

detail.abstract: Generative AI changes platform ecosystems not only by expanding complement supply, but also by making surface plausibility cheap to manufacture. I develop a theory in which a platform allocates scarce exposure between a verified trusted lane and a protected exploration lane, while complementors choose substantive effort, AI-enabled polish, and verification. When AI raises the return to polish faster than the return to substance, complementors privately overinvest in mimicry and underuse verification. The platform's optimal response is often neither openness nor closure but selective permeability: more trusted exposure combined with a protected exploratory frontier. A theory-guided computational application shows that this hybrid architecture becomes optimal in most post-AI categories and materially outperforms openness and closure in discovery-rich environments.

detail.title: Intermediate Input Prices and the Labor Share

detail.abstract:
We argue that the relative price of materials is an important determinant of the labor share of income. When materials and primary inputs are complements and the profit share is positive, a higher price of materials lowers the labor share and raises the profit share of value added, without requiring markups or returns to scale to change. We show that materials-price fluctuations align with U.S. labor-share trends, provide causal evidence on this mechanism across industries and commuting zones, and quantify its importance in a dynamic quantitative model. Finally, we use our mechanism to rationalize differential labor-share trends across countries.

detail.abstract:
This paper argues that the global climate-mobility policy regime is rapidly expanding yet fundamentally under-evaluated, and proposes a strategic framework for rigorous impact evaluation of climate-related mobility and displacement interventions. Drawing on recent case studies of planned relocation, internal labor-mobility programs, and regional free-movement schemes, we synthesize best practices and identify persistent gaps in causal identification, longitudinal monitoring, and rights-based evaluation. 
The paper makes three original contributions: (1) a typology of "climate-mobility policy experiments" amenable to quasi-experimental evaluation; (2) a critique of securitized and technocratic governance designs that systematically undervalue participation and immobility; and (3) a set of concrete, actionable recommendations for embedding impact evaluation into national climate-action plans and global climate-finance architecture. 
The paper calls for a paradigm shift in which climate-mobility governance is explicitly treated as a policy experiment field, with evaluation embedded from design to implementation, to ensure that migration remains a rights-based adaptation strategy rather than a crisis-managed burden.

detail.abstract: I develop a model-based definition of time-varying sovereign bond safety and apply it empirically by constructing a news-based index, the flight-to-safety index (FLY), which measures global safe-asset demand. The FLY captures flight-to-safety episodes, the savings glut, and natural interest rate declines. Estimated FLY loadings allow the classification of bonds as safe, neutral, or risky. Post-Great-Recession, the global set of safe assets has shrunk, but the safety of US assets has increased. I detect regime switches in FLY loadings: positive switches (becoming safe) align with expansions, higher government spending, lower debt, and credit upgrades; negative switches (becoming risky) are associated with contractions, reduced spending, higher debt, and downgrades.

title: Beyond Accuracy: A Validation Framework for Machine Learning in Cryptocurrency Trading

detail.title: Beyond Accuracy: A Validation Framework for Machine Learning in Cryptocurrency Trading

detail.abstract:
Machine learning strategies for cryptocurrency trading routinely report exceptional backtest results, yet practitioners consistently fail to replicate them. We identify three systematic failure modes—directional prediction bias, statistical-economic disconnect, and transaction cost omission—through 340 strategy variants across four timeframes and three cryptocurrency assets. To address these failures, we propose VALID (Validation Architecture for Learning-based Investment Decisions), a 12-item reporting and validation framework for financial ML research—the first domain-specific checklist for this field.

We demonstrate that gradient-boosted models predict long 90–97% of the time without class balancing; that standard validation tools (PBO = 0, permutation p = 0) cannot distinguish exploitable signals from noise; and that transaction costs consume 55–91% of gross alpha. Monte Carlo analysis (200 iterations) shows 27% false positive rates for AUC-based validation alone, reduced to 0% by CPCV with PBO. We provide the first empirical confirmation of Witzany's (2021) PBO critique through null-distribution analysis. A systematic audit of 80 papers reveals that the median study satisfies only 2.5 of 12 VALID items. We release an open-source implementation for reproducibility.

detail.abstract: Central banks increasingly rely on large volumes of policy documents—ranging from monetary policy statements to regulatory guidelines and internal reports—to communicate decisions and maintain institutional accountability. These documents help ground decisions in the most up-to-date economic signals, support internal coordination and strengthen transparency toward markets and the public. Yet their complexity and frequency impose significant administrative and analytical burdens. The emergence of agentic AI, which combines large language models with autonomous goal setting, structured workflows and tool-calling capabilities, offers the potential to automate key tasks such as drafting, summarization, cross-document consistency checks, integration with data sources and the generation of tables and figures. In this paper, we address the question posed in the title by examining the role that recent advances in AI—enhanced by agent-based architectures and coordinated task execution—can play in central bank workflows. We present two simple, ground-up examples showing how open-source tools can be leveraged effectively while keeping development and operating costs under control. The paper concludes by discussing how agentic AI could reshape document processing practices within central banks, highlighting both the efficiency gains and the governance safeguards required for its trustworthy adoption.

detail.abstract:
Aims: To analyse the competitiveness and structural shifts in India's marine product exports over 2004-05 to 2023-24, addressing the gap in understanding long-run market transition patterns using RCA and Markov Chain techniques. 

Methodology: The study uses RCA to evaluate comparative advantage across major marine product categories such as frozen shrimp, frozen fish, cuttle fish, squid, and other products. Markov Chain analysis is applied to examine the direction and stability of export markets, focusing on transition probabilities among major importing regions.

Results: The RCA analysis indicates a strong and consistent comparative advantage in frozen shrimp exports throughout the study period (RCA ranging from 3.08 to 5.27), while other product categories show either temporary or persistent comparative disadvantage (RCA < 1). This reflects a structural dependence on shrimp in India’s marine export basket. Markov Chain results reveal varying degrees of market retention, with South East Asia (0.3306) and China (0.1221) emerging as relatively stable and increasingly significant markets. In contrast, traditional destinations such as the United States and the European Union exhibit more dynamic and shifting patterns. The long-term trends suggest gradual diversification of export destinations and stronger regional integration within Asian markets.

Conclusion: The study highlights the need for diversification, value addition, infrastructure development, and targeted market strategies to sustain export competitiveness and reduce risks associated with product and market concentration. These findings suggest the need for diversification beyond shrimp, strengthening value addition in underperforming segments, and consolidating trade relations with emerging Asian markets.

detail.abstract: We examine how foreign aid relates to citizens' trust in political institutions by combining geocoded information on development projects with geolocated survey data from 22 countries in Eastern Europe and Central Asia (2010-2016). Motivated by the idea that locally visible interventions may generate signals about domestic institutional performance, we exploit spatial proximity and variation in the timing of project implementation to compare individuals residing near projects implemented prior to the survey with individuals residing near projects implemented only later, and complement this design with within-municipality difference-indifferences estimates. Exposure to implemented aid projects is associated with higher trust in a broad set of political institutions. This relationship varies systematically with time since implementation and is sharply heterogeneous across project types and institutional environments. Socially oriented interventions are most strongly linked to trust in political institutions, and the positive relationship is concentrated in countries with lower levels of democratic consolidation, while it is muted in more consolidated democracies. These findings suggest that locally visible development interventions can shape institutional trust in ways that depend on regime context.

reference: NBER Working Paper No. w35115
title: On the Resilience of Payment Methods
affiliations: University of Chicago - Department of Economics, Yale University and Yale University

detail.title: On the Resilience of Payment Methods

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
We study the resilience of payment systems to large disruptions in digital infrastructure caused by natural disasters and outages. While advanced economies have rapidly shifted toward electronic payments, these systems depend critically on electricity and information technology, raising concerns about their reliability during crises. We combine high-frequency county-level electricity outage data with detailed weather records, transaction-level expenditure data, household scanner data, and new representative surveys from the United States, Spain, and Sweden. Event-study evidence shows that natural disasters---especially hurricanes---generate persistent outages that sharply reduce expenditures. Natural disasters by themselves do not alter households' choice of payment method; instead, shifts toward cash arise through three channels: electronic payment methods become unavailable, households increase cash holdings for precautionary reasons, and cash is subsequently spent once available ("cash burn"). Consistent with these mechanisms, payment composition shifts markedly: spending rises before disasters due to stockpiling, largely financed with credit, while after disasters digital payments decline and cash usage rises, particularly in areas experiencing outages. Survey evidence confirms that nearly half of consumers are unable to use their preferred electronic payment during outages and that cash serves as a key fallback. Exploiting variation in cash holdings across households and locations, we find that greater access to cash increases the likelihood of completing transactions during outages and mitigates expenditure declines. Complementary survey evidence and the immediate response to our information treatment show that outages and official guidance increase desired cash holdings. Finally, we embed an RCT in the NielsenIQ panel: roughly half of panel households receive authoritative preparedness guidance, and we follow their realized purchases through the subsequent hurricane season. This design provides a clean framework for causal identification of whether greater cash preparedness smooths consumption during weather shocks. Together, the observational, survey, and experimental components of the paper show that cash plays a critical role in sustaining economic activity during payment-system disruptions and point to the value of offline-capable payment instruments, including CBDCs, in increasingly digital economies.

Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.

reference: NBER Working Paper No. w35117
title: Does Employment Slow Cognitive Decline? Evidence from Labor Market Shocks
affiliations: University of California, Irvine, University of California, Irvine - Department of Economics and University of California, Irvine - Program in Public Health

detail.title: Does Employment Slow Cognitive Decline? Evidence from Labor Market Shocks

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
With large gains in life expectancy, the population share of disability due to cognitive decline and dementia has substantially increased. Many older adults in the United States leave the workforce well before age 65. Correlational evidence suggests that leaving the workforce before retirement age could accelerate the pace of cognitive decline. We offer causal evidence, using HRS data for the United States, exploiting plausibly exogenous shifts in labor demand in local labor markets as a Bartik instrument for employment variation across these markets. We find substantial declines over time in cognitive scores stemming from negative labor demand shocks. These findings are concentrated among men aged 51 to 64, whose employment decisions and outcomes may be more sensitive to local labor market conditions than are these decisions or outcomes for women or for older men. Our evidence extends past work focusing narrowly on the retirement age window and provides further support to the notion that working to older ages may delay age-related cognitive decline.

title: Upcycling and Patent law: finding the contours for Social Innovation and sustainability
affiliations: University of Copenhagen

detail.title: Upcycling and Patent law: finding the contours for Social Innovation and sustainability

declarations.declarationOfInterest: NA
declarations.ethicsApproval: NA
declarations.funderStatement: NA

detail.abstract: The move towards Social innovation is increasingly gaining strength within the UN sustainable development (SDG) goals for 2030. Upcycling forms a part of social innovation in reassessing existing innovation and transforming them value added invention making them socially useful and sustainable for the long run. In contrast to this patent laws protect inventions that are new, inventive and susceptible of industrial application. While this can also contribute to social innovation goals, the question is how far patent laws may enhance or hamper the use or exploitation of such upcycled inventions. In addition it also raises a related question as to whether patents as a system to enhance innovation could be used to incentivize upcycled inventions. The notion of upcycling is innately different from mere repair. Upcycling offers to revitalize old materials to find new ways of using it. This adds the value for the upcycled product. The foundation of patent law rests on the quid pro quo of disclosure of an invention in the interest of the society in exchange for the exclusivity offered by law. Patent law not only protects new inventions but also protects new uses of existing products. However, in many jurisdictions such as EU the new use is limited to known substance or composition. In contrast patent laws in other prominent jurisdictions like USA offers a better scope for considering any new and useful improvement to any existing inventions so long as they meet other stands of patentability. While there is no uniformity in approach to upcycled and transformative uses under patent law both in EU and USA, there is a growing jurisprudence on altered use of patented products that could have implications for value added transformation of existing inventions. This chapter aims to examine the foundation of upcyclying and its implications for patent law. In this effort part I of the chapter will examine the concept of Novelty as a requirement under patent law and how it impacts the approach to upcycling; Part II will examine the judicial discussions from a European and comparative perspective on the intersection of patent law and reconstructive use and finally Part III will identify the policy considerations for encouraging and incentivising upcycled inventions for global justice. In finding a role for intellectual property rights in sustainable development, this chapter will specifically consider the impact of patent law in supporting social innovation.

title: Profit shifting via intragroup lending: measuring and comparing the debt structure and interest rate channels
affiliations: Bank of Italy, Bank of Italy and Bank of Italy

detail.title: Profit shifting via intragroup lending: measuring and comparing the debt structure and interest rate channels

publicationDetails.detailsText: Bank of Italy Temi di Discussione (Working Paper) No. 1529
publicationDetails.journalName: Bank of Italy Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Multinational groups can use intragroup lending to shift their profits to low-tax jurisdictions so as to minimize their tax liability. We provide novel evidence on the extent of profit shifting via intragroup lending. Our findings suggest that firms are more likely to take on a greater share of related foreign party debt than non-related foreign party debt when the multinational group they belong to has affiliates in low-tax jurisdictions; we have also found that the interest rate paid on related party debt tends to be higher than the interest rate paid to non-related counterparties. The importance of tax motivations is confirmed by the disproportionate reliance on internal borrowing from affiliates in countries listed as tax havens among firms with higher EBITDA and spare interest deductibility capacity. Finally, we try to quantify the amount of corporate tax dodged via intragroup lending in Italy over the 2013-2022 period and show that it is relatively modest overall.

title: Motivational Dynamics of Collective Action for Sustainability
affiliations: , Bern University of Applied Sciences (BFH), University of Geneva, University of Geneva - Geneva Finance Research Institute (GFRI) and Information Science Institute, Geneva School of Economics and Management, University of Geneva

detail.title: Motivational Dynamics of Collective Action for Sustainability

declarations.ethicsApproval: Informed consent was obtained from survey participants. Data was anonymised before processing.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Manuscript not published elsewhere. under review in Scientific Reports.

detail.abstract:
Addressing grand challenges like the UN's Sustainable Development Goals requires mobilizing voluntary collective action, yet what motivates sustained participation without traditional incentives remains unclear. We examine hackathons for SDGs – a growing form of collaborative innovation – as a case of collective action for advancing UN sustainability goals. Analyzing 299 participants across 15 SDG hackathons in six countries using pre-post surveys, qualitative interviews, and project outcomes, we reveal participants are primarily motivated by intrinsic factors and the desire to contribute to a higher purpose (~90% rated purpose highly). Critically, the collective action experience itself strengthened intrinsic motivation, with purely intrinsically motivated participants increasing by approximately 20% post-hackathon.

We introduce "purposeful play-and-work"- the integration of playful experimentation with meaningful purpose - as a novel motivational mechanism sustaining voluntary participation. Participants were drawn not only by desire to contribute to sustainability but also by opportunities to experiment, create, and engage in novel social interactions. Personal preference for play and experimentation significantly predicted project success, explaining 42.7% of variance in peer-evaluated outcomes.

These findings advance collective action theory by demonstrating how environments enabling purposeful play-and-work can effectively mobilize and sustain voluntary participation where traditional coordination mechanisms like monetary incentives or institutional monitoring are limited.

title: Supply Chain Credit Contagion Model: A Network-Based Stress-Testing Framework for Corporate Banking

detail.title: Supply Chain Credit Contagion Model: A Network-Based Stress-Testing Framework for Corporate Banking

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest. This research was conducted independently as a portfolio project with no external funding or institutional affiliation beyond EMSI.

detail.abstract:
Standard corporate credit risk models assume borrowers are independent. This assumption is empirically untenable in economies where large industrial groups sustain entire supplier ecosystems. This paper presents the Supply Chain Credit Contagion Model (SC-CCM), a quantitative framework for measuring and stress-testing credit risk propagation across Moroccan industrial supply chain networks.

The model combines three methodological layers: (1) a logistic regression Probability of Default model incorporating firm-level financial ratios and Moroccan macroeconomic factors (Bank Al-Maghrib policy rate, phosphate price index, EUR/MAD); (2) an IFRS 9 Expected Credit Loss engine (PD × LGD × EAD); and (3) a DebtRank network contagion algorithm propagating distress across a 50-firm supply chain graph.

Two stress scenarios are evaluated: a 40% phosphate price crash and a BAM policy rate spike from 3.00% to 5.50%. Monte Carlo simulation (n=500) produces robust uncertainty intervals. Under the commodity shock, portfolio ECL rises 43.3% and DebtRank R reaches 0.1490 — exceeding the 10% systemic materiality threshold. The rate spike produces a 46.6% ECL increase with R=0.1239. Both scenarios imply IFRS 9 Stage 2 reclassification for the majority of tier-2/3 SME exposures.

The framework demonstrates that failure to account for supply chain network contagion understates portfolio ECL by 43–47% under plausible stress conditions, with direct implications for Bank Al-Maghrib macroprudential policy and corporate banking ICAAP design.

title: Designing Decision-Centric Banking Analytics Systems: A Practical Framework from Regional Banking Environments

detail.title: Designing Decision-Centric Banking Analytics Systems: A Practical Framework from Regional Banking Environments

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve human participants or sensitive personal data and does not require ethical approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Analytics systems in financial institutions often fail not due to lack of data, but due to their inability to influence operational decision-making. This challenge is particularly pronounced in regional banking environments, where data is fragmented across multiple sources, reporting processes are manual, and user adoption of analytics tools remains low. This paper presents a practical framework for designing decision-centric analytics systems in low data-maturity environments. Based on a real-world implementation across 27 banking branches, the study outlines a three-layer model consisting of data standardisation, decision-focused dashboard design, and user adoption alignment. The implementation resulted in a 40% reduction in reporting time and a 15% improvement in non-performing asset (NPA) recovery performance. The findings highlight that the effectiveness of analytics systems depends less on technical sophistication and more on their integration into operational workflows and decision making processes.
