detail.title: ABC dei modelli per lo studio delle politiche del clima (ABC of models for the study of climate policies)

publicationDetails.detailsText: Bank of Italy Temi di Discussione (Working Paper) No. 1530
publicationDetails.journalName: Bank of Italy Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Italian Abstract: Questo paper è una rassegna di contributi presenti in letteratura sui modelli di valutazione integrata (MVI) e sulle loro applicazioni. Gli MVI sono modelli econometrici che includono equazioni che riproducono il ciclo del carbonio e i suoi effetti sulla temperatura; prendendo come esempio i modelli DICE e RICE sviluppati dal premio Nobel Nordhaus, il lavoro descrive le modifiche necessarie a far sì che gli MVI siano in grado di dare conto dell'interazione tra economia e clima e consentano di valutare costi e benefici delle politiche di riduzione delle emissioni di CO2. Le principali indicazioni che possono essere tratte dall'uso degli MVI sono che (i) i costi delle politiche necessarie ad eliminare l'esternalità climatica sono di entità sopportabile e non ridurrebbero drammaticamente le prospettive di crescita dell'economia globale; (ii) solo le politiche che incidono sul prezzo delle fonti di energia fossile sono in grado di azzerare le emissioni di gas serra, mentre le politiche monetarie possono contribuire solo in misura marginale; (iii) le strategie che si prefiggono un tetto all'aumento della temperatura o una data entro cui arrivare all'azzeramento delle emissioni sono sub-ottimali, perché non tengono adeguatamente conto degli oneri che misure troppo ambiziose - o troppo blande - impongono alla collettività.
English Abstract: This paper reviews the literature on Integrated Assessment Models (IAMs) and their applications. By augmenting standard econometric models with equations that represent the carbon cycle and its impact on temperature, IAMs can capture the interactions between the economy and the climate system, enabling the assessment of the costs and benefits of policies aimed at reducing CO₂ emissions.The main insights afforded by IAMs are that (i) the costs of the policies required to eliminate the climate externality are manageable and would not dramatically reduce global economic growth prospects; (ii) only policies that affect the price of fossil energy sources can bring greenhouse gas emissions to zero, while monetary policy can contribute only marginally; (iii) strategies that set a temperature cap or a specific date for achieving net‑zero emissions are suboptimal.

title: TAXATION POLICY CONSIDERATIONS: THE EFFECT OF THE PROVISIONS OF THE PETROLEUM INDUSTRY ACT ON INVESTMENTS IN NIGERIA.

detail.title: TAXATION POLICY CONSIDERATIONS: THE EFFECT OF THE PROVISIONS OF THE PETROLEUM INDUSTRY ACT ON INVESTMENTS IN NIGERIA.
detail.abstract: The purpose of this study is to provide insights into the socio-economic impact of the fiscal policies of Petroleum Industry Act 2021. The Petroleum Industry Act 2021 shall be examined primarily alongside relevant statutes using doctrinal approach.  The taxation provisions within the Act introduced certain changes in incentives and allowances to foster an enabling environment for investors in the bid to align with one its core objectives. The Act has elicited mixed reactions from stakeholders; including but not limited to host communities, international oil companies, local companies, the NNPC and the tax man (Federal Inland Revenue Service). Three years after the enactment of the Act, this paper evaluates the accuracy of the prognosis of stakeholders about the Act’s impact and assesses the relevance of its provisions amidst evolving global and local socio-economic and political dynamics. Key factors are considered such as Fuel Subsidy, OPEC production quota, Russia-Ukraine War, Inflation, Security, Naira devaluation, Dangote Refinery, and the election of a new president in Nigeria. These dynamics are analysed to comprehend its influence on the effectiveness of the Act in its capacity to achieve its intended objectives. This paper also provides an overview of petroleum tax regimes in Saudi Arabia, Russia, and the United States, the big players in the international oil scene to draw comparative insights and assess the suitability of their systems. The findings aim to guide regulators and stakeholders in shaping future policies that align with the sector's current realities and global best practices to drive investment in the sector.

title: Informational Mpemba Effect in Financial Markets: Extreme Crises Recover Faster

detail.title: Informational Mpemba Effect in Financial Markets: Extreme Crises Recover Faster
detail.abstract: We report empirical evidence of a recovery-speed inversion in financial markets analogous to the informational Mpemba effect. Analyzing 413 asset-crisis observations (109 assets, 6 crises, 2008-2022), we find that assets whose return distributions diverge more from pre-crisis baselines (higher Kullback-Leibler divergence) recover to pre-crisis levels faster than moderately divergent assets. The partial Spearman correlation controlling for asset class is ρ =-0.151 (permutation p = 0.001, bootstrap 95% CI [-0.250,-0.053]). The effect survives survivorship analysis (high-KL assets are more, not less, likely to recover), operates within individual sectors (emerging markets ρ =-0.69, financials ρ =-0.39), and persists in a model-free rolling-window test over 6,591 drawdown events (ρ =-0.097, p < 10-6). The effect is small (Cliff's δ ≈ 0.28 between moderate and extreme quintiles), strongest for internationally traded assets, and absent for the 2008 financial crisis where structural insolvency dominated recovery dynamics. We discuss connections to resource-theoretic Mpemba frameworks and economic mechanisms (fire-sale repricing, value hunting).

title: The Data Wants Its Physics Back: Lindbladian Dynamics of Institutional Commitment Networks
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Data Wants Its Physics Back: Lindbladian Dynamics of Institutional Commitment Networks
detail.abstract: Promise Theory (Burgess, 2004) abstracted physics into a framework for autonomous agents and voluntary commitments. We apply the framework to institutional data and find that the data returns to physics. The Gorini-Kossakowski-Sudarshan-Lindblad (GKSL) master equation, developed for open quantum systems, fits the state evolution of commitment networks across nine substrates (R 2 = 0.13 to 0.994), with six exceeding 0.90. Substrates include IMF lending conditions, World Bank evaluations, EPA compliance violations, Freedom House democracy scores, World Governance Indicators, Global Fund grant disbursements, and a non-cooperative control (NYC taxi queues). We introduce implicit declaration reconstruction, a technique for recovering truncated pre-verification commitment periods from administrative records, which improved one substrate from R 2 = 0.721 to 0.972. The equation is universal. The parameters are diagnostic. The drift rate g dec , measuring how fast verified commitments decay back toward the unchecked state, is nonzero in most cooperative systems and exactly zero in the non-cooperative control. A distinct "sticky compliance" regime (g dec = 0 with strong remediation pressure) appears in incentive-driven healthcare systems, where met commitments do not revert. Verification acts as a quantum instrument: the act of checking is irreversible, outcome-dependent (post-measurement Weibull k spans 0.733 to 0.913, all pairwise p < 10-18), and leaves persistent backaction (Delta-k = +0.176, p = 0.002). The quantum Zeno effect is confirmed (rho =-0.191): frequent observation suppresses state transitions. The system operates at 75% incoherence, placing it in the classical limit of the GKSL framework where the dissipative terms dominate. The minimal sufficient model has nine parameters, all fitted from data, all with physical interpretation. It provides a common mathematical language for measuring the dynamics of commitment networks across institutions, enforcement mechanisms, and scales. The formal derivation from a microscopic model and extension to additional substrates are future work.

title: Optimizing Service Operations via LLM-Powered Multi-Agent Simulation
affiliations: Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST) and Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST)

detail.title: Optimizing Service Operations via LLM-Powered Multi-Agent Simulation
detail.abstract: Service system performance depends on how participants respond to design choices, but modeling these responses is hard due to the complexity of human behavior. We introduce an LLM-powered multi-agent simulation (LLM-MAS) framework for optimizing service operations. We cast the problem as stochastic optimization with decision-dependent uncertainty: design choices are embedded in prompts and shape the distribution of outcomes from interacting LLM-powered agents. By embedding key numerical information in prompts and extracting it from LLM-generated text, we model this uncertainty as a controlled Markov chain. We develop an on-trajectory learning algorithm that, on a single simulation run, simultaneously constructs zeroth-order gradient estimates and updates design parameters to optimize steady-state performance. We also incorporate variance reduction techniques. In a sustainable supply chain application, our method outperforms several benchmarks, including black-box optimization and using LLMs as numerical solvers or as role-playing system designers. A case study on optimal contest design with real behavioral data shows that LLM-MAS is both a cost-effective evaluator of known designs and an exploratory tool that can uncover viable designs overlooked by traditional approaches.

title: Beyond Risk-Neutrality in Dynamic Pricing: Stochastic Dominance and Target-Based Objectives
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Beyond Risk-Neutrality in Dynamic Pricing: Stochastic Dominance and Target-Based Objectives
detail.abstract: The structure of optimal pricing rules in dynamic pricing models with limited inventory is typically derived under the assumption of expected revenue maximization. We show that this assumption is pivotal in producing the well-known monotonicity properties of optimal prices. We analyze a finite-horizon pricing problem with constrained stock and binary demand in each period. Instead of focusing solely on expected revenue, we consider alternative performance criteria and emphasize properties shared by stochastically undominated strategies. In particular, we examine a targetbased objective that maximizes the probability of achieving a prescribed revenue threshold. Our findings show that monotonicity is not inherent to the model but arises from the choice of objective function. While risk-neutral policies yield prices that are monotone in both time and inventory, target-based objectives can generate non-monotone behavior and more complex pricing patterns. We present analytical results for the single-unit case, a two-period example illustrating the breakdown of monotonicity, and a numerical study of the general model. Together, these results offer a new perspective on dynamic pricing by linking the structure of optimal policies to the form of the objective function and help rationalize empirically observed pricing behaviors that deviate from classical risk-neutral predictions.

title: Fake Plastic Voters: When Political Parties Can Use AI-Simulated Focus Groups
affiliations: Yale University - Digital Ethics Center, Independent, Independent, University of Zurich, Department of Political Science, Independent, Université Libre de Bruxelles and Yale University - Digital Ethics Center

detail.title: Fake Plastic Voters: When Political Parties Can Use AI-Simulated Focus Groups

publicationDetails.detailsText: Centre for Digital Ethics (CEDE) Research Paper (forthcoming)
publicationDetails.journalName: Centre for Digital Ethics (CEDE) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Political parties strive to understand their electorates, and focus groups are a vital tool in these efforts. AI-enhanced simulation technologies (AESTs) enable synthetic focus groups in a fraction of the time (and cost), raising the question of when and how such simulated evidence can be used in campaign research. This paper develops a decision matrix to help party strategists match research needs to appropriate simulation technologies and to identify when to escalate to hybrid or fully human focus groups. The matrix combines three dimensions: strategic purpose, deployment risk, and empirical grounding of the simulation tool. Strategic purpose is the decisive dimension, as it determines what kind of evidence the focus group is meant to produce: observing how political meanings and identities emerge through interaction (Mode 1) or testing and refining campaign messages (Mode 2). The matrix shows that, given documented failure modes such as sycophancy, persona drift, and the suppression of minority viewpoints, AESTs cannot replace human interaction in Mode 1 at any risk level. Within Mode 2, suitability depends instead on deployment risk and on the empirical grounding. Yet even here, we caution that routine reliance on AESTs may erode the qualitative craft on which sound judgment depends.

reference: Stanford Public Law Working Paper (forthcoming)
title: The Disappearance of the Ten-Year Fund
affiliations: Stanford Law School and

detail.title: The Disappearance of the Ten-Year Fund

publicationDetails.journalName: Stanford Law School, Public Law & Legal Theory Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Private equity and venture capital funds are commonly described as ten-year investment vehicles, yet modern funds increasingly realize value over much longer horizons. Using linked quarterly fund cash flow and net asset value (NAV) data from PitchBook for funds formed between 1995 and 2014, together with portfolio-company investment, valuation, and exit data, we examine the sources and consequences of this lengthening of fund lifecycles. We show that unrealized NAV late in fund life has risen sharply across vintages--especially in venture capital--and that many funds continue distributing capital for more than twenty years. We find little evidence that later vintage funds convert NAV into cash more slowly. Instead, elevated late-life NAV primarily reflects greater value creation: these funds hold portfolio companies that reach substantially larger valuations by year ten and exhibit more extreme right-tail outcomes. Funds have sustained NAV-to-cash conversion by shifting exit channels away from IPOs toward acquisitions and secondary transactions, with serial acquirers playing an increasingly important role in venture capital. Extended realization horizons mechanically inflate interim IRRs and complicate performance evaluation and governance as large unrealized positions persist alongside successor fundraising. These findings challenge the use of ten-year fund structures and interim performance metrics as reliable guides to the timing, risk, and performance of private fund investments.

title: Financial disclosure Synergy between generative AI and unstructured social data: a comparison between ChatGPT narrative synthesis and Facebook sentiment shocks
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Financial disclosure Synergy between generative AI and unstructured social data: a comparison between ChatGPT narrative synthesis and Facebook sentiment shocks
detail.abstract: There is a gigantic change in the information presented under financial reporting where static and outdated paperwork is being replaced with more real-time and dynamic information. This paper examines how Generative AI (ChatGPT) and social media data that is not structured (such as Facebook) can be more transparent and predictive of corporate disclosures. Conventional reporting is all about retrospection of the audited statements that may be falling behind the reality on the ground and may be lacking the real-time market sentiments. In this work, I applied a comparative approach to research and triangulation of data to observe the way these techs can cooperate. By using ChatGPT, I discovered that it is an Internal Architect that reduces the time off reporting by approximately 40 percent and keeps documents structurally sound, IFRS compliant, as well as taking on anomalies. Facebook, in its turn, would be the External Sentinel, its sentiment peaks can be used as early warning signals of financial risk, and it regularly raises concerns regarding the troubles approximately 5.2 days before official impairment reports, or stock price changes. The lesson of the big picture is that hybridity between the AI-based story generation and the social media sentiment analysis is the key to the True and Fair View in the environment where information circulates rapidly. I would advise that the companies release data on social media risks, as well as implement AI-enhanced audits, to bridge the transparency gap

reference: Bank of Italy Occasional Paper No. 1005
title: The economic impact of artificial intelligence: evidence from Italian firms
affiliations: Bank of Italy and Bank of Italy

detail.title: The economic impact of artificial intelligence: evidence from Italian firms

publicationDetails.detailsText: Bank of Italy Occasional Paper No. 1005
publicationDetails.journalName: Bank of Italy Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: We study the adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies among Italian firms and their effects on firm–level outcomes, using newly collected survey data linked to administrative balance sheet and employer–employee records. We document that, as of 2024, AI adoption remains limited: about 10 per cent of firms report current use, while nearly 30 per cent plan to adopt AI within the next two years. Adoption is concentrated among larger and more knowledge-intensive firms, as well as among firms with higher labour costs, pointing to the importance of organizational capacity, technological complementarities and efficiency considerations. Using a difference-in-differences framework, we show that AI adoption increases labour productivity and profitability, and leads to a reallocation of employment toward higher-skilled occupations through a statistically significant expansion of white-collar employment and a contraction of blue-collar employment, with no detectable effects on overall employment. Finally, we examine firms’ expectations and find that AI-adopting firms anticipate smaller increases in their own prices and lower medium- to long-term inflation than non-adopters. These patterns suggest that AI adoption is associated with expected efficiency gains that shape both firms’ pricing behaviour and their macroeconomic expectations.

title: Hydrogen Logistics Architecture Standard (HLAS): A Deterministic Architecture for Bankable Hydrogen Infrastructure

detail.title: Hydrogen Logistics Architecture Standard (HLAS): A Deterministic Architecture for Bankable Hydrogen Infrastructure
detail.abstract:
The transition toward hydrogen-based energy systems has accelerated globally; however, the development of hydrogen infrastructure remains fragmented, project-centric, and often misaligned with long-term network efficiency and scalability requirements. Existing approaches typically focus on isolated production facilities, point-to-point logistics, or technology-specific solutions, resulting in suboptimal infrastructure utilization, higher delivered costs, and increased risk of stranded assets.

This standard introduces the Hydrogen Logistics Architecture Standard (HLAS), a deterministic, system-level framework for designing scalable and bankable hydrogen infrastructure networks. HLAS is grounded in formal analysis of endogenous network formation and proposes that optimal hydrogen systems emerge as multi-echelon, hierarchical architectures consisting of centralized production hubs, direct supply to large industrial users, regional aggregation hubs, and distributed demand layers. The framework separates topology selection from transport modality, enabling infrastructure planning that remains robust across evolving technologies and market conditions.

HLAS formalizes architecture classification, topology rules, structural constraints, and a deterministic evaluation framework for assessing system coherence. It further introduces a structured approach to investor triage and project evaluation based on architecture quality rather than isolated project metrics. By prioritizing aggregation, hub-based planning, and phased backbone emergence, HLAS minimizes total system cost while preserving scalability and interoperability.

The standard provides a practical bridge between theoretical network optimization and real-world infrastructure planning, offering governments, developers, and investors a consistent basis for decision-making. HLAS has implications for industrial cluster development, hydrogen corridor planning, export-oriented infrastructure, and capital allocation strategies.

By shifting the focus from individual projects to integrated network architecture, HLAS aims to establish a common reference framework for the design, evaluation, and governance of hydrogen infrastructure systems.

detail.abstract:
This research paper examines the structural basis of NVIDIA's dominance in the global AI accelerator market, which stands at 80–92% market share as of 2026. The central argument is that NVIDIA's competitive advantage is not attributable to hardware specifications but to a 20-year software ecosystem called CUDA — a deliberately engineered platform dependency that produces measurable real-world performance advantages over theoretically superior competing hardware.

The paper presents empirical benchmark evidence showing NVIDIA's H100 delivering 38.7% more real-world throughput than AMD's MI300X despite the latter's 32.1% theoretical TFLOPS advantage across 52 benchmark tests. It analyses the competitive failures of AMD, Intel, and Google TPU through the lens of software ecosystem depth rather than hardware capability, and identifies the principal structural threat to NVIDIA's dominance: the rapid commoditisation of AI inference workloads, where custom ASICs from Amazon, Google, Meta, and Microsoft offer 50–70% cost reductions and are growing at a 44.6% CAGR.

The paper introduces a dual-thesis framework: NVIDIA's training market dominance is assessed as durable within a 2026–2028 horizon; its inference market position is assessed as structurally contested, with one projection placing inference share declining from above 90% to 20–30% by 2028. Four risks are examined — inference market erosion, model architecture shift, open-source abstraction layer development, and TSMC supply chain concentration — with probability, horizon, and impact assessments for each.

A dedicated India analysis covers measurable infrastructure commitments (L&T, Yotta, E2E Networks, IndiaAI Mission's $1.2 billion programme), workforce exposure across India's 5 million IT professionals, the structural pressure on India's labour arbitrage IT services model from Agent-as-a-Service economics, and modelled workforce transition estimates of 500,000–800,000 affected roles over five years.

The paper concludes with three forward scenarios (Best Case, Base Case, Risk Case) and structured recommendations for four stakeholder groups: Indian IT companies, IT professionals, investors, and policymakers.

Research is based on five phases of validated primary and secondary sources including AIMultiple benchmark studies, Bloomberg Intelligence, SemiAnalysis, New Street Research, Xpert.Digital, and NVIDIA's GTC 2026 Keynote. All sources are quality-rated and editorial flags are maintained throughout.

detail.abstract: This paper estimates the causal impact of a regional R&D subsidy funded with EU cohesion funds in favour of small and medium firms operating in Puglia, a region in Southern Italy that has historically lagged behind. I leverage firms’ balance sheets and a unique regional administrative dataset on subsidy payments to study how this policy affected the R&D investments, productivity, and survival probability of recipients. By adopting a recently developed match-in-diff approach and using a control group of eligible but unsubsidized firms, I first show that the treated firms display higher survival compared with control firms. Then, I find that the policy was successful in stimulating additional investments in intangible assets. The policy also had positive effects on the number of workers employed in the treated firms. However, I do not find any impact on tangible assets, value of production, and productivity.

title: Why Tokenized Funds Will Scale Before Tokenized Projects: Fiduciary Risk, Governance Continuity, and the Logic of Sequenced Adoption

detail.title: Why Tokenized Funds Will Scale Before Tokenized Projects: Fiduciary Risk, Governance Continuity, and the Logic of Sequenced Adoption
detail.abstract:
Tokenization of real-world assets is frequently presented as a uniform technological shift across asset classes. In practice, adoption has followed a distinct and predictable pattern — one shaped by institutional structure rather than technological readiness. Tokenized investment funds — particularly money market funds, short-duration government bond vehicles, and similar pooled vehicles — have attracted early institutional participation, while tokenized infrastructure and project-level assets remain largely experimental.

This paper argues that this sequencing reflects structural differences in fiduciary risk, governance complexity, and market design requirements — not technological readiness or regulatory timing. Tokenized funds scale first because they inherit established legal structures, standardized governance, and familiar risk allocation frameworks. Tokenized projects, by contrast, introduce bespoke legal, operational, and governance challenges that institutional investors are structurally constrained to avoid. Fiduciary duty is the binding constraint, not the limiting technology.

The analysis has direct implications for asset managers, regulators, and platform designers seeking to understand how institutional capital absorbs financial innovation — and why governance compatibility, not programmability, determines adoption sequencing.

detail.abstract: Corporate governance plays a critical role in organizational sustainability, investor confidence, and financial stability. Yet, repeated failures across Indian and global firms indicate that formal compliance alone is insufficient to prevent collapse. This paper presents a cross-case analysis of major corporate governance failures, including Satyam, IL&FS, Yes Bank, Enron, Wirecard, and Essar Steel, to identify recurring weaknesses in board oversight, risk governance, financial transparency, and ethical accountability. The study shows that governance failures often follow a systematic cycle beginning with strategic misjudgment and progressing through weak monitoring, risk neglect, and reporting distortion. To address these weaknesses, the paper proposes a Governance Risk Heat Map, a Governance Risk Index (GRI), and the Strategic Governance Oversight Model (SGOM), a five-pillar framework integrating board governance, financial transparency, risk governance, ethical governance, and stakeholder governance. The model offers a practical and scalable approach for identifying governance vulnerabilities and strengthening board-level decision-making. The findings are relevant for corporate boards, policymakers, and governance professionals seeking more proactive and integrated governance systems.

Employment is another issue even when vacancy exists, usually due to the mismatch of course taken, skills or competency mastery, and the industry standards; this triggered the birth of BIT Connect, a website intended to unite the tracing and employment of the graduates. title: What Makes Decommissioning of Legacy IT Systems so Hard?

detail.title: What Makes Decommissioning of Legacy IT Systems so Hard?

publicationDetails.detailsText: Paper at SWEBOK workshop (co-located with ICSE), Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, 2026

detail.abstract: Motivation: Decommissioning, also referred to as retirement, disposal, modernization, shutdown, and replacement of legacy IT systems, is a critical, complex, and high-risk activity in the software life cycle. While software engineering research and industry frameworks acknowledge decommissioning as part of the life cycle of IT systems, they appear to offer little evidence or guidance on how to implement it successfully. Goal: This study aims to enhance the understanding of the challenges organizations face when decommissioning IT systems. Method: We surveyed software professionals, who were asked to assess the importance of potential causes of decommissioning problems. Results: The findings suggest that the two most important reasons for decommissioning problems, as measured by mean perceived importance, are the lack of a proper decommissioning plan and the absence of clear criteria or decision-making authority to shut down the old IT system. Unforeseen technical problems with the new IT system were, on the other hand, rated as the least important reason. Conclusion: The results suggest that problems with decommissioning an old IT system are more closely linked to challenges associated with the old system itself than to those associated with developing the new IT system. We argue that more empirical evidence is needed on effective practices for addressing the most important decommissioning problems, and that reference guides and bodies of knowledge (such as the SWEBOK) should expand their coverage of the decommissioning process.

detail.abstract:
This paper extends the structural framework introduced in the author’s prior work, "Replacing Paper Cash in the Post-Dollar Hegemony Era: From 'Paper Sovereignty' to 'Algorithmic Governance'" (Bishoy Samaan, 2026; SSRN Abstract ID: 6300199). While the earlier study examined the logic of algorithmic governance, the present paper explores its systemic resilience by addressing a central question: who protects the code, and who controls the network that sustains it?

Drawing on recent geopolitical and energy disruptions observed during March and April 2026—including reported constraints on key energy corridors, financial system stress, and rising sovereign debt levels—the paper argues that centralized financial and digital infrastructures may be increasingly vulnerable to systemic shocks.

The study adopts a theoretical and analytical approach, evaluating digital monetary architectures against a set of resilience criteria and proposing a multi-layered transition framework: Model A (Western Digital Liquidity), Model B (Eastern Sovereign Settlement), and Model C (a Neutral, Distributed Network Layer).

By applying the Equation of Exchange (M × V = P × Y), the paper develops a bounded valuation framework for distributed monetary systems, emphasizing the role of verified network participation and transaction velocity in value formation.

The findings suggest that future monetary systems are likely to emerge not solely from political or institutional design, but from the relative resilience of networked infrastructures under conditions of systemic stress.

title: The Hidden Work of Disclosures
affiliations: University of Georgia School of Law and Georgia State University - College of Law

detail.title: The Hidden Work of Disclosures
detail.abstract:
Most investors do not read mutual fund disclosures, yet disclosure remains the central regulatory tool of U.S. securities law. This gap between regulatory design and investor behavior has led many scholars to conclude that disclosure is largely ineffective. This Article shows why that conclusion is wrong.

Drawing on original interviews with investment advisers, fund managers, compliance officers, and fund counsel, we demonstrate that the principal consumer-protection effects of disclosure occur before any document reaches the public. The process of drafting, reviewing, and revising mandated disclosures activates professional norms, legal oversight, and organizational routines that shape how mutual funds design products, market shares, manage portfolios, and comply with the law. Across institutions, disclosure operates as a powerful private-governance mechanism organized around a simple norm: “say what you do and do what you say.”

By revealing the hidden work of disclosure, the Article reframes decades of skeptical scholarship and offers a more accurate account of how modern securities regulation protects the more than 120 million Americans who invest in mutual funds to finance retirement, education, and long-term financial security. Our argument has particular urgency in an era of administrative atrophy, as reduced enforcement capacity has intensified calls to weaken, if not abandon, disclosure-based regulation. Reconceptualizing disclosure as a form of co-regulation that mobilizes private governance inside firms, the Article explains why disclosure may continue to protect investors ex ante even as public oversight weakens. More broadly, the Article offers regulatory design principles for leveraging private governance to protect consumers in complex, information-dense markets.

detail.abstract: The Ogallala (High Plains) Aquifer — supporting approximately 30 per cent of U.S. irrigated agriculture — is being depleted at rates 15 to 53 times faster than natural recharge in its most water-stressed states. This paper develops a six-domain Compound Depletion Index (CDI) integrating hydrological, agricultural, economic, demographic, infrastructural, and ecological fragility into a single threshold metric, parameterised from published USGS High Plains Water-Level Monitoring Study data ([1]), USDA Census of Agriculture 2002–2022, and USDA NASS land value surveys. The CDI rose 265 per cent from 0.016 in 2002 to 0.068 in 2026, driven primarily by the Ecological Collapse domain (0.667) and Infrastructure Degradation domain (0.481). Simulation-based Granger causality tests — conducted in first differences on the parameterised time series — confirm 13 of 30 directed cascade pathways at p<0.05; the Ecological→Infrastructure link survives Bonferroni correction (p=0.001, adjusted threshold p<0.0017 for 30 simultaneous tests), constituting the most robust empirical finding. Four 25-year scenario analyses show that business-as-usual depletion reaches CDI 0.229 by 2038, while compound intervention — managed aquifer recharge, crop transition support, and a 3 per cent annual withdrawal reduction — stabilises the CDI at the 2026 baseline. The paper's central methodological contribution is an intergenerational irreversibility cost framework grounded in Arrow and Fisher (1974) [19] quasi-option value theory and Daly (1996) [12] strong sustainability criterion: the effective discount rate for aquifer depletion should be modified by the physical irreversibility factor φ = 1 − (recharge rate / withdrawal rate), which ranges from 0.75 (Nebraska) to 0.98 (Texas and Kansas), reducing a 7 per cent market discount rate to an effective rate of 0.13–1.75 per cent. This framework demonstrates that the standard cost-benefit case against aquifer conservation investment is an artefact of a technical category error — applying a reversible-asset discount rate to a physically irreversible resource loss — rather than a genuine economic verdict.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Bank of Italy Temi di Discussione (Working Paper) No. 1524

detail.abstract: We use CPI microdata for nine euro-area countries to document new evidence on consumer price stickiness in the euro area during the 2021-2024 inflation cycle. In 2022, the monthly frequency of price changes reached 12 per cent, compared with an average of 8 per cent over 2010–2019, roughly a 4 percentage point increase; it then fell quickly in 2023 and more slowly in 2024, ending close to its pre-pandemic level. The decline in the frequency of price changes was faster for food and non-energy industrial goods (NEIG) than for services, where frequencies remained elevated in 2024. The overall frequency rose mainly because there were more price increases, while the magnitude of the average size of the price increases or decreases changed only marginally during the surge. Products with a larger imported-energy cost share responded more strongly, and hazard-rate evidence shows that the probability of price adjustments increases with the gap between actual and optimal prices, consistent with state-dependent pricing and a steepening of the Phillips curve. To illustrate the implications of this state dependence, a macro model suggests that peak inflation would have been almost 1 percentage point lower if the frequency had not responded to the inflation surge.

title: Fragile Links: Private Credit Tokenization and DeFi Contagion
affiliations: Marquette University

detail.title: Fragile Links: Private Credit Tokenization and DeFi Contagion
detail.abstract: Private credit has grown into a multi-trillion-dollar asset class embedded within modern financial networks, yet the pathways through which stress in that sector can propagate into digital asset markets remain poorly understood. This paper examines two distinct contagion channels linking macroeconomic shocks to decentralized finance (DeFi): a macro deleveraging channel in which broad risk-off behavior spreads from traditional markets into cryptocurrencies, and a direct tokenization channel in which blockchain-based tokens representing private credit portfolios serve as collateral within automated DeFi lending protocols. Drawing on recent empirical developments, including the redemption restrictions imposed by a large BlackRock private credit fund in early 2026, the bankruptcy of First Brands Group in September 2025, and the associated stress in tokenized credit instruments on the Morpho lending protocol, the analysis constructs a conceptual contagion framework. The paper also situates these dynamics within the shadow banking theory of Gennaioli, Shleifer, and Vishny (2013), arguing that tokenized private credit instruments exhibit a liquidity paradox: while blockchain infrastructure enables continuous trading, the underlying credit exposures remain illiquid. The paper concludes that as tokenization expands the integration between traditional and digital finance, regulatory frameworks must evolve to monitor cross-market contagion channels, enforce transparency in tokenized asset structures, and account for the systemic implications of automated liquidation mechanisms.

title: The Price of Diversity: A Costly Choice Screens for Cooperative Intent and Yields Higher Performance in Mixed-Gender Teams
affiliations: University of Texas at Dallas, University College Cork, University of Texas at Dallas - Department of Organizations, Strategy & International Management and Columbia University

detail.title: The Price of Diversity: A Costly Choice Screens for Cooperative Intent and Yields Higher Performance in Mixed-Gender Teams

declarations.funderStatement: The authors acknowledge support from US National Science Foundation (grant 240402 to SSL), European Research Council (grant 695256 to DCS), and Center on Organizational Innovation, Columbia University.

detail.abstract: As gender segregation wanes, the performance of gender-diverse teams has become a central organizational challenge. While prevailing theories emphasize status hierarchies or homophily to explain why such teams may underperform, we probe an alternative, expectations-based, performance-risk mechanism. Across three incentivized experiments (N = 1,609), we examine how gender composition shapes expectations, contributions, reciprocity, and allocation behavior in public-goods teamwork. Study 1 provides causal evidence on mechanism: when group gender composition is assigned exogenously, gender-diverse groups underperform relative to gender-segregated groups, an effect driven not by average gender differences but by high variance in male cooperation and the expectations this variance induces. Building on this diagnostic insight, Studies 2 and 3 shift from mechanism to organizational design. We introduce a costly choice architecture that allows participants to select group composition. Willingness to bear cost functions as a screening device: a subset of men elects to pay to join groups with women, and these men exhibit substantially higher contributions, reciprocity, and alignment of behavior with expectations. A preregistered replication confirms the screening pattern and shows that differences between payers and non-payers are largely statistically mediated by expectations of peer cooperation, with little residual association once beliefs are accounted for. Taken together, the findings demonstrate that the underperformance of gender-diverse teams is not inevitable. It reflects behavioral uncertainty concentrated among a subset of men and can be mitigated through organizational designs that screen for cooperative intent, enabling the formation of high-performing mixed-gender teams without reverting to segregation.

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the strategic role of human resource management (HRM) practices and organizational communication in cultivating sustainable competitive advantage within conventional print media organizations in the United Kingdom. Drawing on a qualitative, multi-case study design spanning six major UK national newspapers-The Daily Telegraph, The Times, the Daily Mail, The Observer, The Guardian, and The Sun-the study employs semi-structured in-depth interviews with sixty respondents drawn from editorial, managerial, and operational tiers. Thematic analysis, informed by both inductive coding and deductive interpretive frameworks, is applied to primary and secondary data. Findings confirm that bundled high-commitment HRM practices-encompassing selective recruitment, performance-contingent compensation, extensive training, participative decision-making, and employee voice mechanisms-function as primary antecedents of firm-level competitive advantage. The study further reveals that alignment between corporate competitive strategy and HR strategy remains critically underdeveloped across the sampled organizations, representing a significant strategic gap. Practical implications for HR practitioners and media executives are discussed, together with directions for future quantitative and longitudinal inquiry.

title: From Implicit Execution to Deterministic Control A Unified Control-Plane Architecture for Network and Execution Security

detail.title: From Implicit Execution to Deterministic Control A Unified Control-Plane Architecture for Network and Execution Security

declarations.funderStatement: This research was self-funded by Sinteag Ventures, Inc. No external funding was received.

detail.abstract:
Modern security failures share a common structural flaw: systems grant execution authority implicitly. Network infrastructures forward traffic based on reachability rather than intent. Application and AI-driven systems execute code and actions based on origin or context rather than admissibility.

This paper defines implicit execution as the dominant failure mode across both network-layer and execution-layer systems and introduces a unified control-plane architecture that enforces deterministic admissibility prior to action. Two implementations are presented. IVD-N (Invariant Vector Defense, Network) addresses network-layer attack formation by enforcing upstream control over traffic behavior prior to aggregation, using Psi-vector pattern extraction, macro-object formation, and BGP FlowSpec policy propagation. IVD-ACP (IVD, Admissibility Control Plane) addresses execution-layer risk by intercepting all candidate actions before execution and assigning bounded authority states deterministically. Both systems share the same foundational properties: removal of implicit trust, deterministic pre-action evaluation, bounded control state under scale, and full auditability of every classification decision.

Validation is presented for IVD-ACP in a live agent environment. Application to software supply chain execution authority is discussed with reference to the Axios npm compromise. Together, these implementations demonstrate that security can be reframed from detection and mitigation to bounded, pre-authorized execution.

title: Historical Patterns of Economic Collapse: A Comparative Global Analysis-A Literature-Based Comparative Study

detail.title: Historical Patterns of Economic Collapse: A Comparative Global Analysis-A Literature-Based Comparative Study
detail.abstract: This research investigates how economies have fallen apart in the past by looking at many major financial crises around the world over the last 140 years, for example, the Great Depression, the financial issues in Asia, and the worldwide financial crisis of 2007 to 2009. By comparing what is already known from research across different countries and over long periods of time regarding these crises, the paper brings together empirical results to determine the repeating indicators of trouble, to contrast how collapses have progressed in different historical situations, and to determine how useful looking at the past is for predicting future crises. The investigation reveals that a very fast increase in credit, increasing prices of assets, more borrowing, and problems with the balance of payments between countries, are frequently the first indications of weakness in an entire system. Although these warnings are present in many different collapses, the seriousness and length of an economic decline are dependent on the strength of a country's institutions, how the government reacts, the system of exchange rates, and the size of the external shock. The study is also conclusive in stating that understanding historical trends is useful for discovering fundamental weaknesses and to improve the observation of macro-financial risks, but they are not very accurate in predicting precisely when or how large a future crisis will be. By combining evidence from history with theories about increases in credit, alterations to the money supply, and the build-up of debt, this paper suggests a combined method of analysis for understanding how economies collapse, and for making the financial system more robust in the present.

detail.abstract: Households exposed to temperature shocks often face a short-run trade-off between keeping cool or warm and maintaining food consumption. This paper quantifies how food and energy budget shares adjust over time after hot and cold shocks, and how these dynamics differ by household wealth. Using nationally representative household panel data from India linked to state-level temperature shock measures, we estimate panel local projection models to trace the time path of consumption-share responses. We find that both hot and cold shocks induce significant reallocation between food and energy. Poorer households exhibit larger and more persistent trade-offs, consistent with tighter liquidity and limited capacity to smooth consumption. Wealthier households adjust more gradually and preserve relatively higher spending on essential goods during shocks. Interactions between temperature shocks and wealth reveal substantial heterogeneity in adaptive capacity. A battery of robustness checks indicates that the results are not driven by time-invariant household characteristics, price-induced expenditure effects, alternative shock definitions, and state-specific heterogeneity. Overall, temperature shocks reshape household consumption trajectories in ways that are dynamic and unequal, with implications for welfare policy design and climate adaptation in low-and middleincome settings.

title: Labor Market Dynamics after Cost-of-Living Shocks *

detail.title: Labor Market Dynamics after Cost-of-Living Shocks *

detail.abstract: This paper provides causal microevidence on how idiosyncratic cost-of-living shocks are transmitted to labor market outcomes. Using the case of energy price changes, I combine 20 years of German employer-employee data with a representative household expenditure survey and rely on regional differences in energy expenditure patterns to identify the pass-through of energy cost shocks into earnings. A one-standard-deviation shock raises annual earnings growth by 0.4 percentage points, offsetting 30-35% of local cost increases within a year and compensating for 80% over five years. Job-to-job mobility is a key mechanism: higher exposure to energy price changes both increases the likelihood of switching and makes switches more profitable. Through the lens of an equilibrium model of the labor market, I clarify that while labor market responses substantially mitigate the distributional impact of relative price changes, they impose additional non-pecuniary costs on workers.

title: BALI: Solvency-Constrained Batch Liquidation as a Cryptoeconomic Control Mechanism
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: BALI: Solvency-Constrained Batch Liquidation as a Cryptoeconomic Control Mechanism
detail.abstract: We study liquidation in onchain perpetual markets as a stochastic control problem with delayed marks and finite liquidity. We evaluate batch liquidation (BALI), a solvency-constrained mechanism with stress triggers, uniform-price clearing, concentration caps, and deterministic fallback, against a mathematically comparable continuous liquidation baseline. Results are conditional: BALI consistently reduces cascade depth, while impact and bad debt improve only when auction participation is sufficiently elastic and fallback activates before uncovered residuals approach bankruptcy. Under weaker participation or larger effective delay, continuous liquidation can perform better on impact or bad debt. These findings position batch liquidation (BALI) as a state-contingent control layer rather than a universal replacement.

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence in Transit Corridor Management: Economic Efficiency Prospects of the Zangezur Corridor
detail.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming transit corridor management by enhancing operational efficiency, enabling predictive logistics, and optimizing cross-border trade flows. The Zangezur Corridor, as a strategically important transport route connecting Azerbaijan with regional and global markets, offers substantial opportunities for AI-driven modernization. The integration of intelligent transport systems, real-time data analytics, automated customs procedures, and predictive risk assessment mechanisms can significantly reduce operational costs, shorten delivery times, and improve reliability in freight movement. Moreover, AI-based coordination platforms can strengthen institutional cooperation among regional stakeholders and enhance supply chain transparency. The digitalization of corridor infrastructure is expected to improve resilience, sustainability, and long-term economic competitiveness. By leveraging AI technologies in transport planning, monitoring, and logistics management, the Zangezur Corridor can evolve into a technologically advanced transit hub, contributing to economic diversification and sustainable growth in the South Caucasus region.

title: The K-A-T Framework: Macro-Financial Propagation across Funding Constraints, Input-Output Networks, and Policy Backstops

detail.title: The K-A-T Framework: Macro-Financial Propagation across Funding Constraints, Input-Output Networks, and Policy Backstops
detail.abstract: We propose and test a framework linking funding constraints (K), input-output network centrality (A), and policy backstop credibility (T) to explain the amplitude and persistence of macro-financial stress. Using LP-IV on a panel of 42 economies (1999-2025) with a CIP basis measure constructed from ECB EURIBOR and FRED market data, we document strong first-stage diagnostics, network amplification, and a natural experiment (the February-March 2026 private credit gate wave) where T is approximately zero. The framework formalizes the interaction between USD funding shocks (K), input-output network density and hub centrality (A), and OMT/TPI/SRF policy backstop half-life (T) as joint determinants of macro-financial propagation. Hypotheses tested: (H1/H1B) USD funding shocks propagate to global FCI under IV identification; (H2/H2B) network amplification produces Q4/Q1 ratios of 1.5-2x in production networks, with NAV lending and bank credit lines amplifying K-shocks via financial network density; (H3) backstop credibility reduces stress half-life, with the February-March 2026 private credit gate wave (BCRED, HLEND, Cliffwater 14%, Morgan Stanley, Blue Owl, New Mountain — six funds gated; JPMorgan collateral markdowns; Deutsche Bank $30B exposure disclosed) providing a natural experiment where T is approximately zero; (H4-H6) BaaS intensity, hub centrality, and backstop clarity moderate propagation. The repository contains LaTeX source, replication packages for K-A-T and three sibling papers (Network Contagion, NPL-ML, Retailization), and supporting documentation. title: Bootstrapping Risk-Bearing Capital: Solver Economics for Coordinated Liquidation in Onchain Perpetual Markets
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Bootstrapping Risk-Bearing Capital: Solver Economics for Coordinated Liquidation in Onchain Perpetual Markets
detail.abstract: Coordinated batch liquidation mechanisms such as BALI can reduce cascade depth in onchain perpetual markets, but their effectiveness depends on whether rational solvers participate. This paper addresses the participation bottleneck with four contributions: (1) participation conditions under a cost model with dual-channel adverse selection, stress-dependent slippage, and multihour inventory risk, robust to β ∈ [2, 8]; (2) a concrete batch auction architecture specifying stress detection, coverage gating, sealed-bid clearing, settlement, and fallback logic; (3) a two-phase bootstrapping model (shadow mode → activation) resolving the paradox that BALI harms at low coverage yet must cold-start from zero, at total cost ∼$220K; and (4) stress simulations on 3 exchanges showing 70%+ coverage eliminates cascades (t =-21.1, p < 0.001) while coverage below 50% increases bad debt 20-100×. Correlated default analysis shows maintaining 70% effective coverage requires diversification (ρ c ≤ 0.15, nominal 88%).

detail.abstract: Spec-driven development (SDD) tools — GitHub’s Spec Kit, Amazon’s Kiro, and others — claim that writing specifications before implementation reduces defects, prevents rework, and improves code quality. These claims lack empirical evidence. We provide the first large-scale test: 100,247 pull requests across 119 open-source repositories, using SZZ defect tracing and within-author fixed-effects estimation. Five hypotheses derived from vendor claims are tested. None are supported. Within-author, specifications are associated with higher defect rates (+1.4pp, p = 0.056) and higher rework (+5.0pp, p < 0.001). Specification quality has zero effect on rework (p = 0.997). The AI scope-constraint claim is null (p = 0.617). Four robustness checks — alternative outcomes, JIT defect features, individual quality dimensions, and repo-level aggregation — all confirm. Specification artifacts proxy for task complexity, not quality improvement.

title: Governance-Aware Resource Allocation for Distributed Acoustic Positioning Systems Using Centrality-Entropy Optimization
affiliations: University of the Cumberlands

detail.title: Governance-Aware Resource Allocation for Distributed Acoustic Positioning Systems Using Centrality-Entropy Optimization
detail.abstract: Distributed acoustic positioning systems are critical for underwater navigation in GPS-denied defense environments. These systems operate under severe constraints: acoustic modems deliver 5-20 Kb/s data rates, propagation delay reaches 67 ms per 100 m, and channel quality varies continuously with ocean thermodynamics. Reactive schedulers produce oscillatory allocation that wastes scarce acoustic bandwidth; static schedulers cannot adapt to non-stationary channel conditions. This paper proposes a governance-aware resource allocation framework based on the Centrality-Entropy Index (CEI) for distributed underwater acoustic positioning networks. We derive three formal results: (1) an oscillation frequency bound proving that CEI with hysteresis parameter H limits each node to at most floor(T/H) allocation changes over T slots; (2) a positioning availability guarantee for networks satisfying a minimum channel margin condition; and (3) an O(|V|(|E|+W)) per-slot complexity characterization of the full algorithm. We validate the framework through a Thorp-model Python simulation of a 12-node acoustic network in a 15 km × 15 km area over 600 scheduling slots with non-stationary thermocline and shipping noise channel perturbations. Results show CEI reduces scheduling oscillations by 50.0% relative to reactive-with-governance baselines, maintains 100% positioning availability, and achieves 24.2% bandwidth savings versus static allocation. Simulation source code is provided for reproducibility.

detail.abstract: Through this study, I examine how we can revolutionize traditional financial reporting processes by integrating blockchain technology, automation, and artificial intelligence (AI) into a single model. Conventional accounting is still characterized by periodic closings, manual reconciliation and retrospective auditing that are known to introduce delays, human errors, and increased exposure to fraud. This study verifies whether a reporting system involving technology can be used to enhance productivity, accuracy and reliability within such limitations. I operated two accounting systems in parallel during a three-month comparative case study with one mediumsized e-commerce company: a traditional manual reporting system and a technology-powered platform where AI automation was enforced on a permissioned blockchain ledger. I analyzed five common indicators of performance (Bizri et al., 2021) which are monthly closing time, rate of transaction error, audit hours, accuracy of fraud detection and cost of reporting which were determined on approximately 10,000 transactions. The results indicate that there is a remarkable improvement of AI-blockchain environment. There was an increase of 29 % in the accuracy of fraud detection, a reduction of 46 in the auditing hours, time saved in the monthly closing of books, the error rates were to be reduced by 76 percent and the costs of reporting were to be reduced by 39. The implications of these findings are as follows: with the help of real-time processing, reinforcing internal controls, and enhancing transparency, combining AI and blockchain can positively influence the financial reporting considerably. But the first incurred expenses and uncertainty on the part of regulations are still major factors to mass adoption.

title: Wave Liquidity Redistribution Theory (WLRT): Third Law — Scale Invariance and Structural Universality
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Wave Liquidity Redistribution Theory (WLRT): Third Law — Scale Invariance and Structural Universality
detail.abstract:
This paper presents the Third Law of Wave Liquidity Redistribution Theory (WLRT), which defines the scale invariance of structural states and transitions within liquidity redistribution environments.

In WLRT, systems are modeled as environments in which stability is defined by the relation between compensation and fragility (First Law), and development proceeds through cyclic structural states (Second Law). The Third Law establishes that the structure of these states and transitions is invariant with respect to scale.

Scale in WLRT is not limited to temporal dimensions and includes variations in magnitude, intensity, and the type of environment. The law clarifies that scale invariance does not imply visual self-similarity, pattern repetition, or fractal identity, but applies exclusively to the structure of admissible states and transitions.

The Third Law completes the canonical law-based formulation of WLRT by establishing the universality of structural dynamics across scales.

First Law (Stability): https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19854961  
Second Law (Cyclicity): https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19860828  
Third Law (Scale Invariance): https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19861942

title: Accessing Weak Password Vulnerabilities through Penetration Testing
affiliations: EC-Council University

detail.title: Accessing Weak Password Vulnerabilities through Penetration Testing
detail.abstract:
This study investigates the identification and exploitation of weak password vulnerabilities through systematic penetration testing methodologies. In contemporary cybersecurity landscapes, inadequate authentication practices remain a dominant cause of security breaches, exposing critical systems to unauthorized access. This research positions penetration testing as a proactive and structured approach to evaluating system defenses by simulating real-world attack scenarios.

A critical review of existing literature reveals persistent user and organizational weaknesses in password creation and management, including predictable patterns, reuse of credentials, and insufficient enforcement of security policies. The study further analyzes prevalent password attack techniques, such as brute force, dictionary attacks, credential stuffing, and social engineering, demonstrating how these methods exploit both technical and human factors.

The research adopts a multi-phase penetration testing framework comprising reconnaissance, enumeration, vulnerability scanning, and exploitation. Using industry-standard tools, the study evaluates password security across multiple platforms, including desktop, server, and mobile environments. A controlled laboratory experiment illustrates the successful compromise of weak credentials via Secure Shell (SSH) brute-force attacks, reinforcing the practical implications of poor password hygiene.

Findings indicate that weak password policies, lack of multi-factor authentication, and limited user awareness significantly heighten organizational vulnerability. The study highlights inconsistencies in password security implementations across systems, emphasizing the need for standardized and enforced controls.

The paper concludes that penetration testing is a critical instrument for identifying authentication weaknesses and strengthening cybersecurity defenses. Continuous assessment, combined with robust password policies and user education, is essential for mitigating risks associated with weak credentials in complex digital ecosystems.

title: Exporting Sovereign Risk and the Extraterritorial Limits of Digital Financial Assets

detail.title: Exporting Sovereign Risk and the Extraterritorial Limits of Digital Financial Assets
detail.abstract: The unilateral legalization of Digital Financial Assets (DFAs) for cross-border trade by the Russian Federation attempts to bypass the traditional correspondent banking network through distributed ledger technology. However, this statutory framework generates a legal fiction, as it fails to extinguish the underlying sovereign risk of the issuer. This article analyzes the jurisdictional tethering of Russian DFAs, demonstrating that domestic data localization and rigid platform control render tokenized claims structurally incapable of extraterritorial mobility. Confronting an algorithmically enforced global compliance architecture, including strict liability standards under U.S. Executive Order 14114 and targeted SDN designations against core infrastructure operators, foreign financial endpoints systematically reject these digital assets. The resulting institutional over-compliance drives commercial actors toward dual-tier shadow clearing mechanisms reliant on private stablecoins, which introduce severe private-law vulnerabilities and FATF Travel Rule compliance bottlenecks. The Russian tokenization paradigm demonstrates that domestic technological isolation cannot override global sanctions enforcement architectures. Unilateral legal fictions possess no extraterritorial validity against a unified sanctions enforcement network, rendering diplomatic initiatives within BRICS and the SCO legally impotent.

detail.title: Four Irreducible Entities: A Systems-Theoretic Proof of Structural Necessity and Sufficiency in Persistent Economic Systems

The paper is sole-authored. detail.abstract: This paper develops a formal systems-theoretic account of persistence in economic systems. Its central claim is that four entity categories are both necessary and sufficient at the level of primitive structure: Individual, Firm, Governance, and Commons. Theorem 1 establishes irreducibility: no entity's function can be reproduced by any combination of the other three without loss of required informational or operational properties. Proposition 4.1 establishes closure of the entity set: no fifth primitive entity is required. Theorem 2 applies Ashby's Law of Requisite Variety to show that a regulator whose model omits any entity faces an irreducible variety deficit. Theorem 3 shows that entity-incomplete systems are non-persistent under extraction pressure, reaching at least one collapse condition in finite time. Theorem 4 gives a worked formalization of one derived rule, showing how a bounded productivity-gate mechanism prevents accumulation failure on cultivable land. Theorem 5 grounds the closure of the entity set in the cybernetic structure of feedback-controlled systems, putting Proposition 4.1 on the same foundation as Theorem 2's application of Ashby's Law. The framework provides a single structural diagnosis for a wide range of major economic failures previously analyzed as unrelated phenomena: each case examined — ecological commons collapse, financial confidence loss, agrarian abandonment, salinization-led productive failure, displaced pastoral commons, and the debt-driven dynamics of the contemporary global system — traces to a specific absence of one or more of the four entities or a specific violation of one or more of the eleven derived rules. Historical cases serve not as substitutes for proof but as external tests of the framework's explanatory reach. The paper's contribution is a compact formal architecture for analyzing persistence, non-persistence, and rule-derived failure in economic systems, with the implication that the trajectory of accumulating contemporary crises is a structural output of the dominant architecture rather than a coincidence of unrelated phenomena.

detail.abstract: Amidst high market volatility in emerging economies, investors often struggle to identify stocks that offer both capital appreciation and consistent passive income. This study aims to formulate a systematic stock selection framework through the Dividend Growth Investing (DGI) strategy, specifically tailored for the Indonesian Stock Exchange (IDX). By integrating earnings sustainability as the core metric, this research develops a multi-layered screening process involving key financial indicators such as the Dividend Payout Ratio (DPR), Free Cash Flow (FCF), and historical dividend growth consistency. The methodology employs a qualitativedescriptive approach supported by fundamental analysis of selected blue-chip and mid-cap stocks. The findings suggest that a disciplined DGI framework effectively filters companies with robust financial health, reducing the risk of "dividend traps" while ensuring long-term portfolio resilience. This paper contributes to the literature on portfolio management by providing a practical roadmap for individual and institutional investors to achieve sustainable financial growth in the Indonesian capital market.

title: The Impact of Recent Banking Regulations on the Market for Corporate Control
affiliations: George Mason University - Antonin Scalia Law School and

detail.title: The Impact of Recent Banking Regulations on the Market for Corporate Control

publicationDetails.detailsText: Washington University Law Quarterly, Vol. 68, pp. 861–883 (1990)

detail.abstract:
The efficacy of the market for corporate control as a powerful mechanism for disciplining disloyal and inept corporate managers has been demonstrated by numerous empirical studies and validated by the extreme efforts to which some corporate leaders have gone to influence public policies affecting the market for corporate control. Efforts to restrict the takeover market have been manifest in numerous public policies and policy proposals. Legal commentators have correctly identified the passage of state takeover statutes, increased and expanded enforcement of insider trading regulations, proposed changes in the federal income tax treatment of certain corporate interest payments, plant closing legislation, and antitrust enforcement as poorly disguised attempts to impede the market for corporate control. Such restrictions undoubtedly harm the efficiency of the United States economy.

One aspect of regulating the market for corporate control that has yet to be addressed is the impact of banking regulations on takeover activity. Banks and savings and loan associations are important to takeover activity for two reasons. First, commercial banks often provide financing to acquiring firms at the crucial early stages of the takeover process. Banks might make short-term “bridge” loans and commitments to the acquiring firm while the deal is being consummated and before long-term financing can be arranged. Often these short-term loans are paid off when the acquiring firm sells so-called “junk bonds.” Occasionally banks also make long-term loans to acquiring firms. Second, during the 1980s, savings and loan associations became an important buyer of junk bonds-that is, an important source of funds for takeovers. The development of junk bonds presented savings and loans (S&Ls) with another investment opportunity that was far superior in basic financial terms to many of the other investment options allowed under thrift regulations. 

These two areas of banking regulation that affect takeovers have undergone substantial changes in recent years. First, changes in bank capital adequacy guidelines and related regulations have altered the treatment of loans to finance changes in corporate control in a manner that increases the bank financing cost of takeovers. Second, statutory changes have eliminated the ability of thrifts to purchase junk bonds, thereby eliminating an important source of funds for corporate control transactions. In both instances, the new regulations do not come close to attaining their stated goals of increased safety and soundness in the banking system. In fact, both sets of regulations have the potential to increase the riskiness of bank asset portfolios. Thus, the regulatory changes not only adversely affect bank safety and soundness, they also decrease overall corporate efficiency.

Part II of this Article briefly discusses the historical development of the regulation of bank capital, focusing on the 1989 risk-based capital adequacy regulations as well as the 1989 highly leveraged transaction guidelines and their impact on the banking industry's involvement in takeover transactions. This section also shows how the perverse incentives created by the present system of federal deposit insurance impact on the takeover market. Part III discusses the role of thrifts in corporate takeovers and the effect of the Financial Institutions Reform, Recovery and Enforcement Act of 1989, including its prohibition on thrifts' purchasing junk bonds. The concluding section speculates as to why these seemingly unwise regulations were adopted.

title: The effect of education on corruption in sub-Saharan Africa: does gender matter?

detail.title: The effect of education on corruption in sub-Saharan Africa: does gender matter?
detail.abstract: This study investigates the impact of educational attainment on corruption in 33 Sub-Saharan African (SSA) countries from 2001 to 2017, with a specific focus on gender-disaggregated effects. Using a System Generalized Method of Moments (GMM) estimator, the analysis finds that while primary education is associated with lower corruption levels, tertiary education has a significant positive relationship with corruption. These findings suggest that higher education may provide individuals with the tools to navigate or exploit corrupt systems in environments with weak institutional safeguards. Notably, this effect persists regardless of gender. The study recommends integrating ethical character formation and anti-corruption modules into the regional education curriculum to produce more patriotic and conscientious graduates.

detail.abstract: The rise of Artificial Intelligence and zero-marginal-cost production has rendered traditional labor-for-income models obsolete. This paper proposes a revolutionary socioeconomic architecture: The Algorithmic State. This system replaces fiat currency with a multivariate Contribution Index (CI) and transitions governance from majoritarian populism to Epistocratic Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (EDAO). Using agent-based modeling (N = 10 6), we demonstrate that this framework reduces the Gini Coefficient from 0.82 to 0.29 while mathematically neutralizing resource hoarding. This paper outlines the four pillars of this new civilization: Algorithmic Economics, Epistocratic Governance, Adaptive Education, and Restorative Justice. Furthermore, to empirically validate the theoretical framework and prevent logical fallacies in long-term execution, this paper introduces a bifurcated simulation methodology. While macro-level stability is proven through a 1,000,000-agent Python backend simulation, we also present an interactive, WebGL-based Agent-Based Model (ABM) micro-simulation (N=300). Utilizing Reinforcement Learning (RL) heuristics, this live environment demonstrates real-time Epistocratic smart-contract execution, dynamic fiat reserve management, and restorative justice mechanics (Neural Detox), proving the system's self-regulating resilience against resource hoarding and corruption.

title: Synthetic Harm? Understanding the Effects of Generative AI on Offline Sexual Crime

detail.abstract: This study investigates whether the expanded effective availability of generative AI influences offline sexual crime. We exploit the May 2023 launch of the ChatGPT iOS application in Japan as a quasi-exogenous shock to GenAI accessibility and combine monthly crime statistics from Japan’s National Police Agency with platform-level engagement data from one of the country’s largest digital creator platforms. Using difference-in-differences and difference-in-difference-in-differences models, we estimate the effect of GenAI diffusion on reported rape incidence relative to murder and examine whether this effect varies with aggregate engagement in AI-generated explicit content. The results indicate a statistically significant post-launch increase in reported rape relative to murder, amounting to approximately 12 additional cases per month. Moreover, this effect is significantly amplified during periods of greater engagement with AI-generated adult sexual content. Supplemental analyses further show that engagement with minor-tagged AI-generated explicit content is associated with even stronger post-launch increases, particularly for offenses involving victims under age 20. Collectively, the findings are more consistent with stimulation and social learning mechanisms than with cathartic substitution. The study contributes early causal evidence that generative AI may produce harmful offline behavioral externalities and underscores the need for regulatory and platform-level safeguards.

detail.abstract: Employee attrition has emerged as one of the most critical human resource challenges in India's rapidly growing industrial sector. Despite extensive research at the national level, attrition dynamics in Tier-2 industrial cities such as Raipur, Chhattisgarh-home to over 200 steel and manufacturing enterprisesremain largely unexplored. This study investigates the key factors driving employee attrition and examines their impact on organizational performance in the steel and manufacturing sector, with specific reference to Bhilai Steel Plant (BSP). Using a descriptive and analytical research design, primary data was collected from 120 employees and HR managers at BSP through a structured 20-item Likert-scale questionnaire. The reliability of the instrument was confirmed through a Cronbach's Alpha of 0.846. Statistical tools including descriptive statistics, Pearson Correlation Analysis, and Multiple Regression Analysis were employed using SPSS. Findings reveal that lack of career growth opportunities (Mean = 2.28), salary dissatisfaction (Mean = 2.41), and excessive workload stress (Mean = 3.82) are the primary attrition drivers. The regression model explains 71.7% of variance in employees' intention to leave (R2 = 0.717, F = 46.83, p < 0.001). All six organizational performance indicators recorded mean scores above 3.70, confirming that attrition significantly erodes productivity, team morale, and operational efficiency. Both research hypotheses were accepted at the 1% level of significance. The study concludes with eight evidence-based HR recommendations for reducing attrition in the Raipur steel and manufacturing sector. This paper contributes a region-specific empirical dataset to the existing attrition literature and offers actionable insights for HR practitioners and policy makers.
