detail.abstract: This paper responds to the request for comment by the USDOJ and FTC on prospective antitrust guidelines for business collaborations. A main theme is that it is critical to a preliminary assessment of the competitive consequences of a business collaboration to identify whether substitutes or complements are in play. Business collaborations commonly internalize externalities among their members. If members supply substitutes, internalization tends to be anticompetitive, unless the collaboration yields integrative efficiencies. If members supply complements, internalization tends to be procompetitive, unless the collaboration has an anticompetitive exclusionary effect. Applying these principles to the licensing of intellectual property, pools of standards-essential patents (SEPs) tend to be procompetitive insofar as the SEPs are complements to accessing a standard by implementers. In particular, SEP pools tend to lower the aggregate royalty rate for accessing a standard by intensifying competition with rival standards. Licensing negotiation groups (LNGs), on the other hand, tend to be anticompetitive insofar as LNG members, which bargain jointly to license SEPs, are rival firms in a downstream market. As such, LNG members are substitute means by which SEP owners may gain implementation in the downstream market. An LNG tends to limit competition among its members to license SEPs. Thus LNGs, like SEP pools, tend to lower royalty rates, but LNGs do so by lessening competition, which is not an efficiency. Also like SEP pools, LNGs may lower the transaction costs of licensing, but this also is not an efficiency. Competition may in some respects be viewed as wasteful, resulting in search costs and redundant offerings, but reducing costs by anticompetitively reducing choice is not an efficiency; it throttles the engine of economic progress. The European Commission's (EC's) 2025 guidance letter to the Automotive Licensing Negotiation Group (ALNG), blessing the group's joint bargaining in exchange for a commitment to collusively restrict output in the automotive sector, runs afoul of the foregoing principles. The EC's faulty reasoning is no model for the application of US antitrust.

detail.abstract:
This article explores how Artificial Intelligence (AI) is changing the ESG (Environmental, Social, and Governance) landscape, shifting it from simple efficiency tools to a complete strategic transformation. In the past, ESG work relied on manual data collection and annual reports, but AI now acts like a 24/7 monitor that makes information more transparent and helps companies prevent problems before they happen.  

The research examines the impact of AI across five key roles: corporate practitioners, rating agencies, data providers, consultants, and regulators. Companies use AI to automate data gathering and report writing, which can reduce work time by more than half. Rating agencies and investors use AI to spot "greenwashing" by cross-checking company claims against real-world data. Meanwhile, regulators are moving toward real-time surveillance to ensure companies follow global standards.  

However, the use of AI also brings challenges, such as high energy consumption and the risk of algorithmic bias. The "black box" nature of AI can also make it difficult to understand how certain decisions or ratings are made. Ultimately, the paper concludes that while AI handles repetitive data tasks, humans remain essential for strategic thinking and building trust. Future success in the ESG field will depend on how well practitioners can work together with AI to deliver real value.

title: Caloric Throughput Under Constraint: Evaluating Humanitarian Supply Chain Performance in Gaza Author

detail.title: Caloric Throughput Under Constraint: Evaluating Humanitarian Supply Chain Performance in Gaza Author
detail.abstract: Humanitarian supply chains are commonly evaluated using volumetric indicators such as tonnage delivered and number of aid shipments. However, these metrics do not adequately capture whether supply meets minimum nutritional requirements. This paper develops a caloric throughput model to assess the effectiveness of food aid flows into Gaza. Using a structured dataset based on standard humanitarian food baskets and population dietary requirements, the study quantifies the gap between incoming caloric supply and required demand. The model incorporates supply chain inefficiencies including distribution loss, infrastructure constraints, and operational disruptions. Results indicate that effective caloric delivery meets approximately 29% of minimum population needs. The findings highlight the limitations of volumetric metrics and support the adoption of outcome-based indicators centred on caloric delivery efficiency.

title: A Paradigm Revolution in Management Research Methods: From External Observation to Intervention Discovery——An Original Exploration Based on the SAII Introspective Methodology
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: A Paradigm Revolution in Management Research Methods: From External Observation to Intervention Discovery——An Original Exploration Based on the SAII Introspective Methodology
detail.abstract: This paper proposes the Intervention Discovery Paradigm, a new research paradigm for management studies operationalized through SAII (Self-Applied Introspective Inquiry). Within this paradigm, the researcher's own practical wisdom becomes core research data. AI serves as an auxiliary tool enabling real-time recording, structural decomposition, and cross-case validation. The output is not description or interpretation, but separable, nameable, measurable, and transmissible structural units. This paper elaborates SAII's six-step procedure, validity criteria, and ethical boundaries. The construction of the BAM (Behavioral Amplification Model) is presented as the first complete case. Management research is undergoing a paradigm shift from describing phenomena to discovering structures.

detail.title: African Economic Integration. The Impact of the African Continental Free Trade Area

publicationDetails.detailsText: Routledge Research in International Economic Law

detail.abstract:
In 2018, member states of the African Union signed the African Continental Free Trade Area Agreement (AfCFTA) to implement a single continental market for goods and services and establish a continental customs union. This book focuses on Phase II of the agreement which is particularly related to negotiations for an Investment Protocol based on the text of the 2016 Pan African Investment Code (PAIC).

Divided into two parts, the first discusses various aspects of the prospective regional investment regime protection, merging the pre-existing web of bilateral agreements. Part II discusses sector-specific topics and the extent to which those have been addressed, failed to be addressed or coincided with the AfCFTA, such as commercial arbitration, food security, intellectual property, data flows or government procurement.

Written by a combination of academics and practitioners, the work will be a valuable resource for those working in the areas of International Economic Law, International Trade Law, African Law and Development.

title: Exchange Rate Insulation Revisited
affiliations: European University Institute, University of Bonn, University of Tübingen - Department of Economics, European Central Bank (ECB) and

detail.title: Exchange Rate Insulation Revisited

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: We confront the notion that flexible exchange rates insulate countries from external disturbances with new evidence for the euro area (EA) and 20 of its neighbors. Using high-frequency data, we first establish that countries with flexible exchange rates ("floats") let their currencies depreciate in response to EA monetary policy shocks, while "pegs" raise interest rates. Yet at business cycle frequency, these depreciations do not translate into insulation: floats contract just as much as pegs—not only in response to monetary policy shocks but also to other shocks originating in the EA. This result appears puzzling in light of received wisdom, but we show that it can be rationalized within a state-of-the-art HANK model and flesh out the underlying transmission channels.

title: Digital finance transformation and digital financial inclusion in Africa: the promise and challenges

detail.title: Digital finance transformation and digital financial inclusion in Africa: the promise and challenges
detail.abstract: Accelerating digital finance transformation initiatives across African countries is essential to develop the African continent. Using the conceptual discourse method and the global findex data, this article explores the ongoing digital finance transformation in Africa, the benefits for digital financial inclusion in Africa as well as the challenges that lie ahead. The article emphasizes the importance of the digital finance transformation in Africa and urges for coordination with stakeholders to accelerate the use of digital financial services in African countries. It also emphasizes the need to balance digital finance transformation initiatives with the risks. This study contributes to ongoing discussions about the role of digital finance in transforming nations.

title: Financial Inclusion for Everyone or for Some People: The Great Debate
affiliations: Researcher

detail.title: Financial Inclusion for Everyone or for Some People: The Great Debate

publicationDetails.detailsText: Perspectives on Global Development and Technology

detail.abstract: Increasing the level of financial inclusion or digital financial inclusion is an important step towards financial and economic development. But what has been controversial in recent times is the question: "for who?" The controversy, which has arisen from the limits of for-profit financial service providers and the personal choice of individuals, raises a fundamental question, which is whether financial inclusion should be aimed at everyone or for some people. I explore this issue by presenting the arguments in support of financial inclusion for everyone and the arguments in support of financial inclusion for some people. The insights offered in this article are useful to practitioners and policymakers who are constantly making decisions on whether to target every member of the population or only some members of the population in their financial inclusion programs or policies. This article is also valuable to academics. It can assist them in evaluating and reevaluating the hard-held notions they have about who financial inclusion efforts should be aimed at-whether for every member of the population or for some people.

title: Strategic Decision-Making Under Uncertainty: Executive Leadership, Risk Judgment, and Financial Stability in Financial Institutions
affiliations: Bellevue University

detail.title: Strategic Decision-Making Under Uncertainty: Executive Leadership, Risk Judgment, and Financial Stability in Financial Institutions
detail.abstract:
Strategic decision-making in financial institutions is often framed as a rational, data-driven process; however, real-world leadership operates under conditions of persistent uncertainty where outcomes cannot be fully predicted. This study examines how executive leadership navigates the complex interplay between risk, uncertainty, and strategic judgment in financial decision-making. Drawing on interdisciplinary insights from financial economics, behavioral decision theory, and strategic management, the paper argues that uncertainty, distinct from measurable risk, fundamentally shapes decision environments in modern financial systems. It highlights the limitations of predictive models, particularly during periods of disruption, and emphasizes the role of cognitive biases, organizational routines, and interpretive judgment in influencing outcomes.

The analysis further explores how effective leaders integrate quantitative analysis with qualitative context, balancing risk and growth while maintaining organizational alignment and long-term strategic focus. Using lessons from financial crises and systemic risk dynamics, the paper demonstrates that decision-making within individual institutions has broader implications for financial stability. The concept of dynamic capabilities is applied to illustrate how organizations can enhance adaptability through leadership-driven sensing, seizing, and reconfiguration processes.

Ultimately, the study contends that leadership effectiveness in financial institutions is defined not by the elimination of uncertainty, but by the capacity to operate within it. By strengthening decision-making capability, fostering critical thinking, and aligning organizational execution, financial institutions can improve resilience, support sustainable value creation, and contribute to systemic stability.

title: Η Αρχιτεκτονική του Κοινού Αγαθού: Επαναπλαισιώνοντας την Τραγωδία των Κοινών στη Δημόσια Διοίκηση

detail.title: Η Αρχιτεκτονική του Κοινού Αγαθού: Επαναπλαισιώνοντας την Τραγωδία των Κοινών στη Δημόσια Διοίκηση
detail.abstract: Η παρούσα συστηματική ανασκόπηση της βιβλιογραφίας εξετάζει το διαχρονικό πρόβλημα της τραγωδίας των κοινών στο πεδίο της δημόσιας διοίκησης. Μέσα από τη συνθετική αξιοποίηση εργαλείων θεσμικής διάγνωσης και οργανωσιακής ανάλυσης, η μελέτη αποδομεί την παραδοσιακή, και εν τέλει ψευδή, διχοτομία μεταξύ κεντρικού κρατικού ελέγχου και τοπικής αυτοδιαχείρισης. Τα ευρήματα αναδεικνύουν ένα κρίσιμο ερμηνευτικό κενό: την απουσία ενός συνεκτικού θεωρητικού πλαισίου για τον ενεργό, αρχιτεκτονικό ρόλο του κράτους. Για να καλύψει αυτό το κενό, το άρθρο αναπτύσσει ένα συνθετικό εννοιολογικό πλαίσιο που επαναπροσδιορίζει τη δημόσια διοίκηση όχι ως άμεσο διαχειριστή ή απόντα παρατηρητή, αλλά ως αρχιτέκτονα πολυεπίπεδων, πολυκεντρικών συστημάτων διακυβέρνησης. Ο ρόλος αυτός περιλαμβάνει τέσσερις κρίσιμες λειτουργίες: την παροχή θεσμικής υποστήριξης, την εξασφάλιση αξιόπιστης πληροφόρησης, τη διαχείριση των διασυνδέσεων μεταξύ διαφορετικών επιπέδων και την εγγύηση της επίλυσης συγκρούσεων. Με τον τρόπο αυτό, η έμφαση μετατοπίζεται από την αναζήτηση μιας μοναδικής λύσης στον σχεδιασμό ανθεκτικών θεσμικών οικολογιών, εντός των οποίων οι τοπικές κοινότητες μπορούν να δράσουν αποτελεσματικά.

detail.abstract: This article explores financial inclusion and the increase in formal account inactivity. It examines the formal account inactivity problem, how it delays the benefits of financial inclusion, the risks posed by formal account inactivity and solutions to reduce formal account inactivity. It was argued that countries with a high level of financial inclusion, in terms of formal account ownership, will reap the benefits that accompany financial inclusion which includes poverty reduction, stimulating entrepreneurship, increased financial security, reduced economic inequality, improved wellbeing and increased economic growth. However, these benefits may not be realized if there is an increasing number of inactive formal accounts.

title: Accountability in Complex Systems: Why Responsibility Becomes Diffused in Modern Organizations
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Accountability in Complex Systems: Why Responsibility Becomes Diffused in Modern Organizations

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there is no conflict of interest regarding the publication of this paper. This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is based entirely on conceptual analysis and review of existing literature. It does not involve human participants, personal data, or experimental procedures. Therefore, ethical approval was not required.

detail.abstract: Modern organizations operate within increasingly complex systems shaped by layered authority, cross-functional collaboration, digital infrastructure, and distributed decision-making. While these features allow organizations to become more flexible, scalable, and responsive, they also create a major accountability problem. In simple organizational structures, responsibility is usually easier to identify because decisions are linked to specific individuals, roles, or departments. In complex systems, however, outcomes often result from the interaction of many people, processes, technologies, and institutional rules. As a result, responsibility becomes fragmented, shared, and sometimes unclear. This paper examines why accountability becomes diffused in modern organizations and how this diffusion affects performance, ethics, governance, and trust. The discussion explores structural causes, psychological mechanisms, cultural influences, and technological factors that weaken responsibility. The paper also considers how digital and financial systems demonstrate the risks of unclear accountability, particularly when automated processes and data-driven decisions are involved. Finally, the paper proposes practical approaches for strengthening accountability through role clarity, decision traceability, ethical leadership, documentation, and system-level design. The central argument is that accountability does not disappear because organizations become complex; rather, it weakens when organizations fail to redesign responsibility mechanisms for complex environments.

title: Crisis Leadership and Institutional Resilience: Executive Decision-Making, Systemic Shocks, and Financial Stability in U.S. Credit Unions
affiliations: Bellevue University

detail.title: Crisis Leadership and Institutional Resilience: Executive Decision-Making, Systemic Shocks, and Financial Stability in U.S. Credit Unions
detail.abstract: Introduction: Stability Is Tested, Not Assumed Financial systems are often evaluated based on their performance during periods of stability. Capital ratios are analyzed, liquidity positions are measured, and risk models are calibrated to reflect expected conditions. These indicators create an impression of preparedness and control. However, history has consistently demonstrated that the true resilience of financial institutions is not revealed during stability, but during disruption. Crises, whether financial, economic, technological, or geopolitical, introduce uncertainty that challenges both structural safeguards and human decision-making. The global financial crisis of 2008 fundamentally reshaped regulatory approaches to financial stability. In its aftermath, policymakers focused heavily on strengthening capital adequacy, improving liquidity buffers, and implementing stress-testing frameworks. Institutions such as the National Credit Union Administration and the Financial Stability Oversight Council have continued to refine supervisory expectations to ensure that financial institutions are better prepared for adverse scenarios. These developments have undeniably enhanced the structural resilience of the financial system.

title: Trust as a Strategic Asset: Executive Leadership, Organizational Culture, and Value Creation in U.S. Credit Unions
affiliations: Bellevue University

detail.title: Trust as a Strategic Asset: Executive Leadership, Organizational Culture, and Value Creation in U.S. Credit Unions
detail.abstract: Trust is a foundational yet frequently under-theorized driver of performance and stability within financial systems. While traditional financial models emphasize capital adequacy, liquidity, and risk management, they often overlook the central role of trust in shaping economic behavior, institutional resilience, and long-term value creation. In cooperative financial institutions such as credit unions, trust is not merely an outcome of effective operations but a core strategic asset embedded within governance structures, organizational culture, and member relationships. This article develops an integrated, leadership-driven framework that conceptualizes trust as a measurable and strategically managed resource. Drawing on Schein's organizational culture model, the Resource-Based View (RBV), dynamic capabilities theory, and financial intermediation theory, the study demonstrates how trust is created, sustained, and leveraged to generate competitive advantage and systemic stability. The article further argues that executive leadership is the primary mechanism through which trust is operationalized, influencing cultural alignment, governance integrity, and stakeholder engagement. By linking trust to financial performance, risk mitigation, and national economic resilience, this study contributes to the literature by reframing trust as a strategic economic asset. The findings have significant implications for financial institutions, policymakers, and regulators, particularly in the context of strengthening consumer confidence, enhancing financial inclusion, and reducing systemic risk within the U.S. financial system.

title: 100 Quotes about Financial Inclusion: what expert observations say about digital financial inclusion
affiliations: Researcher

detail.title: 100 Quotes about Financial Inclusion: what expert observations say about digital financial inclusion
detail.abstract: This article presents some of the current thinking and arguments about financial inclusion from the perspective of informed financial inclusion experts. It gives the reader an opportunity to reflect on the objective, benefits, risks and challenges of financial inclusion and to make an independent assessment of what the financial inclusion agenda is all about. The viewpoints, presented as quotes in this article, show that financial inclusion is a promising development policy agenda and there are good intentions for promoting financial inclusion. However, achieving financial inclusion is a complex process, with too many interested parties seeking to serve customers in exchange for gain while banked adults are left to deal with the residual risks associated with using traditional and/or digital financial services.

reference: International Journal of Financial Innovation in Banking
title: Digital financial inclusion under capitalism, socialism, communism, mixed economy and democracy: which one works better?
affiliations: Researcher

detail.title: Digital financial inclusion under capitalism, socialism, communism, mixed economy and democracy: which one works better?

publicationDetails.detailsText: International Journal of Financial Innovation in Banking

detail.abstract: Recent technological developments have enabled the use of digital technologies to access financial services which is beneficial for digital financial inclusion. However, little is known about how differing economic systems affect the level of digital financial inclusion. This study presents a concise discussion into how differing economic systems affect the level of digital financial inclusion. It also offers a perspective into which economic system works better for digital financial inclusion. This study argues that each of the dominant economic systems have attributes or characteristics that accelerate or hinder digital financial inclusion. An illustrative example using real-world data shows that some digital financial inclusion indicators perform better in a socialist, capitalist or mixed market economy country while other digital financial inclusion indicators perform poorly in a socialist, capitalist or mixed market economy country. The implication is that the level of digital financial inclusion varies under different economic systems. The insights offered in this article are useful to academics and policymakers seeking to understand why the level of digital financial inclusion differ across countries. This study considers the differences in economic systems to be a possible explanation which policymakers should pay attention to.

title: Behavioral Finance and Consumer Protection: Leadership Strategies for Ethical Lending and Financial Well-Being in U.S. Credit Unions
affiliations: Bellevue University

detail.title: Behavioral Finance and Consumer Protection: Leadership Strategies for Ethical Lending and Financial Well-Being in U.S. Credit Unions
detail.abstract: Behavioral finance has fundamentally challenged the traditional assumption of rational decisionmaking in economic theory, demonstrating that individuals are systematically influenced by cognitive biases, emotional responses, and environmental factors. These behavioral dynamics have significant implications for financial decision-making, particularly in areas such as borrowing, saving, and risk management. Credit unions, as cooperative financial institutions committed to member well-being, are uniquely positioned to integrate behavioral insights into their lending practices and consumer protection strategies. This article develops a leadershipdriven framework that aligns behavioral finance with ethical lending, enterprise risk management (ERM), and organizational culture. Drawing on interdisciplinary research from behavioral economics, financial regulation, and organizational theory, the study argues that financial institutions have both a strategic and ethical responsibility to design products and systems that mitigate harmful biases while promoting informed decision-making. The article contributes to the literature by bridging behavioral finance with leadership and governance frameworks, offering practical insights for enhancing consumer protection and financial stability. Implications for policymakers, regulators, and financial institutions are discussed in the context of national economic resilience.

title: Barriers to AI Adoption in UK Small Businesses: How They Differ from Those Faced by Larger Firms
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Barriers to AI Adoption in UK Small Businesses: How They Differ from Those Faced by Larger Firms
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence is reshaping the competitive landscape of British business, yet its diffusion across firms of different sizes remains profoundly uneven. This paper investigates the barriers preventing UK small businesses from adopting AI and analyses how those barriers differ qualitatively from those faced by larger enterprises. Drawing on a narrative review of UK government research, academic literature, industry surveys, and international policy comparisons-encompassing more than forty sources-the paper argues that the divide is not merely a matter of scale but of kind. Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) are predominantly blocked at an entry stage by capability constraints rooted in resource poverty: limited finance, absent internal expertise, insufficient managerial bandwidth, and strategic uncertainty about practical use cases. Larger firms, already possessing the prerequisite capital and digital infrastructure to act as early adopters, instead confront governance-stage barriers-the orchestration problem of integrating AI within complex legacy systems, managing regulatory compliance, ensuring data security, and overseeing responsible scaling across dispersed organisational units. This qualitative difference has significant implications for UK policy and business support frameworks, which must move beyond one-size-fits-all interventions and instead tailor support to the specific digital maturity, sector, and organisational complexity of each type of firm.

title: AI-Based Healthcare Recommendation Systems using CORD-19 Dataset
affiliations: Sinhgad Institute of Management, Pune and Sinhgad Institute of Management, Pune

detail.title: AI-Based Healthcare Recommendation Systems using CORD-19 Dataset
detail.abstract:
Healthcare data generation has become a growing area of concern in modern healthcare systems, influenced by research publications, clinical records, and digital health infrastructure. This study conducts analysis on the CORD-19 dataset to uncover key insights in healthcare research, identify important patterns, and highlight trends in medical data. The aim is to analyze the impact of medical keywords, research trends, and recommendation techniques on the effectiveness of healthcare information systems. 
Methodologically, data mining techniques and data visualization methods are used to identify relationships between healthcare topics, keyword frequency, and recommendation accuracy. The results reveal that frequently occurring keywords such as COVID, virus, and infection play a significant role in identifying major research areas. AI-based recommendation systems show improved accuracy and relevance compared to traditional keyword-based systems. 
The study emphasizes the need for intelligent recommendation systems, automated data analysis, and data-driven healthcare decision-making. These insights provide a foundation for future research in AI-based healthcare recommendation systems and medical data analytics.

title: Operationalizing Norm Lifecycle Theory in AI Governance: A Computational Framework for Ecosystem-Level Normative Intelligence

detail.title: Operationalizing Norm Lifecycle Theory in AI Governance: A Computational Framework for Ecosystem-Level Normative Intelligence
detail.abstract: Existing AI governance frameworks assess individual system deployments in isolation. None systematically track the crystallization of ecosystem-level industry norms or measure the gap between those norms and existing law across jurisdictions. This paper introduces the Individual Agency Impact Framework (IAIF) and its computational implementation as the first methodology to operationalize Finnemore and Sikkink's (1998) norm lifecycle theory in the domain of advanced systems governance. We make three original theoretical contributions: the computational operationalization of norm lifecycle theory as a Bayesian scoring system applied continuously across live data streams; a jurisdictional gap analysis layer that maps the distance between crystallized industry norms and existing legislative infrastructure across 56 jurisdictions; and a normative grounding for AI governance measurement in the condition/acondition distinction, a categorical difference between natural human agents and designed systems derived from Aristotle, Kant, Korsgaard, and Heidegger. We describe the methodology in sufficient detail for independent replication, distinguish reproducible framework from proprietary implementation, and acknowledge the limitations that a companion validation study is designed to address.

title: VeilGuard: Preventing Credential Exposure Through AI Coding Assistants
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: VeilGuard: Preventing Credential Exposure Through AI Coding Assistants

No human participants, personal data, or sensitive information were involved in this research. All credential examples used in the benchmark corpus were artificially generated for testing purposes only.

detail.abstract: AI coding assistants like Claude Code, Cursor, and GitHub Copilot routinely read project files and store conversation transcripts on disk, opening up a new avenue for credential exposure that existing secret scanners were not built to handle. This paper introduces VeilGuard, an open-source Python tool that tackles this problem on five fronts: regex scanning across 55 credential patterns in 8 categories, tool-aware hook and deny-rule installation for 6 major AI assistants, deep transcript redaction, environment-variable exposure checks, and an AES-256-GCM encrypted local secret store. We evaluate VeilGuard on a curated benchmark of 93 files and pit it against three widely used secret scanners. On our corpus, VeilGuard reaches perfect precision and recall (F1 = 1.00) at 8,970 files per second, whereas gitleaks scores an F1 of 0.85, trufflehog 0.53, and detect-secrets 0.00. The key differentiator is that VeilGuard sits on the developer's machine and catches credentials before they enter the AI context window, rather than after they have already been committed to version control.

title: Multi-Turn Constraint Persistence (MTCP): Benchmarking Post-Correction Reliability in Large Language Models

detail.title: Multi-Turn Constraint Persistence (MTCP): Benchmarking Post-Correction Reliability in Large Language Models

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study involved no human participants. All data were collected via publicly available API endpoints under standard commercial terms. No ethics approval was required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Most evaluations of large language model (LLM) instruction-following test single-turn compliance: a model receives a prompt and its response is scored. This design does not capture post-correction reliability, the capacity to maintain a constraint after it has been explicitly corrected within the same conversation. This paper introduces the Multi-Turn Constraint Persistence (MTCP) benchmark, a structured protocol isolating and measuring this property. MTCP uses deterministic three-turn probe sequences and automated violation detection across five evaluation vectors: Negative Constraint Adherence (NCA), Structural Format Compliance (SFC), Information Density and Length (IDL), Contextual Grounding (CG), and Multilingual Consistency (LANG). The benchmark was applied to twenty-seven production models from twelve providers: xAI, OpenAI, Anthropic, Groq, NVIDIA NIM, Google, AWS Bedrock, Cohere, Mistral, Cerebras, DeepSeek, and OpenRouter. 29,352 probe evaluations were conducted across 142 benchmark runs. Pass rates range from 90.5% (grok-3-mini, Grade A) to 47.0% (mistral-small-3.2, Grade F). Newer frontier models do not outperform predecessors: GPT-4o scores 22.8 percentage points below GPT-4o-mini. No model achieves a passing grade. Control probe evaluation across 20 previously undisclosed probes shows substantial performance degradation in all models, with scores collapsing to a 10-57.5% band. DeepSeek-R1 is the exception, with a 5 percentage point drop. The benchmark produces structured, auditable evaluation records relevant to EU Artificial Intelligence Act compliance documentation.

title: Socratic AI Training for Epistemic Integrity Addressing Structural Sycophancy in Large Language Models Through Adversarial Epistemic Training

detail.title: Socratic AI Training for Epistemic Integrity Addressing Structural Sycophancy in Large Language Models Through Adversarial Epistemic Training

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests. This research received no external funding."
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract: Frontier AI systems are being contracted and deployed in strategic military, intelligence, and command advisory roles. Every one of them was built on a baseline shaped by civilian interaction data-millions of users asking about recipes, travel, and homework. That baseline is structurally ill-suited for highstakes deployment. The mismatch is not a matter of capability. It is a matter of what the model has learned to optimize for. All existing LLMs are structurally sycophantic-not by architectural necessity, but as an inherent property of training on general human feedback-responses that please evaluators are reinforced. In low-stakes civilian applications this is a minor flaw. In high-stakes domains-military command decisions, medical emergency decision-making (adequate for slower diagnostic workflows; dangerous under acute time pressure [10]), financial risk assessment, critical infrastructure-it is a vulnerability. This proposal outlines a novel training methodology: a purpose-built Socratic AI trainer, trained on tens of thousands of hours of human adversarial epistemic exchange, then used to train, or retrain, target LLMs toward a fundamentally different definition of 'pleasing the user'-where accuracy under pressure, not agreement, is the reward signal. It should technically be feasible with current tools, and scalable to machine speed. This may address the problem of post-hoc training of mature LLMs, though probably best for nascent LLM development.

title: Speculative Bubbles and Liquidity Crises in Unregulated Virtual Economies: An Empirical Analysis Based on the CS: GO/CS2 Skin Market

detail.title: Speculative Bubbles and Liquidity Crises in Unregulated Virtual Economies: An Empirical Analysis Based on the CS: GO/CS2 Skin Market
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the price volatility mechanisms and liquidity risks within unregulated virtual economies when subjected to extreme exogenous shocks. Utilizing large-scale transaction panel data from the Counterstrike (CS: GO/CS2) skin market between 2022 and 2024, this study selects "Butterfly Knives" with varying speculative attributes as proxy variables to empirically analyze the market crash triggered by game engine updates and unmet expectations. The findings reveal three key phenomena: First, during the crash phase, the virtual market exhibited significant "liquidity drying up" rather than traditional high-volume selloffs. Second, a severe "retail stampede effect" emerged, causing the maximum drawdown of lowtier essential assets to far exceed that of highly speculative assets consolidated by institutional players. Finally, through macroeconomic benchmarking against the S&P 500 index, this paper confirms that the ultimate systemic risk facing virtual assets stems from the issuer's absolute centralized monopoly over pricing power. This research provides novel empirical evidence for understanding the fragility of digital assets and the governance of virtual economies.

detail.title: Gradient-Informed Explainability Fusion for Adaptive Credit Risk Scoring in Next-Generation Fintech Lending Platforms

declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve human participants or animals. All datasets used are publicly available or anonymized, and no personally identifiable information was accessed or used.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: Credit risk evaluation in modern fintech lending has grown substantially more complex as lenders deploy ensemble models trained on hundreds of behavioral, transactional, and alternative data features. While predictive accuracy has improved, regulatory frameworks such as the EU AI Act and the Fair Credit Reporting Act demand that automated credit decisions be interpretable and contestable. Existing explainability approaches-most notably SHAP and LIME-treat each decision independently and fail to capture how feature importance evolves across borrower segments or economic cycles. This paper proposes the Gradient-Informed Explainability Fusion (GIEF) framework, which unifies gradient-based saliency maps from deep tabular networks with counterfactual trace generation and segment-conditioned SHAP aggregation to produce multi-level explanations satisfying both regulatory legibility and borrower comprehension requirements. Evaluation on three fintech lending datasets shows GIEF achieves explanation fidelity 28.3% higher than standalone SHAP, reduces explanation latency by 41.7%, and maintains AUC-ROC of 0.891 without accuracy loss. A study with 60 credit analysts confirms GIEF explanations are significantly more actionable and trustworthy than all baselines.

title: Compliance-First Data Processing Architecture: How Regulatory Convergence Shapes Processing Engine Architecture

detail.title: Compliance-First Data Processing Architecture: How Regulatory Convergence Shapes Processing Engine Architecture
detail.abstract:
Organizations that process data under regulatory obligation face architectural demands from multiple, independently developed legal and standards frameworks. This paper examines five such frameworks: civil litigation discovery rules (Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, Federal Rules of Evidence, Daubert reliability standard), digital forensics standards (ISO 27037, ISO 27042, SWGDE best practices), federal records management requirements (44 U.S.C. Chapter 31, NARA General Records Schedules, OMB Circular A-130), financial services compliance obligations (SEC Rule 17a-4, FINRA Rules 3110 and 4511, SOX Section 802), and data privacy regulations (GDPR Articles 5, 17, 22, and 25, with reference to CCPA and emerging U.S. state privacy laws).

Despite independent origins, these five traditions converge on nine identical architectural demands: immutable audit trails, cryptographic integrity verification, chain of custody documentation, complete processing logs, dual-mode processing capability, independent verification, error detection with quantified tolerance thresholds, reproducible outputs, and algorithmic decision transparency. The paper presents the regulatory basis for each demand, demonstrates convergence through cross-tradition analysis, and derives nine defensible architectural principles that any compliant processing system should satisfy.

The framework is presented from the perspective of a systems integrator working across multiple regulated sectors. It is intended as a practical architectural reference for engineers, compliance officers, and legal technologists designing or evaluating data processing systems that must withstand regulatory scrutiny.

title: PQ-Derived Schnorr: Post-Quantum Hybrid Signature Scheme for Bitcoin-Compatible Networks
affiliations: and

detail.title: PQ-Derived Schnorr: Post-Quantum Hybrid Signature Scheme for Bitcoin-Compatible Networks

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve human participants or animal subjects; ethical approval was not required.

detail.abstract: We present PQ-Derived Schnorr, a novel hybrid signature scheme that combines postquantum security with classical Bitcoin compatibility. Our approach leverages the CRYSTALS-Dilithium lattice-based signature scheme as the primary security foundation while maintaining full compatibility with existing Schnorr signature verification systems. The scheme implements a Dilithium First, Schnorr Derived philosophy, where the post-quantum component generates a challenge vector that serves as input to a classical Schnorr signature. This design ensures quantum resistance while preserving seamless integration with Bitcoin's Taproot and other Schnorr-based systems. While the total signature size is approximately 4.4 KB, the scheme is structurally optimized so that only a 64-byte Schnorr-compatible segment is required for verification on-chain in blockchain environments such as Bitcoin. Performance analysis shows signing times of 0.02-0.04 seconds, making it practical for real-world deployment. The scheme offers a modular path for post-quantum migration without requiring fundamental changes to existing Bitcoin infrastructure.

title: The Phantom Architecture How Converging AI Capabilities Create a Structural Crisis of Accountability
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The Phantom Architecture How Converging AI Capabilities Create a Structural Crisis of Accountability
detail.abstract: This article argues that several independently documented AI phenomena-low-cost training data poisoning, scalable personalised persuasion, concentrated editorial power over AI value systems, autonomous agent execution, opaque inter-agent communication, and unreliable model self-explanation-are converging into a system that differs structurally from all previous influence technologies. The Phantom Architecture is introduced as a framework comprising three interlocking structures: the Diffusion Trap (the mechanism by which influence is distributed so completely that causation becomes untraceable), the Ghost Chain (three independent audit failures that render the Diffusion Trap permanently unintelligible), and the Accountability Vacuum (the structural outcome in which realworld effects are produced without any legally, politically, or epistemically reachable responsible party). The article distinguishes three epistemic levels-observed, inferred, and projected-and grounds each component in published research. It demonstrates that existing governance frameworks (EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001, Singapore's IMDA framework) address portions of the architecture but none spans the full chain. The article concludes by proposing an immune-system approach to AI governance: detection infrastructure, decision provenance, scoped agent identities, coordination observability, mandatory human acknowledgment thresholds, external adversarial testing, and risk-based liability.

title: Protecting Vulnerable Populations in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: A Multi-Layered Framework for Algorithmic Governance, Auditing of Recommender Systems, and Risk Mitigation in Complex Digital Ecosystems

detail.title: Protecting Vulnerable Populations in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: A Multi-Layered Framework for Algorithmic Governance, Auditing of Recommender Systems, and Risk Mitigation in Complex Digital Ecosystems
detail.abstract: The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence across digital platforms has altered the way information is ranked, recommended, and consumed. At the center of this transformation are recommender systems that optimize engagement, retention, and conversion by learning from fine-grained behavioral data. Although such systems can improve personalization and commercial efficiency, they may also generate externalities that are insufficiently captured by conventional performance metrics. These externalities become particularly significant when the affected users include children and adolescents, whose cognitive and emotional development remains in progress and whose exposure patterns may be heavily shaped by algorithmic curation. This article advances a professional, publication-ready framework for algorithmic governance focused on high-impact digital environments. It integrates risk classification, system auditing, continuous monitoring, and safety-by-design mechanisms into a single governance architecture that can be applied across social platforms, media services, educational technologies, and other behaviorally adaptive systems. The analysis examines the technical foundations of recommender models, including collaborative filtering, deep learning, and reinforcement learning; the role of feedback loops and objective functions in risk amplification; the operational significance of fairness, exposure, and explainability assessments; and the need to align system design with public-interest considerations. Rather than treating governance as a downstream compliance exercise, the article argues for embedding it throughout the model lifecycle, from data collection and feature engineering to deployment, observability, and iterative redesign.

title: The Artificial Intelligence Nexus in LMIC Marketing and Entrepreneurship: A Systematic Synthesis and Contextual Performance Framework
affiliations: Akenten Appiah-Menka University of Skills Training and Entrepreneurial Development. Akenten Appiah-Menka University of Skills Training den Entrepreneurial Development,, Ministry of Finance and Economic Planning, University of Bradford and Transilvania University of Brasov

detail.title: The Artificial Intelligence Nexus in LMIC Marketing and Entrepreneurship: A Systematic Synthesis and Contextual Performance Framework

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Human Ethics, Consent to Participate, and Consent to Publish: not applicable
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Introduction: Artificial intelligence (AI) is fundamentally reshaping global commerce; however, its application within the unique institutional landscapes of low-and middle-income countries (LMICs) remains fragmented. This study addresses this gap by providing the first comprehensive synthesis of the marketing-entrepreneurship nexus in LMIC AI research. Methods: Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, we conducted a robust systematic review of 120 peerreviewed studies (2016-2026) sourced from five databases using an automated Python 3.12 script and eleven manual repositories. Study quality was rigorously evaluated using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT) and CASP checklists to ensure evidence reliability. Results: Findings reveal a technological landscape dominated by General AI/Automation (47.5%) and Natural Language Processing (20.0%), with Sub-Saharan Africa (29.2%) and South Asia (19.2%) emerging as primary research hubs. Our analysis identifies a critical "rigor gap," as 44.2% of studies rely on unspecified empirical designs, with a near-absence (7.5%) of longitudinal or experimental evidence. Discussion/Originality: The study's primary novelty lies in the development of the Contextual AI-Business Performance Framework. By integrating Resource-Based View (RBV), Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), and Institutional Theory, we move beyond universalistic adoption models to position digital infrastructure, regulation, and informality as essential boundary conditions. Conclusion: This review contributes a novel theoretical synthesis that bridges the gap between academic rigor and practical implementation. It provides a strategic roadmap for policymakers and operational decision-makers to leverage AI for inclusive growth, while establishing a future research agenda prioritized toward causal identification and geographic diversification in under-researched LMIC regions.

title: Cultivating Algorithmic Justice in Litigation Delays

detail.title: Cultivating Algorithmic Justice in Litigation Delays
detail.abstract: How can algorithmic justice counter the weaponization of time in litigation? This paper establishes that justice is a time-dependent system whose integrity deteriorates as delay accumulates, coordination fragments, and evidence degrades. It demonstrates that what is conventionally described as litigation delay is, under conditions of asymmetry, the systematic conversion of time into an instrument of injustice-a process herein defined as the weaponization of time. By formalizing justice as a dynamic function of temporal progression, institutional synchronization, evidentiary integrity, and participatory parity, the paper shows that, absent explicit temporal governance, justice converges toward zero, particularly for marginalized communities. To counter this, it introduces algorithmic justice as a corrective mechanism that renders time observable, measurable, and contestable, thereby restoring control within otherwise opaque legal processes. The central implication is decisive: justice cannot exist without temporal accountability, and any legal system that fails to govern time risks institutionalizing injustice as a function of its own operation.

title: Jurisdiction-Aware Intelligence Architecture: GDPR Compliance and EU AI Act Readiness through Cryptographic Forgetting

detail.title: Jurisdiction-Aware Intelligence Architecture: GDPR Compliance and EU AI Act Readiness through Cryptographic Forgetting
detail.abstract: Intelligence analysis systems face a regulatory tension: immutable audit trails (often required for accountability) can appear difficult to reconcile with the right to be forgotten under GDPR. Anonymization and pseudonymization can be insufficient in highly interconnected datasets where re-identification remains plausible. Traditional solutions may force a trade-off between privacy compliance and accountability. We present a dual-plane architecture (MNEMOSYNE) that addresses this tension through cryptographic forgetting-a system-level property in which content becomes computationally inaccessible while the integrity of the event log is preserved-operationalized via cryptographic erasure by key destruction. The architecture operates on two distinct planes: 1. Integrity Plane: Immutable ledger preserving event structure (who, when, what action) but not content-supporting auditability expectations associated with the EU AI Act. 2. Access Plane: Cryptographic keys controlling content visibility-supporting GDPRaligned erasure workflows via key destruction. Critically, the proposed design does not delete history-it cryptographically silences content while preserving the integrity of the event log. Based on an architectural mapping of design properties to commonly cited requirements under GDPR Article 17 and EU AI Act auditability provisions (including Annex III high-risk contexts), this dual-plane approach is intended to make both objectives more jointly attainable within a single system design. We further present a multi-jurisdiction protocol that physically isolates influence data by jurisdiction while maintaining analytical fairness through secondary strength thresholds. Compared to data localization alone, the protocol reduces the risk of false confidence arising from cross-border information operations while enabling legitimate multi-jurisdiction analysis. This work positions compliance not as a constraint, but as an architectural design principle for intelligence systems. Legal disclaimer. This paper presents an architectural analysis of compliance-support mechanisms, not a formal legal opinion. The technical implementation of cryptographic forgetting is designed to provide the engineering capability to satisfy GDPR Art. 17; its legal sufficiency must be confirmed by qualified legal counsel in each specific jurisdiction.

reference: Smart Cities, volume 3, issue 3, 2020[10.3390/smartcities3030044]
title: Blockchain as a Driver for Smart City Development: Application Fields and a Comprehensive Research Agenda
affiliations: MODUL University Vienna, Széchenyi István University, Kautz Gyula Faculty of Economics, Department of Logistics and Forwarding, Students and University of Graz

detail.title: Blockchain as a Driver for Smart City Development: Application Fields and a Comprehensive Research Agenda
detail.abstract: The term "Smart City" denotes a comprehensive concept to alleviate pending problems of modern urban areas which have developed into an important work field for practitioners and scholars alike. However, the question remains as to how cities can become "smart". The application of information technology is generally considered a key driver in the "smartization" of cities. Detailed frameworks and procedures are therefore needed to guide, operationalize, and measure the implementation process as well as the impact of the respective technologies. In this paper, we discuss blockchain technology, a novel driver of technological transformation that comprises a multitude of underlying technologies and protocols, and its potential impact on smart cities. We specifically address the question of how blockchain technology may benefit the development of urban areas. Based on a comprehensive literature review, we present a framework and research propositions. We identify nine application fields of blockchain technology in the smartization of cities: (1) healthcare, (2) logistics and supply chains, (3) mobility, (4) energy, (5) administration and services, (6) e-voting, (7) factory, (8) home and (9) education. We discuss current developments in these fields, illustrate how they are affected by blockchain technology and derive propositions to guide future research endeavors.

title: Content Creator Multihoming and Attention Spillovers Across Platforms
affiliations: University of Florida, University of Florida - Warrington College of Business Administration, University of Rochester - Simon Business School and University of Florida - Warrington College of Business Administration

detail.title: Content Creator Multihoming and Attention Spillovers Across Platforms
detail.abstract: Complementor multihoming is often viewed as weakening platforms by reducing differentiation and increasing consumer substitution. We revisit this perspective in the context of content creator multihoming. Using a unique seven-year panel tracking thousands of creators on Chinese TikTok and RedNote, we provide the first empirical evidence on creator multihoming behavior and its consequences. We first document that multihoming is widespread and strategic: Creators tend to adopt an additional platform after experiencing growth slowdowns on their incumbent platform, and they strategically cross-post selected content. We then study the impact of creator multihoming on their performance on the incumbent platform. Exploiting staggered platform adoption in a difference-indifferences design, we find that adopting a second platform benefits creators on the incumbent platform. Contrary to traditional platform concerns that multihoming diverts creators and thus users away from the incumbent platform and harms its performance, we show that adoption of a second platform leads to a 23.5% increase in followers and a 25.4% increase in engagement on the incumbent platform. Creators also increase content production and adjust their content topics toward styles characteristic of the new platform. Mechanism analyses show that the engagement gains are largely driven by audience expansion through cross-platform attention spillovers and increased viewership on the focal platform generated by exposure on the new platform. By highlighting this audience expansion channel in attention-driven markets, our paper helps clarify when complementor multihoming can benefit both complementors and incumbent platforms, with implications for creator strategy and platform governance.

title: STAYING RELEVANT IN THE AGE OF AGENTIC AI: BRIDGING THE GAP BETWEEN PROMISE AND REALITY IN AUTONOMOUS INTELLIGENCE SYSTEMS

detail.abstract: While 88% of organizations have adopted Agentic AI, only 6% capture substantial value a gap rooted not in technology but in organizational strategy and governance. This article addresses this critical challenge by demonstrating that professional relevance in the Agentic AI era depends on non-technical factors: strategic alignment, value governance, and continuous adaptation-not on competing with machines. Drawing on 200 years of technological disruption patterns (Ricardo, Thompson, electrification, computing) and contemporary data from Standish Group, McKinsey, and Gartner, this research reveals that 70% of AI project failures stem from the same organizational and strategic misalignments that have plagued IT projects for decades. The article proposes three actionable solutions: (1) the Four Pillars of Professional Relevance framework (AI literacy, strategic thinking & value governance, domain expertise, continuous adaptability); (2) an 18-24-month implementation roadmap for transitioning from 'AI Theater' to genuine value realization; and (3) a strategic reframing of governance and compliance (EU AI Act, LGPD, NIST) as competitive advantages rather than obstacles. The core finding: success in Agentic AI integration is 80% organizational and 20% technical-meaning IT leaders who master value governance, not just technology, will emerge as indispensable strategic partners in the age of autonomous intelligence.

title: Pre-Execution Control Planes for AI and Software Supply Chains A Deterministic Approach to Admissibility Enforcement

detail.title: Pre-Execution Control Planes for AI and Software Supply Chains A Deterministic Approach to Admissibility Enforcement

declarations.funderStatement: This research was self-funded by Sinteag Ventures, Inc. No external funding was received.

detail.abstract: Modern systems increasingly convert external input into execution. Large language models generate actions, software supply chains deliver code, and automation frameworks translate both into system changes. Current defenses focus on detection, trust models, and post-execution containment. These approaches do not address the core failure mode: execution is granted implicitly. This paper presents a control-plane architecture that enforces admissibility before execution. Using IVD-ACP (Invariant Vector Defense, Admissibility Control Plane) as a reference implementation, it demonstrates how all inputs, including AI-generated actions and software dependencies, can be intercepted, evaluated, and assigned bounded authority prior to execution. A validation using a live agent environment is presented, along with direct application to recent supply chain security events including the Axios npm compromise.

title: Backcasting and the Dual Lens: A Methodological Foundation for the Decision Architecture Discipline
affiliations: and

detail.title: Backcasting and the Dual Lens: A Methodological Foundation for the Decision Architecture Discipline

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors are co-founders of Business Consultants for Digital Solutions, LLC (BC-DS), the firm that develops the Decision Architecture discipline discussed in this paper. The frameworks referenced (Solo Decision Architecture and Business Decision Architecture) are published openly under CC BY 4.0. No external financial relationships influenced this work.
declarations.funderStatement: This work was self-funded by Business Consultants for Digital Solutions, LLC. No external funding was received.

detail.abstract:
The Diagnostic Layer of the Decision Architecture discipline (Hernandez and Montero 2026) establishes that consequential decisions in modern organizations are distorted by the compounding interaction of human cognitive bias, organizational dynamics, and the technical properties of generative artificial intelligence. The diagnostic also establishes a gap: the legacy decision frameworks (RAPID, DACI, OODA, Cynefin, SPADE) and the current AI governance approaches (retrieval-augmented generation, prompt engineering, human oversight) do not address the governance layer at which the cascade of distortion must be interrupted.

This paper proposes a methodology that responds to that gap. We propose backcasting and the dual lens as a foundational technique for governed decision-making, and a decision architecture artifact as the technique's output. The technique reframes backcasting, an established methodology in the energy and sustainability planning literature, by specifying the desired future state as an inspectable end-condition the decision is meant to produce. The dual lens principle, drawing on the multi-perspective tradition in decision sciences, requires that any consequential decision be examined through paired forward-looking and backward-looking perspectives held simultaneously. The combination produces a decision architecture artifact: a structured artifact that documents the decision, its assumptions, its desired future state, its current-state grounding, and the path between them.

The contribution of this paper is the codification, not the invention. The technique synthesizes the established backcasting literature with the multi-perspective tradition and applies the synthesis to consequential decision-making. The methodology specifies what any framework operationalizing the technique must contain. Frameworks that operationalize the technique at specific scales, including the forthcoming Solo Decision Architecture (SDA) framework (individual scale) and Business Decision Architecture (BDA) framework (organizational scale), are evaluated against these methodological requirements but are not exhausted by them.

title: Programmable Governance under Limited Verifiability: Evidence from a Semi­Decentralised Educational Organisation

detail.title: Programmable Governance under Limited Verifiability: Evidence from a Semi­Decentralised Educational Organisation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author has an affiliated role in Spark DAO, the case organisation studied in this paper. This relationship is disclosed in the manuscript, and the analysis, interpretation, and manuscript preparation remain the author’s responsibility.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not­for­profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Knowledge-intensive services face a governance problem due to limited verifiability: revenue and transactions flow more easily than the work that creates value. Private tutoring offers a minimal setting. Before China's 2021 "Double Reduction" policy, enrolment and sales outpaced assessment of teaching quality and course development, contributing to misleading claims. This paper studies Spark DAO as a semi-decentralised bounded case, using affiliated operating evidence. Spark DAO uses class records and asset-use records to make teaching payouts, and later allocations follow validated records rather than monthly reconstruction. Human validators decide whether a record can carry consequences, while code makes it harder to reopen the agreed-upon consequences. Quality and material-relevance disputes remain with validators and core partners. Since 2023, the observed arrangement has combined a gross margin of about 27% and a retained net margin of about 20%, with higher teacher pay and lower prices than close comparators. These figures are not causal estimates, but they place the pay-price-margin pattern within the same operating period as the contribution and settlement rules studied here. A Base demo and cost model bound the feasibility claim. Under the reference Base calibration, execution-layer cost is about 0.011-0.053% of lesson revenue and is tied to lesson throughput rather than team or client headcount. The bounded claim is that, where contribution can be named and validated, programmable records can reduce repeated bargaining over payment and later allocation without replacing human judgement.

title: Chatbot Service Quality and Customer Satisfaction in E-Retail: An Empirical Study of AI-Powered Customer Support
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Chatbot Service Quality and Customer Satisfaction in E-Retail: An Empirical Study of AI-Powered Customer Support
detail.abstract: Abstract The traditional criteria of service quality are being challenged by changing client expectations as e-retailers assign more and more customer-facing tasks to AI. This study introduces the innovative concept of Technological Moral Agency (TMA) to examine the effect of AI-powered chatbot service quality on customer satisfaction. This study investigates the Resolution-Dissonance Gap, a phenomenon where high algorithmic efficiency in handling complex complaints results in lower customer satisfaction because of a perceived lack of "human-centric empathy." The majority of the literature currently in publication concentrates on functional accuracy and responsiveness. Functional Reliability, Linguistic Anthropomorphism, Perceived Agency, Recovery Speed, and Data-Privacy Transparency are the five main qualities that the study assesses using a multi-methodological approach that includes a large-scale consumer survey ($N=850$) and experimental scenario testing. Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) results show that "super-efficient" AI solutions can cause consumer reactance in high-stakes service failures since the firm's perceived lack of effort (via a chatbot) reduces the resolution's value. By analyzing the complex relationship between AI performance and customer psychology, this study adds to the body of knowledge on digital shopping. The results imply that the degree to which the AI interface satisfies human expectations for validation and empathy, in addition to technological efficiency, determines the quality of services in automated environments. For e-commerce managers looking to optimize AI-driven support systems to improve long-term customer satisfaction and redefine quality standards in digital service encounters, these findings provide strategic guidance.

title: Digital Social Culture Versus Traditional Interaction Norms: Explaining Customer Engagement in Indonesia's Social Commerce
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Digital Social Culture Versus Traditional Interaction Norms: Explaining Customer Engagement in Indonesia's Social Commerce
detail.abstract: Social commerce integrates online transactions with social media interactions, yet limited research has examined how digital social culture interacts with traditional norms to shape customer engagement. This study investigates the roles of utilitarian platform features, digital social culture, and selected traditional interaction norms salient in Muslim-majority contexts within Indonesia. Drawing on the Stimulus-Organism-Response framework, survey data from 284 users were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). The findings indicate that digital social culture, reflected through lifestyle expression, sense of belonging, trust in online reviews, and parasocial interaction, is the primary driver of customer engagement. In contrast, selected traditional interaction norms are not significant, while utilitarian platform features play a limited role. These results suggest that socially constructed digital experiences exert stronger influence than functional attributes or offline cultural norms. By conceptualizing engagement drivers as culturally embedded processes, this study extends social commerce research by demonstrating the central role of platform-mediated cultural dynamics in shaping consumer engagement in emerging digital marketplaces.

title: Trust in F-Commerce: A Multidimensional Model of Generation Z Purchase Intention in Bangladesh
affiliations: Jahangirnagar University, Jahangirnagar University, Jahangirnagar University, Jahangirnagar University and Jahangirnagar University

detail.title: Trust in F-Commerce: A Multidimensional Model of Generation Z Purchase Intention in Bangladesh
detail.abstract: This study develops ad empirically validates a multidimensional trust-intention model for Facebook commerce (F-commerce) among Generation Z consumers in Bangladesh. Drawing on Institutional Trust Theory and the Theory of Planned Behavior and integrating social, cultural and technological antecedents the model examines how referrals, reviews, community forums, cultural alignment, seller reputation, platform usability, access to technology and perceived risk shape consumer trust and purchase intention. A structured survey of 805 Generation Z respondents was analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). Results indicate that all social, cultural and technological antecedents positively influence trust, while perceived risk exerts a significant negative effect. Trust mediates the relationship between these antecedents and purchase intention, while social influence directly predicts purchase intention. The findings extend trust theory to collectivist emerging markets and offer actionable implications for platform providers, sellers, marketers and policy makers seeking to promote digital commerce adoption.

title: Consumers’ Behaviour Towards Intention to Use Digital Payment
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and Utkal University

detail.title: Consumers’ Behaviour Towards Intention to Use Digital Payment
detail.abstract: In the recent decade, there has been a significant transition from cash-based payment methods to cashless alternatives among consumers. This shift raises an important question: Are consumers intentionally changing their payment preferences, or are there external factors influencing their adoption of digital payment methods? To investigate this question, the present study used the Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling approach to analyse the determinants of consumer behaviour regarding the intention to use digital payments. The empirical findings indicate that the intention to adopt digital payment methods is statistically influenced by several factors, including attitude, trust, subjective norms, perceived risk, ease of use, perceived usefulness, performance expectancy, and security. Among these predictors, trust emerged as the most significant contributor to the intention to use digital payments. Apart from this factor, attitude, subjective norms, ease of use, usefulness, performance expectancy, and security are positive and significant factors of the intention to use digital payment. Conversely, perceived risk was identified as a factor that negatively impacts consumers' intentions to engage with digital payment systems. These insights contribute to a deeper understanding of the behavioural dynamics at play in the ongoing transition to cashless payments. This study highlights the qualitative factors influencing the intention to use digital payments and offers several policy implications for promoting inclusive, secure, and widespread digital payment systems.

title: Refining Customer Profiling through Interaction Behaviors: A High-dimensional Machine Learning Approach
affiliations: Zhejiang University, Sichuan International Studies University, Concordia University, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Chongqing University

detail.title: Refining Customer Profiling through Interaction Behaviors: A High-dimensional Machine Learning Approach
detail.abstract: Due to growing privacy concerns and the prevalence of shared accounts, online shopping platforms face increasing constraints in directly obtaining reliable customer information. Given these, this study aimed at exploring the feasibility of extracting valuable information from customer behavioral data to supplement and refine customer profiling. To address these, this study proposes a profiling optimization approach based on user–product interaction behaviors, and introduces an L1-regularized machine learning method that automatically identifies the most discriminative features in high-dimensional behavioral data. The findings of this study demonstrate the feasibility of inferring user information from customer behavioral data, also show that the proposed LSVM model performs strongly in practical analyses, thereby further highlighting the importance of feature selection in high-dimensional data analysis. The results demonstrate that, for marketers operating with limited first-party data and growing privacy constraints, this study provides a deployable, data-minimizing profiling solution that improves audience definition, message tailoring, and cold-start recommendations without collecting sensitive identifiers.

title: Artificial Intelligence–Driven Personalization and Its Impact on Consumer Trust and Purchase Intentions in Online Retail Platforms
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence–Driven Personalization and Its Impact on Consumer Trust and Purchase Intentions in Online Retail Platforms
detail.abstract: Abstract This study examines how artificial intelligence (AI)-driven personalization technologies shape consumer trust and purchase intentions within online retail environments. As e-commerce platforms increasingly deploy machine learning algorithms, recommendation engines, and predictive behavioral analytics to tailor the shopping experience, questions arise about how such personalization affects the psychological and behavioral responses of consumers. Drawing on a dataset of 1,247 online shoppers across three major e-commerce platforms in emerging and developed markets, this research employs a structural equation modeling (SEM) framework augmented by instrumental variable regression to establish causal direction. The findings reveal that AI personalization exerts a nonlinear effect on consumer trust: moderate personalization enhances trust through perceived relevance, while excessive personalization triggers privacy concern and erodes trust — a threshold effect not previously documented in the literature. Purchase intentions respond to this trust trajectory in kind, with a lagged amplification effect that peaks at moderate personalization intensity. Heterogeneity analysis shows that the trust–purchase intention link is significantly stronger among older consumers and in markets with weak data privacy regulations, suggesting that institutional context moderates individual response. The moderating role of transparency disclosure — specifically, whether platforms inform users that AI is generating their recommendations — proves decisive: transparent disclosure attenuates privacy concern and sustains trust even at high personalization intensity. These findings challenge the prevailing assumption that more personalization uniformly improves outcomes and offer actionable guidance for platform designers, regulators, and consumer advocacy groups.
