detail.abstract: For any business entity that wishes to retain their clients and prevent loss of revenue, predicting client churn is of primary importance. This article discusses the application of the machine learning technique in predicting client churn using a structured data set. Data preparation techniques are applied to handle the problem of missing data, data encoding, and feature scaling in order to ensure the quality of the data. A variety of machine learning classifiers, including Random Forest, Decision Tree, and Logistic Regression, are applied in categorizing the clients as churn or non-churn clients. Current studies have proven that ensemble methods are superior in accuracy and reliability [1] [8][26]. Moreover, it has been established that deep learning methods are more accurate in detecting complex patterns of customer behavior [2][27]. The Random Forest algorithm is more accurate than other algorithms in terms of accuracy, based on the test results. The proposed system may help to identify potential churners and initiate client retention activities.

title: An Explainable Expert System for Tokenized Carbon Credit Market Monitoring: Quantum-Enhanced
affiliations: National Taiwan Normal University

detail.title: An Explainable Expert System for Tokenized Carbon Credit Market Monitoring: Quantum-Enhanced
detail.abstract: Blockchain-based carbon credit markets create new opportunities for traceable digital trading, but they also introduce monitoring challenges because transaction records are high-dimensional, temporally irregular, and difficult for human analysts to interpret directly. This study proposes an explainable expert-system framework for tokenized carbon credit market monitoring. The framework integrates three components: risk-oriented blockchain transaction preprocessing, quantum-enhanced feature learning, and AI-agent-based interpretation. Raw MCO2 transaction records are first transformed into structured representations that preserve behaviors relevant to suspicious flow detection. Classical clustering, random quantum feature augmentation, and fully trained quantum neural network embeddings are then compared to examine whether quantum-enhanced representations improve latent behavioral separation in blockchain transaction data. Finally, an AI agent translates clustering outputs into analyst-facing explanations by describing cluster characteristics, comparing cross-cluster differences, and surfacing anomalyoriented patterns. Empirical results show that quantum-enhanced representations substantially improve internal clustering quality over classical features, while the AI-agent interpretation layer reveals distinct monitoring roles for random quantum features and trained QNN embeddings. The trained QNN is especially effective for isolating high-impact or anomalous transaction profiles, whereas random quantum features preserve broader ecosystemlevel diversity. The study contributes to expert and intelligent systems research by showing how representation learning and semantic explanation can be integrated into an auditable decision-support workflow for fraud-sensitive blockchain market monitoring.

title: "Impact of Online Shopping on Local Small Businesses". [ A Study in Pune]
affiliations: Savitribai Phule Pune University (SPPU) - Savitribai Phule Pune University, Pune

detail.title: "Impact of Online Shopping on Local Small Businesses". [ A Study in Pune]

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there is no conflict of interest regarding the publication of this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study was conducted through a survey of local small business owners in Pune. Participation was voluntary, and informed consent was obtained from all participants. No personal or confidential information was disclosed.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was self-funded by the author and did not receive any financial support from any organization or institution.

detail.abstract:
Abstract:

The rapid expansion of e-commerce and digital technology has significantly transformed consumer buying behavior in India. Online shopping platforms such as Amazon, Flipkart, Zepto, and Blinkit have become increasingly popular due to their lower prices, convenience, wider product variety, home delivery, and attractive discount offers. While these developments provide benefits to consumers, they have created serious challenges for local small businesses that depend mainly on regular neighbourhood customers. This study examines the impact of online shopping on local small businesses in Pune, with special reference to the Bhopodi and Aundh areas.The study is based on both primary and secondary data. Primary data were collected through structured questionnaires and informal interviews with 25 respondents, including 20 customers and 5 local shopkeepers. Secondary data were collected from books, journals, newspapers, government reports, and published studies related to e-commerce and retail business. A descriptive research design and convenience sampling method were used to analyse customer preferences, changes in sales, and the difficulties faced by small retailers. The findings of the study reveal that a large majority of customers prefer online shopping over local shopping because of lower prices, discounts, home delivery, product variety, and easy comparison facilities. The study also shows that clothing shops, mobile accessory shops, stationery shops, and grocery stores are among the most affected businesses. Most local shopkeepers reported a decline in customer footfall and sales due to the growing popularity of online shopping. Many small retailers find it difficult to compete with large e-commerce companies because they cannot provide similar discounts, return policies, or delivery services. However, the study also indicates that online shopping has encouraged some local businesses to adopt digital methods such as UPI payments, social media marketing, WhatsApp orders, and home delivery services. Retailers who make use of such digital tools are more likely to survive and improve their business performance. The study concludes that although online shopping has negatively affected local small businesses in Pune, these effects can be reduced through government support, digital training, financial assistance, and the adoption of modern business practices. Strengthening the digital capabilities of local retailers can help them remain competitive in the changing retail environment.

Key Words: E-commerce; Local Small Businesses; Consumer Behaviour; Customer Preferences; Digital Payments; Retail Sector; Pune.

title: The Verification Architecture Problem: Why Internal AI Legal Output Remedies Face a Structural Efficacy Ceiling

detail.title: The Verification Architecture Problem: Why Internal AI Legal Output Remedies Face a Structural Efficacy Ceiling

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the inventor of the VARI technology and principal of Thirty Seven Inc., which holds the associated patent applications.

detail.abstract: The deployment of AI-generated legal research and drafting tools at enterprise scale has created a documented pattern of citation failures, including fabricated case references, mischaracterized holdings, and overruled precedent submitted without disclosure. This paper argues that all three principal internal verification approaches available to AI legal technology companies — self-review, cross-vendor second-opinion, and citator database-lookup — impose a structural efficacy ceiling that cannot be overcome by engineering effort alone. The ceiling arises from a single constraint: no system can adversarially verify its own outputs. The paper identifies four structural properties required for genuinely adversarial verification, analyzes why internal builds cannot satisfy all four simultaneously, and describes the compliance documentation gap that persists regardless of which internal architecture is adopted. The paper further argues that the gap extends beyond court filings to AI-generated legal opinions, contract analyses, and regulatory interpretations that never reach a tribunal, and examines how the EU AI Act's August 2026 enforcement deadline transforms the compliance documentation gap from a liability management question into a statutory obligation under Article 12. The analysis is offered as a framework for legal practitioners, in-house counsel, technologists, and regulators evaluating verification claims made by AI legal tool vendors.

reference: NBER Working Paper No. w35107
title: The Domestic Political Economy of War: Evidence from Russia
affiliations: , University of California, San Diego (UCSD) and New Economic School (NES)

detail.title: The Domestic Political Economy of War: Evidence from Russia

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Wars are often framed as responses to external threats or shifts in the regional balance of power. Yet they can also serve domestic political ends. This paper studies how Russia’s escalations against Ukraine reshaped support for the regime and redistributed the burdens of war across the population. Combining ethnic Russian shares with election and independent polling data, we exploit two sharp geopolitical shocks, the 2014 annexation of Crimea and the 2022 full-scale invasion, in a difference-in-differences event-study design. We find that provinces with larger ethnic Russian populations exhibit sharp increases in support for President Putin following both episodes. At the same time, battlefield casualties fall disproportionately on regions with lower ethnic Russian shares, and attitudes toward the US and EU deteriorate sharply. On the Ukrainian side, Russian attacks are concentrated in areas with higher ethnic Russian shares rather than in resource-rich provinces. Explanations based on material extraction, Soviet symbolism, or differential exposure to external threats do not account for these patterns. Instead, the evidence is more consistent with ethnic identity playing a central role in the domestic political economy of the war. Our conclusions remain similar in fraud-adjusted electoral outcomes, with alternative ethnicity measures, under bounded departures from parallel trends, and after accounting for several baseline regional differences.

Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.

reference: CESifo Working Paper No. 12623
title: Trade Policy and Access to Intermediate Inputs: Quantifying the Welfare Costs of a Fertilizer Shortage
affiliations: World Bank,  and World Bank - International Trade Division

detail.title: Trade Policy and Access to Intermediate Inputs: Quantifying the Welfare Costs of a Fertilizer Shortage

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper leverages Sri Lanka's 2021 chemical fertilizer import ban to quantify the costs of restricted fertilizer access for agriculture, trade, and welfare. Leveraging trade and production data, satellite-based yield estimates, and event studies, we document sharp declines in fertilizer imports, agricultural output, and exports. A quantitative spatial model of trade and agriculture estimates the ban's average welfare cost at 7.3%, with farmers, estate workers, and fertilizer-intensive regions bearing disproportionate losses. Model-implied partial-equilibrium elasticities line up with the experimental evidence, but once we account for general-equilibrium price and wage adjustments, the elasticities are much smaller—implying that using partial equilibrium estimates to assess large, economy-wide fertilizer shocks (like those seen during recent conflicts) would substantially overstate their effects. Domestic and trade policy interact: by curtailing fertilizer use, the import ban effectively contracted the country's fertilizer subsidy program and its implicit transfers from mobile workers to farmers, thereby mitigating the former's welfare losses.

reference: CESifo Working Paper No. 12624
title: Firm-Level Geopolitical Risk and Bank Debt Financing: Global Evidence
affiliations: University of Nottingham, University of Sussex , University of Bradford and University of Bradford School of Management

detail.title: Firm-Level Geopolitical Risk and Bank Debt Financing: Global Evidence

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper constructs a novel firm-level measure of geopolitical risk using textual analysis of 130,061 earnings conference call transcripts and examines its impact on firms' reliance on bank-based financing. Using a panel of 4,692 listed firms across 38 countries over 2005–2024, we find that higher firm-level geopolitical risk is associated with a significant increase in the bank debt ratio. Instrument-level analysis shows that this effect is driven by greater reliance on term loans, while revolving credit facilities exhibit no systematic response. The relationship holds across United States and non-United States firms, as well as across developed and emerging economies, with stronger effects in emerging markets and in institutional environments that facilitate contracting and enforcement. A comprehensive set of robustness tests confirms that the results are not driven by industry composition, regional concentration, crisis periods, or omitted institutional factors. Difference-in-differences evidence around the Russia–Ukraine war provides additional support, showing that firms with higher pre-war geopolitical risk increase their reliance on bank debt after 2022. Overall, the findings identify geopolitical risk as a time-varying determinant of corporate financing decisions.

reference: CESifo Working Paper No. 12625
title: Mobility-Based Gerrymandering: Theory and Evidence
affiliations: Simon Fraser University (SFU) - Department of Economics, University of Turin,  and University of Turin

detail.title: Mobility-Based Gerrymandering: Theory and Evidence

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper models theoretically and tests empirically the hypothesis that the decision about the location of a public bad within a multi-tiered structure of government (a facility providing benefits throughout the federation but inflicting damage to the region hosting it) can be driven by strategic electoral considerations exploiting the heterogeneous migration responses to the location of the public bad by voters of different ideologies - a sort of mobility-based gerrymandering. As long as the average utility loss from living close to the public bad is larger for progressives than it is for conservatives, conservative and progressive central governments will pursue opposite strategies. The former locate the public bad in an electorally tight region to induce progressive voters to exit and gain the region for the conservative party, while the latter attempt to spread progressive voters out of safe and into electorally tight regions. An application to waste treatment plant locations across Italian municipalities returns evidence in support of the model's main hypotheses.

reference: CESifo Working Paper No. 12627
title: The Cultural and Political Foundations of Quality of Institutions: The Role of Tightness and Looseness
affiliations: University of Napoli Parthenope and Università degli Studi della Basilicata

detail.title: The Cultural and Political Foundations of Quality of Institutions: The Role of Tightness and Looseness

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper examines how cultural and political dimensions of normative looseness shape institutional quality across European regions. Drawing on the Regional Index of Looseness (RIL) developed by Alfano and Ercolano (2026), which distinguishes between a vertical dimension and a horizontal dimension of tightness-looseness, we estimate fractional probit models for 142 NUTS-2 regions using measureas of institutional quality (the European Quality of Government Index-EQI, and its pillars) as dependent variables. Our results show that overall looseness is negatively associated with institutional quality, but this aggregate effect is driven (almost) entirely by the vertical dimension, reflecting tolerance for defying hierarchical authority. On the other hand, the horizontal dimension proves largely insignificant. These findings suggest that the relationship between culture and governance operates primarily through the vertical legitimacy of state authority rather than through peer-level normative pluralism, with important implications for the debate on institutional reform and regional divergence in Europe.
